Before you start: what this review is and how to use it

0:00–0:05

This review closes the first half of CS (Computer Science) 251 — Integrative Project 1. It brings together, in one place, everything you need for the Mid-Term Assessment of Friday, November 20, 2026: the ideas of every class module, the formulas and conventions you must apply without a book, twenty case studies written as twins of the exam questions, and a bank of practice questions with their answers and the reason behind each answer.

The review is planned for three hours. The first hour and a quarter goes through the content, chapter by chapter. The second part works through the case studies. The last part is a question drill and a short-essay workshop. Questions that are not finished in class are your homework: each one carries its answer, so you can correct yourself.

Two rules apply to the whole document.

  • No new theory. Everything here was taught in the class modules. If a sentence looks new to you, it points to a gap in your notes, not to new material.
  • One case, one dataset. All examples use the fictional consultancy Boréal Studio (Montréal, five staff, six routines) and its synthetic file boreal_routines_2026.csv, or a small twin of it with new numbers. The exam is written on the same basis.

Chapter 1

Welcome: One Real Problem, Three Courses, One Team

0:05–0:20

Class 1 module · 4 sub-chapters · tick Reviewed when you can answer the exam-angle box without looking.

1.1

Welcome, routines and the one rule

What the course is. CS (Computer Science) 251 is a three-credit integrative project. It adds no new theory: it uses three courses you have already passed — Principles of Microeconomics, Introduction to Object-Oriented Programming in Python and Statistics — together, on one real business problem, until the team has a working tool and a recommendation a business owner can act on. The instructor, Asen Grozdanov (Cyber), brings about twenty-five years of industry practice; the course direction is "from the industry to the classroom".

Routine versus event. A routine is a task that repeats on a regular schedule (every day, every week) and follows more or less the same steps each time: triaging the mailbox every morning, writing the Friday status report. A task that happens once, such as registering for a course or graduating, is an event, not a routine. The whole project is about routines: which ones can be automated and which ones cannot.

Expectations, both ways. Every week each student attends the Friday session, the team submits the week's Brick by Thursday 23:59 on the LMS (Learning Management System) and on GitHub, every member commits code to the team repository, and questions are asked openly (unanswered ones go to the Parking Lot and are answered the next Friday). In return, the rhythm of every Friday is the same, each Brick is graded within a week (complete, partial or missing, with one comment), and every team receives one specific, true, positive sentence each week.

The personal time log. From Class 1, every student is a pilot user and keeps a 14-day time log of study and work routines: date, routine, minutes, interruptions — about two minutes a day. The file data/timelog_<initials>.csv (at least five rows per member) is a deliverable of Brick 1, and Brick 4 analyses it with the same statistics as the studio data.

Privacy rule. A time log is personal data. It stays in the private team repository, anonymised: routine names, minutes and timestamps only — no names of other people, no message contents, never on a public page. The relevant sections of the Cyber.SoHo Notice (https://cyber-soho.github.io/prevmon/00.01.%20cyber.soho%20-%20legal.htmlVirusTotal) are 6.7 (data and privacy in laboratories) and 20 (personal information).

Exam angle Be able to tell a routine from an event, to name the four columns of the personal log, and to state the privacy rule in one sentence.

1.2

What an integrative project is

The official definition, piece by piece. An integrative project provides a sustained period of independent study and research, combined with interaction with other students. It starts from a real-world business problem (provided by the instructor or an industrial partner), and a research-based solution is sought that integrates the knowledge acquired in previous courses, reproducing real-world consulting activities. The course includes no additional theoretical content. Every part of that sentence is a requirement: independent research and team work; a real problem; a solution based on evidence, not opinion; integration of earlier courses; the work of a consultant.

The consulting habit. A consulting engagement is a contract in which a client asks an outside expert to analyse a problem and recommend a decision. Consultants work in a fixed order, and every Brick keeps it:

  1. Problem — state what the client actually asks: not "e-mail is annoying" but "which routine should we automate first, how much time would it save, and is a free assistant good enough?"
  2. Evidence — collect data and analyse it with methods you can name and defend. Evidence is what makes the solution research-based.
  3. Recommendation — turn the evidence into a decision the client can act on, with its expected impact and its risk.

The textbook, Leedy and Ormrod's Practical Research: Planning and Design (12th edition), describes the research side of the same order: a research problem is split into sub-problems, each sub-problem becomes a research question (RQ), and data is collected to answer each question.

Why three courses are needed together. The owner's question splits into three sub-problems, one per course:

Sub-problem Course Tools it supplies
What is an hour of staff time worth, and what does automation cost? Principles of Microeconomics opportunity cost, marginal benefit versus marginal cost, fixed and variable cost, break-even, payback
What does the time log actually show? Statistics mean, median, standard deviation, correlation, before/after comparison
How do we automate a routine and measure the saving? Introduction to OOP (Object-Oriented Programming) in Python classes, objects, the csv, statistics and sqlite3 modules

None of the three answers the question alone: economics without data is a guess, statistics without a tool is a spreadsheet nobody maintains, and a program without economics automates the wrong routine. CS (Computer Science) 251 lives in the intersection Microeconomics ∩ Python ∩ Statistics, and so does every question of the Mid-Term.

JARVIS in one sentence. JARVIS is the name of the assistant (a name, not an abbreviation). By January it must log and automate routine work, measure the time it saves with statistics, price that time with microeconomics, and recommend what to automate first and whether the free tier is enough.

The worked chain (Boréal Studio, e-mail triage). Seven days of triage minutes for one person: 62, 35, 30, 33, 40, 31, 38. The mean is 269 ÷ 7 = 38.4 minutes; the median (sorted: 30, 31, 33, 35, 38, 40, 62) is 35 minutes. Because the Monday value of 62 is extreme, the median is the honest typical day. Monthly cost for five people: 35 ÷ 60 × 28 $/h × 20 days × 5 staff ≈ 1 633 $. In Python the same computation becomes one method, EconEngine.routine_cost(...). The recommendation is written in four parts: finding, evidence, decision, risk.

Exam angle Expect to match a tool (opportunity cost, the median, a class with __init__) to its course, and to name the three steps of the consulting habit in order.

Six dates to memorise: November 13 (Mid-Term Review), November 20 (Mid-Term), December 4, 11 and 18 (Sprints), January 15 (Final Review), January 22 (Final). Two more: October 22 (Brick 4 closes Phase 1) and November 6 (Alpha Demo).

The 1 : 2 : 2 rhythm. Every Friday: 1 hour of lecture in short parts of eleven to fifteen minutes, each followed by a three-to-five-minute activity; 2 hours of in-class workshop on the week's Brick, ending with a checkpoint (each team shows its result for thirty to sixty seconds); 2 hours at home (finish the Brick, read a short extract of Leedy and Ormrod (https://www.pearson.com/en-us/subject-catalog/p/practical-research-planning-and-design/P200000001398VirusTotal), write the Weekly Progress Report). Three credit hours correspond to 135 to 180 total study hours.

Grading: 30 / 30 / 40.

Component Weight Details

Midterm Assessment 30 % Friday, November 20: two hours, individual, Part A computational, Part B application

Letter scale: 93–100 A · 90–92 A− · 87–89 B+ · 83–86 B · 80–82 B− · 77–79 C+ · 73–76 C · 70–72 C− · 60–69 D · 59 and below F.

The Brick system. A Brick is the one deliverable of the week (a document, a script, a diagram, a set of tests). Twelve Bricks assemble into JARVIS, and nothing is thrown away: even the corrected Part A of the Mid-Term becomes the first draft of the report's Results section. The Mid-Term is written on the JARVIS basis, so every Brick submitted on time is a page of your own exam preparation; Bricks 1 to 7 had to be complete by Thursday, November 12. The five rules: due Thursday 23:59 (LMS (Learning Management System) + GitHub, tagged where asked); one team submission plus one individual Weekly Progress Report (ten lines); commits from every member count; a missing Brick must still be submitted; every source — code, documentation, AI (Artificial Intelligence) assistance — is cited in APA (American Psychological Association) 7 style.

Worked grade (Maya, all Bricks complete). 12 × 2.5 = 30 points; Mid-Term 78/100 × 0.30 = 23.4; Final 85/100 × 0.40 = 34.0; total 87.4 % → B+. With the same exams and two missing Bricks: 25 + 23.4 + 34.0 = 82.4 % → B−. Two missing Bricks cost five points and a full letter step, before counting the exam questions that were written on those Bricks.

1.4

The client, the dataset and the toolbox

The client. Boréal Studio is a fictional five-person consultancy in Montréal; its data are synthetic, so no real person's working hours are exposed. Six routines: e-mail triage, daily report, scheduling, invoice check, stand-up notes and social posts. The owner's question: "Which of these routines should we automate first, how much time would it really save, and is a free assistant good enough — or should we pay for one?"

The dataset boreal_routines_2026.csv: a CSV (Comma-Separated Values) file — plain text, one line per record, values separated by commas, a header line with the column names. About 420 rows = 14 working days × 5 staff × 6 routines, one row per routine run.

Column Meaning Python type
date day of the run, yyyy-mm-dd datetime.date
staff_id anonymous code S1 … S5 str
routine email_triage, daily_report, … str
category communication, reporting, planning, finance, marketing str
start_hour hour the run started, 0–23 int
minutes duration of the run int
interruptions number of interruptions during the run int
tool manual, template or jarvis str
done completed: 1 yes, 0 no bool (stored as 0/1)

Two deliberate events are built into the data so that a before/after comparison can be computed honestly: a report template introduced on day 8 and a pilot automation (assistant-triaged e-mail) from day 10.

The three given numbers (inputs to the economics, not columns of the data):

  • 28 $ per hour — the hourly value of staff time, a loaded cost (salary plus the employer's overhead per hour worked);
  • 20 $ per user per month — the price of a paid assistant tier, a fixed cost per period;
  • the free API (Application Programming Interface) quota — the number of requests the free tier of an API (Application Programming Interface) allows (an API (Application Programming Interface) is the way a program talks to another program over the network); free tiers change, so the number and the date it was read are posted on the LMS (Learning Management System) and recorded in your notes.

The toolbox — Python only, no Java anywhere. Python 3.12 or newer (https://www.python.org/VirusTotal) with its standard library (csv, sqlite3, statistics, dataclasses); VS Code (Visual Studio Code) (https://code.visualstudio.com/VirusTotal) with the Python extension; a virtual environment (python -m venv .venv, a private copy of Python for one project so that packages never conflict); pip, the Package Installer for Python; Git and GitHub (versions, the private team repository, GitHub Actions (https://docs.github.com/en/actionsVirusTotal) for scheduled scripts, GitHub Pages (https://docs.github.com/en/pages/getting-started-with-github-pages/configuring-a-publishing-source-for-your-github-pages-siteVirusTotal) for a public page); pytest (https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/VirusTotal) (from Class 10) and matplotlib (charts) (https://matplotlib.org/VirusTotal); the LMS (Learning Management System) and the textbook.

The JARVIS loop — five stages.

  1. Request — a user types a sentence, for example log 25 min email_triage.
  2. Intent — a provider turns the sentence into a structured intent: a name (log_time) and arguments (minutes = 25, routine = email_triage). The first provider is offline: rules and regular expressions, deterministic, no key, no network.
  3. Tool — the agent looks up the intent name in its table of tools and selects one (LogTimeTool).
  4. Result — the tool runs and changes the store (a new entry in data/jarvis.db).
  5. Log — the run is recorded: timestamp, request, intent, tool, provider, success, milliseconds. This log is JARVIS's own dataset.

The offline fallback rule. JARVIS must run with no API (Application Programming Interface) key and no network. Tests, the exam and the demos never depend on the internet. The API (Application Programming Interface) provider of Class 10 (a free LLM (Large Language Model) tier) is an upgrade that drops into the same loop, never a dependency.

Exam angle Name the nine columns and their types, the three given numbers with their units, and the five stages of the loop in order; explain what the offline fallback rule guarantees.

Chapter 2

The Problem Before the Code: Requirements and the Research Process

0:05–0:20

Class 2 module · 5 sub-chapters · tick Reviewed when you can answer the exam-angle box without looking.

2.1

From a business problem to a research problem

Research and the research problem. Leedy and Ormrod (https://www.pearson.com/en-us/subject-catalog/p/practical-research-planning-and-design/P200000001398VirusTotal) define research as a systematic process of collecting, analysing and interpreting data in order to increase our understanding of a phenomenon. Every project starts from a research problem: a question or situation that can be resolved only by collecting data and interpreting it.

Complaint versus problem statement. The owner's message — "Mornings disappear into the mailbox, the daily report is always late, and a vendor wants 20 $ per person per month for an assistant" — is a complaint: it describes a difficulty, but names no measurement, no decision and no method. A problem statement is one short paragraph (at most 150 words in Brick 2) that names three things: the situation, the decision the research must support, and the evidence that will be collected. The Boréal Studio version (93 words) names the five-person studio and its six routines, the decision (what to automate first; free assistant or paid tier at 20 $ per user per month), and the evidence (time per routine priced at 28 $ per hour, an assistant that automates at least one routine, and a comparison of the time saved with the cost of each option).

Leedy and Ormrod's guidance for stating a problem: state it clearly and completely; make sure it is feasible with your time and resources (fifteen Fridays, a team of two or three, free tools); define the words that could be read in two ways; keep an open mind — do not write the conclusion into the problem.

What is not a research problem (four cases): a task whose only purpose is to inform yourself ("learn about chatbots"); comparing two sets of data without interpreting the difference; computing a correlation only to show that one exists; a question answered by yes or no ("Is automation good?"). In each case nothing has to be interpreted, so no new understanding is produced.

Sub-problems. Large problems are divided into sub-problems, which have four properties: each is a researchable unit by itself; each is tied to the interpretation of data; together they add up to the whole problem, no more and no less; and they are few (usually two to six). Boréal Studio has three, one per course: the cost of each routine and of each option (Microeconomics); the duration and variability of each routine and the effect of the template and the pilot (Statistics); how an assistant can run a routine and measure the minutes it saves (Python and object-oriented programming).

Pseudo-sub-problems. "Which chart library do we use?" or "How do we split the work?" are planning decisions: they must be made, but they require no interpretation of data, so they do not belong in the problem tree.

Research questions and the four checks. A research question is a sub-problem written as an open question that the project's data and methods can answer. Before accepting one, check that it is (1) an open question — not answerable by yes or no; (2) measurable — it names something in the data or in the given numbers (minutes, interruptions, runs, dollars); (3) tied to one sub-problem; (4) answerable by January 22 with your data. The course template:

  • RQ1 (Research Question 1), the Statistics question: Which routines cost the most time, and which are the most variable?
  • RQ2 (Research Question 2), the Microeconomics question: What is an hour of staff time worth, what does automation cost, and where is the break-even between the free tier and a paid assistant?
  • RQ3 (Research Question 3), the integration question: Which routines should JARVIS automate first, how much time does it save, and what is the risk?

"How can the studio become more productive?" fails check 2 (productive has no unit in the data); "Is automation good?" fails checks 1 and 2. In January, the Results and the conclusions of the report must answer these questions and nothing else; Part B of the Mid-Term asks for a problem, one sub-problem and one research question for a new small-business scenario.

Research question Data that answers it Method Answered in
RQ1 (Research Question 1) — most minutes, most variable routine, minutes, staff_id, date mean, median, SD (Standard Deviation) per routine; histogram; outliers Brick 4; Brick 11
RQ2 (Research Question 2) — monthly cost, break-even of the 20 $ tier minutes, routine + 28 $/h, 20 $/user/month, free quota monthly cost, opportunity cost, break-even hours, payback Brick 3; Brick 11
RQ3 (Research Question 3) — what first, minutes saved, risk tool, minutes, date (before/after day 10) before/after comparison; recommendation pattern Brick 7; Brick 11; Final

Exam angle Turn a complaint into a problem statement, give one sub-problem and one research question, and reject a weak question by naming the check it fails.

2.2

Requirements analysis

Requirement and requirements analysis. A requirement is a statement of something a system must do, or of a property it must have, written so that someone can check whether the delivered system satisfies it. Requirements analysis is the work of discovering, writing, classifying, checking and agreeing on requirements with the stakeholders — the people who use the system or are affected by it (for JARVIS: the owner, the staff, and the assessors of the Product Defense).

The standard. ISO/IEC/IEEE (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission / Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 29148:2018 (https://www.iso.org/standard/72089.htmlVirusTotal) (Requirements engineering) lists the characteristics of a well-formed requirement: necessary, appropriate, unambiguous, complete, singular, feasible, verifiable, correct and conforming. Three matter most here: unambiguous (one reading only), singular (one requirement per statement) and verifiable (a test, an inspection or a measurement can prove it). The same standard fixes the wording convention: "shall" marks a binding requirement; "should" marks a goal or a wish.

Functional versus non-functional. A functional requirement (FR) describes a behaviour: given an input or event, the system produces an output or changes its data ("The assistant shall log a routine from one command"). A non-functional requirement (NFR) describes a quality or a constraint on how the system performs its functions. The quality model ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission) 25010:2023 (https://www.iso.org/standard/78176.htmlVirusTotal) groups qualities into nine characteristics; four matter to JARVIS: performance efficiency, reliability, security and maintainability. Quick test: an FR (Functional Requirement) answers what does it do?; an NFR (Non-Functional Requirement) answers how well, or under which limits?

JARVIS has four non-functional requirements written into the course: it runs from a fresh clone in under 2 minutes; it works with no API (Application Programming Interface) key and no network; it never crashes on an empty cell (a bad row is skipped and counted); the database file data/jarvis.db stays under 1 MB (megabyte). An NFR (Non-Functional Requirement) without a number cannot be verified: "JARVIS shall be fast" is not yet a requirement; "JARVIS shall answer a log command in under one second on the lab computer" is one, because a stopwatch can decide.

User stories. A user story describes one requirement from the point of view of the person who benefits: As a ⟨role⟩, I want ⟨goal⟩, so that ⟨benefit⟩. The Agile Alliance (https://www.agilealliance.org/glossary/user-stories/VirusTotal) dates this template to 2001. Brick 2 asks for five stories with at least three kinds of role, for example: "As the owner, I want a monthly cost for each routine, so that I can decide what to automate first"; "As a staff member, I want to log a routine with one command, so that recording my time takes seconds"; "As JARVIS with no API (Application Programming Interface) key, I want to understand requests with rules, so that the assistant still works offline" (the system itself, in a degraded condition, as the role). The INVEST (Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable) checklist (Bill Wake, 2003) lists the six properties of a good story; T for Testable matters most here.

Acceptance criteria. Acceptance criteria are the conditions a story must satisfy to be accepted as finished, often written in the BDD (Behaviour-Driven Development) format supported by Gherkin (https://cucumber.io/docs/gherkin/reference/VirusTotal): Given the starting situation, When an action happens, Then an observable result follows. Example: Given an empty log, when I type log 25 min email_triage, then one entry is stored with routine email_triage and minutes 25. A second criterion covers bad input: Given an empty log, when I type log twenty min email_triage, then nothing is stored and JARVIS replies with the expected format. Each criterion becomes one automated test in Class 10. Two rules: a story without acceptance criteria can never be declared finished, and an NFR (Non-Functional Requirement) without a threshold can never be tested.

The interview example. Six statements were collected in a 20-minute interview. Statements 1 (record a run from one command) and 2 (compute the monthly cost at 28 $/h) are functional; statements 3 (fresh clone under 2 minutes), 4 (no key, no network), 5 (database under one megabyte) and 6 ("JARVIS should be fast and easy to use") are non-functional. Statement 6 is flagged — no threshold, and "should" marks a wish — and is rewritten as two verifiable NFRs (Non-Functional Requirements): "JARVIS shall answer a log command in under one second on the lab computer" and "A new user shall log a first routine within 5 minutes, using only the README".

Exam angle Classify statements as FR (Functional Requirement) or NFR (Non-Functional Requirement), rewrite a vague statement with a number and a unit, and write a user story with two Given/When/Then criteria.

2.3

Scope, SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) objectives and project selection

Scope and delimitations. The scope is the set of results the project will deliver (features, documents, data) and the work needed to deliver them, and no more — the view of the PMI (Project Management Institute) (https://www.pmi.org/VirusTotal), which publishes the PMBOK (Project Management Body of Knowledge) Guide. Leedy and Ormrod (https://www.pearson.com/en-us/subject-catalog/p/practical-research-planning-and-design/P200000001398VirusTotal) add the delimitations: an explicit list of what the study will not do. Writing both prevents scope creep, the uncontrolled growth of features week after week until nothing works on defense day.

  • JARVIS scope: the six routines, the 14-day log, the statistics and economics engines, the offline provider plus one free API (Application Programming Interface) tier, the tiny SQLite (https://www.sqlite.org/VirusTotal) database, an aggregated dashboard, the report and the defense.
  • JARVIS delimitations: no voice commands, no reading of real mailboxes or calendars, no mobile application, no paid service, no data about real people other than the team's own anonymised logs.

Assumptions versus constraints. An assumption is treated as true for planning without proof, and must be written down because the results change if it is false (28 $/h is a fair loaded cost; the fourteen days are typical; staff logged honestly; the pilot saving continues). A constraint is a limit the project cannot change (fifteen Fridays and the January 22 defense; teams of two or three; Python only; free API (Application Programming Interface) tiers whose quotas change; no personal data in public repositories; a database under one megabyte). Assumptions are tested and discussed (the Sprint 2 recommendation lists its risks and assumptions); constraints are respected.

SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) objectives. An objective is a result the team commits to deliver by a date. The SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) test was first published by George T. Doran in 1981 (his letters were Specific, Measurable, Assignable, Realistic, Time-related); the course uses the common modern set:

Letter The objective…
Specific names exactly what will be delivered
Measurable states a number or an observable test of success
Achievable fits the team's hours and the allowed tools
Relevant serves one of the research questions
Time-bound has a date

"Make JARVIS smart" fails all five letters. "Log 14 days of routines and compute the SD (Standard Deviation) of minutes per routine by October 22" passes all five. The course adds the January test: can we demonstrate this at the Product Defense on January 22? If not, the objective is outside the scope or must become smaller.

Checking Achievable with capacity. Capacity = members × hours per week × weeks. Three members × 4 h per week = 12 h per week: 24 h before October 22, 60 h before November 6, 132 h before December 18. "Connect JARVIS to voice, calendar and e-mail by December 18" needs about 160 h and forbidden tools (a voice service, real mailboxes), so it fails Achievable twice and is rewritten inside the scope: "By November 6, JARVIS logs e-mail triage from one command, offline."

Project selection. Every team works on the same problem with the default synthetic file. A team may use its own real small-business data only if all three conditions hold: the data is anonymised; the organization gives written permission (section 7.9 of the Cyber.SoHo Notice (https://cyber-soho.github.io/prevmon/00.01.%20cyber.soho%20-%20legal.htmlVirusTotal) — a relative who owns the business is not automatically the person entitled to give it); and the instructor approves it, at the latest with Brick 2. Otherwise the default dataset is used; the rubric is the same.

Exam angle Score an objective letter by letter, compare hours needed with capacity, and classify a statement as an assumption or a constraint.

2.4

References and experts

Reference and citation. A reference describes a source precisely enough for a reader to find it (in the list at the end); a citation is the short pointer in the text — (Author, Year) — that sends the reader to it. Citation lets the reader verify a claim and gives credit to the work you build on. In CS (Computer Science) 251 you cite four kinds of material: books and articles, documentation pages of the functions you call, code you reuse, and any AI (Artificial Intelligence) assistance.

Where credible sources come from. Textbooks and scholarly books (Leedy and Ormrod (https://www.pearson.com/en-us/subject-catalog/p/practical-research-planning-and-design/P200000001398VirusTotal); the free peer-reviewed OpenStax textbooks of Rice University); scholarly articles through library databases and Google Scholar (https://scholar.google.com/VirusTotal) (in Québec, BAnQ (Bibliothèque et Archives nationales du Québec) (https://www.banq.qc.ca/VirusTotal) gives every resident free access to many databases); official documentation (the Python documentation (https://docs.python.org/3/VirusTotal); the API (Application Programming Interface) provider's own quota pages, cited with the date read); official statistics agencies such as Statistics Canada (https://www.statcan.gc.ca/en/startVirusTotal).

The CRAAP (Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose) test (Sarah Blakeslee, 2004) — five questions for any source:

Letter Question
Currency When was it published or updated?
Relevance Does it answer my question?
Authority Who wrote it, and what qualifies them?
Accuracy Is there evidence, are there references, can it be checked?
Purpose Does it inform, sell or persuade?

An anonymous blog post selling a productivity course fails Authority, Accuracy and Purpose even when its advice sounds right. Wikipedia is useful to find the primary sources it cites — read and cite those instead.

APA (American Psychological Association) 7 (https://apastyle.apa.org/VirusTotal) in one pattern: Author. (Date). Title. Source.

  • Book: Leedy, P. D., & Ormrod, J. E. (2019). Practical research: Planning and design (12th ed.). Pearson Education.
  • Web page that changes, no date: Python Software Foundation. (n.d.). statistics — Mathematical statistics functions. Python documentation. Retrieved October 1, 2026, from https://docs.python.org/3/library/statistics.html
  • Software: Author. (Year). Title (Version) [Computer software]. Publisher. URL (Uniform Resource Locator)
  • Generative AI (Artificial Intelligence): Company. (Year). Name of the tool (version) [Large language model]. URL (Uniform Resource Locator) — and describe in the text how you used it.

In the text: (Leedy & Ormrod, 2019) or "Leedy and Ormrod (2019) state…"; with three or more authors, (Shapiro et al., 2022). The list is sorted alphabetically by the first author's surname. A DOI (Digital Object Identifier) is a permanent address written https://doi.org/… and replaces the URL (Uniform Resource Locator) when it exists. A retrieval date is added for pages designed to change.

The worked list. Of five candidates, the textbook, the two OpenStax books and the Python documentation page pass all five CRAAP (Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose) questions; the blog "10 AI (Artificial Intelligence) hacks that save 5 hours a day" (no author, no date, ends with a paid course) passes only Relevance and is rejected. Sorted list: Illowsky & Dean (2023); Leedy & Ormrod (2019); Python Software Foundation (n.d.); Shapiro et al. (2022). Brick 2 asks for at least five sources.

Finding one expert. An expert is a person with direct experience of the problem (a small-business owner, an office manager, a statistics tutor). The message states who you are, the purpose, a 20-minute limit, three open questions linked to the research questions, a request for permission to take notes, and how answers will be anonymised (job title in the report, not the name, unless the expert agrees in writing).

Exam angle Apply CRAAP (Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose) to a described source, format a book and a documentation page in APA (American Psychological Association) 7, and write the matching in-text citations.

2.5

The data dictionary and personal data

Data dictionary. A data dictionary documents every column of a data set: name, meaning, data type, unit or format, allowed values, an example, and what could be wrong with it. It states the rules that both the people who collect the data and the code that reads it must follow. Brick 2 asks for the dictionary of the nine columns with a "possible issue" filled in for every row.

Python types and conversions. When Python reads a CSV (Comma-Separated Values) file, every value arrives as text (str). The loader converts each one; the type decides which operations are allowed (you can add two integers, not two dates).

Column Type Conversion
date datetime.date date.fromisoformat("2026-09-07")
staff_id, routine, category, tool str none
start_hour, minutes, interruptions int int("42")
done bool, stored as 0/1 row["done"] == "1"

Two traps: int("25 min") raises a ValueError (the unit belongs in the dictionary, not in the cell), and bool("0") is True, because every non-empty text is true — never convert done with bool(). The type float appears later, for averages and dollar amounts.

Four checks of individual values.

Check Meaning Failing examples
Completeness a value is present empty minutes cell
Validity right type, format and range −5 minutes; "25 min"; 08/09/2026; start hour 27
Consistency agrees with the agreed list and the rest of the data emial_triage; "Manual" with a capital letter
Uniqueness each run recorded once two identical rows double the minutes

These rules return as code: the loader skips and counts bad rows (Brick 5); the database refuses negative minutes and duplicates with CHECK (minutes >= 0) and UNIQUE (date, staff_id, routine, start_hour) (Brick 6); Sprint 1 demonstrates three bad-input cases (Brick 10). In the seven-row example of the class, nine problems were found in seven rows; row 7 alone had four (a real name instead of a code, a free-text note with message contents, an hour of 27 and the value "25 min").

A time log is personal information. Personal information is information about an identifiable individual: the definition of PIPEDA (Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act) (https://www.priv.gc.ca/en/privacy-topics/privacy-laws-in-canada/the-personal-information-protection-and-electronic-documents-act-pipeda/VirusTotal), Canada's federal private-sector privacy law, explained by the OPC (Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada) (https://www.priv.gc.ca/en/VirusTotal). Québec's private-sector act, as amended by Law 25 (https://www.legisquebec.gouv.qc.ca/en/document/cs/P-39.1VirusTotal) and supervised by the CAI (Commission d'accès à l'information du Québec) (https://www.cai.gouv.qc.ca/VirusTotal), uses a similar definition. A time log says when a person worked, on what, for how long and how often they were interrupted: it is personal information.

De-identified versus anonymized. De-identified data no longer identifies a person directly (a code such as S3 replaces the name) but can still be linked back — it remains personal information. Anonymized data can never be linked back, directly or indirectly, and the operation is irreversible. The staff codes S1–S5 are de-identification, so the data stays private.

Risks and mitigations. Risks: a real name typed where a code is expected; message contents in a free-text column; small groups (with five staff, a chart per person identifies the person); public repositories. Mitigations: codes instead of names (the loader accepts only S1–S5); no message contents, ever; raw logs only in the private repository (data/timelog_*.csv in .gitignore); dashboards with aggregated numbers per routine, never per person.

Exam angle Give the Python type of a column, explain the bool("0") trap, classify a data problem by the four checks, and tell de-identified from anonymized.

Chapter 3

Microeconomics Refresher: What Is an Hour Worth?

0:20–0:35

Class 3 module · 4 sub-chapters · tick Reviewed when you can answer the exam-angle box without looking.

3.1

Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost

Scarcity and microeconomics. A resource is scarce when there is less of it than people would like to use; scarcity forces a choice, and every choice has two sides: what you take and what you leave. For Boréal Studio the scarce resource is staff time (five people, about eight hours a day). Microeconomics studies these choices one decision-maker at a time (a household, a firm, an owner). The owner's question uses three microeconomic words: first asks for a ranking, how much for a measurement, good enough for a comparison between the free and the paid option. Chapter 3 is the method of RQ2 (Research Question 2).

The cost of a routine.

Formula cost per month = minutes per run ÷ 60 × hourly value × runs per month

Board example (e-mail triage): about 35 minutes per run, five staff once a day, 20 working days → 100 runs per month; at 28 $/h: 35 ÷ 60 × 28 × 100 = 1 633.33 $ per month. On the file itself the mean is 35.15 minutes, which gives 1 640.12 $. Applied to the six routines, the studio's monthly routine bill is about 5 821 $ and 208 staff hours; e-mail triage is the largest line (28.2 %).

Routine Minutes per run Runs per month Hours per month Cost per month ($) Share
email_triage 35.1 100 58.6 1 640.12 28.2 %
daily_report 21.8 100 36.4 1 018.67 17.5 %
social_post 21.3 100 35.5 994.67 17.1 %
invoice_check 20.8 100 34.7 972.67 16.7 %
scheduling 15.7 100 26.2 732.67 12.6 %
standup_notes 9.9 100 16.5 462.67 7.9 %
Studio total 207.9 5 821.45 100 %

The fifteen pilot runs (tool = jarvis) are left out of this bill: they are an experiment, not the current practice.

Loaded hourly cost. The loaded cost of an hour is the salary for that hour plus the employer's overhead (contributions, vacation pay, equipment, office): what the hour costs the business, not what the employee sees on a pay slip. A real figure starts from published wage data (for example the earnings tables of Statistics Canada (https://www.statcan.gc.ca/en/startVirusTotal)) and adds the overhead. In the project, 28 $/h is a given number: write it once, at the top of the script, as a named constant — never repeated inside formulas.

Opportunity cost. The 1 633 $ above is an explicit cost (money actually paid for the hours). The opportunity cost of using an hour in one way is the value of its next-best use, the best alternative given up. If a consultant's hour could be sold to a client at 65 $, an hour of manual triage gives up 65 $ of revenue, whatever the salary. This is why "free" software still costs something: installing, learning, setting up and checking it take hours, and those hours have a next-best use. For the studio, the 208 routine hours are worth about 5 821 $ at the loaded cost and about 13 514 $ of client work at the 65 $ billable rate. Both numbers are correct; they answer different questions.

Two consequences for code: the hourly value is an input (a parameter), not a fact of nature; and opportunity cost is always relative to a named alternative.

Exam angle Compute a monthly routine cost, convert minutes to hours, value the same hours at a second rate, and explain why both values are legitimate.

3.2

Marginal analysis

Thinking at the margin. The owner automates one routine, then decides about the next one. A decision about one more unit is a decision at the margin, and marginal analysis compares the extra benefit and the extra cost of that unit.

Formula MB (marginal benefit) per month = net minutes saved per run ÷ 60 × hourly value × runs per month

Formula. MC (marginal cost) per month = paid requests × price per request + set-up cost ÷ horizon in months

The marginal benefit (MB) is the value of the time saved per month; net minutes saved = manual minutes − assisted minutes − review minutes. The marginal cost (MC) has two parts: requests sent to the language-model API (Application Programming Interface) beyond the free quota (zero inside the quota) and a monthly share of the set-up (team hours × hourly value, spread over the 12-month planning horizon of the course).

The rule and the ranking. Automate while MB (marginal benefit) ≥ MC (marginal cost). The difference MB (marginal benefit) − MC (marginal cost) is the net benefit; ranking candidates by net benefit, largest first, answers the owner's word "first".

Worked e-mail case: the pilot participants took 35.9 minutes by hand and 13.7 minutes with the assistant → 22.1 minutes saved; minus 2 minutes of review → 20.1 net minutes. MB (marginal benefit) = 20.1 ÷ 60 × 28 × 100 = 938 $/month. The tool sends three requests per run (300 per month, far inside a 3 000 quota), and set-up is estimated at 40 h → 1 120 $ ÷ 12 = 93.33 $. MC (marginal cost) = 0 + 93.33 = 93.33 $/month → net benefit 844.67 $/month: automate.

Routine MB (marginal benefit), $/month MC (marginal cost), $/month Net benefit Rule Rank
email_triage 938.00 93.33 844.67 automate 1
social_post 326.67 35.00 291.67 automate 2
daily_report 280.00 46.67 233.33 automate 3
scheduling 233.33 58.33 175.00 automate 4
standup_notes 93.33 58.33 35.00 automate 5
invoice_check −46.67 70.00 −116.67 do not automate —

The invoice check fails: the assistant saves 5 minutes, but a person must verify every flagged invoice for 6 minutes, so the net saving is negative and the routine stays manual for now. Savings for routines without a pilot are stated assumptions written at the top of the program — stating an assumption openly is not a weakness; hiding it would be.

Diminishing returns. As more of something is done, each additional unit brings less than the one before: the first tool saves 845 $ net, the fifth adds 35 $. This is why three tools that work beat ten that do not (the January test). Inside one routine, automation can be pushed in levels, each judged on its own increment: sort and label (700 $ against 46.67 $ → add), draft replies (233.33 $ against 58.33 $ → add), send without review (93.33 $ against 105 $ → stop; it also carries the unmeasured risk of an e-mail sent by mistake). Stop at the first level whose extra MB (marginal benefit) no longer covers its extra MC (marginal cost).

Exam angle Compute MB (marginal benefit), MC (marginal cost) and the net benefit of two or three candidates, apply MB (marginal benefit) ≥ MC (marginal cost), rank them, and explain why the ranking matters even when all pass.

3.3

Fixed, variable, total, average and marginal cost; the sunk cost

Fixed and variable. A fixed cost (FC) does not change with the quantity during the period: the paid tier is 20 $ per user per month whatever the usage (100 $ for five seats); the team's set-up time is fixed too, but paid once (40 h × 28 $/h = 1 120 $). A variable cost (VC) changes with the quantity: requests beyond the free quota (each adds the price per request), staff minutes per run (the whole bill of 3.1 is variable). The classification depends on the question: a subscription is fixed with respect to the number of requests but variable with respect to the number of users. Always say "fixed with respect to what".

Formula TC (total cost) = FC (fixed cost) + VC (variable cost) · AC (average cost) = TC (total cost) ÷ quantity · MC (marginal cost) = ΔTC (total cost) ÷ Δquantity

Total, average and marginal. The total cost (TC) of the period is the number to compare between options over the same period and quantity. The average cost (AC) is the cost per run or per request: the paid tier's AC (average cost) falls as volume grows (the same 100 $ spread over more runs). The marginal cost (MC) is the change in total cost for one more unit: 0 $ per request inside the free quota, the price per request beyond it (0.02 $ in the teaching example). The free tier's total cost curve therefore has a kink at the quota: flat at zero, then rising in a straight line.

Free versus paid by volume (teaching assumptions: quota 3 000 requests/month, 0.02 $ per extra request; paid tier 100 $/month for five seats; three requests per run):

Requests/month Runs TC (total cost) free ($) AC (average cost) free ($/run) TC (total cost) paid ($) AC (average cost) paid ($/run)
1 000 333 0.00 0.000 100.00 0.300
3 000 1 000 0.00 0.000 100.00 0.100
4 000 1 333 20.00 0.015 100.00 0.075
8 000 2 667 100.00 0.038 100.00 0.038
12 000 4 000 180.00 0.045 100.00 0.025

The two totals cross at 8 000 requests (quota 3 000 + 100 $ ÷ 0.02 $ = 3 000 + 5 000). The studio needs about 300, so the free tier wins by a wide margin — as long as the quota stays where it is, which is why Brick 3 records the quota with the date it was read.

Units. AC (average cost) is "per run" or "per request"; MC (marginal cost) is "per additional run/request"; FC (fixed cost) is "per period" or "once". Mixing units is the second most common error in this topic.

Sunk cost. A sunk cost has already been incurred and no present or future decision can recover it. Rule: a sunk cost must not influence a decision, because it is the same under every alternative. The trap: in month one of the pilot, benefit 938 $, running cost 28 $ (one maintenance hour); someone subtracts the 1 120 $ set-up and announces a 210 $ loss. Wrong logic, not wrong arithmetic: stopping does not return the 1 120 $; looking forward, the choice is +910 $ a month (continue) against 0 $ (stop). The set-up belongs in two places only: before the decision to build, as a monthly share in MC (marginal cost); after it, in the payback computation (how long to recover, not whether to continue). The sentence to write in a report: "The set-up cost is sunk; the decision to continue compares future benefits with future costs."

Exam angle Classify a cost as fixed, variable or sunk with respect to a stated quantity, compute TC (total cost) and AC (average cost), find the volume where two options cost the same, and correct a sunk-cost argument.

3.4

Break-even, payback and make-or-buy

Break-even hours. The break-even point of an option is the quantity at which its benefit exactly covers its cost. For a paid assistant priced per month, the natural quantity is hours saved per month:

Formula break-even hours = monthly cost of the paid option ÷ hourly value

20 ÷ 28 = 0.714 h ≈ 43 minutes per user per month; for five seats, 100 ÷ 28 = 3.57 h per month. The pilot measured 20.1 net minutes per run × 20 runs per user per month = 6.7 h per user — about nine times the break-even. The answer to the owner is therefore: any assistant that does what the pilot did pays for itself many times over; choose on fit and risk, not on the seat price. The set-up hours are not in this formula. Guard for the engine: an hourly value of zero or less makes no sense, so break_even_hours() raises a ValueError.

Payback period.

Formula payback months = set-up cost ÷ monthly net saving

Set-up 1 120 $; monthly net saving 938.86 − 28 = 910.86 $ → 1.23 months (about five weeks). Special case: when the monthly net saving is zero or negative, the set-up is never recovered and the engine returns math.inf ("never") instead of crashing. Payback is simple and widely used, but it ignores what happens after recovery and does not discount the future, so the report shows it next to the monthly net saving.

Make-or-buy. Build (JARVIS: one-time set-up, monthly maintenance, requests inside the free quota) or buy (a paid seat: no set-up, a subscription every month), compared over the same horizon:

Formula build = set-up + maintenance per month × months · buy = subscription per month × months

Horizon Build Buy Cheaper
12 months 1 120 + 28 × 12 = 1 456 $ 100 × 12 = 1 200 $ buy
24 months 1 120 + 28 × 24 = 1 792 $ 100 × 24 = 2 400 $ build

The horizon decides, because the set-up is paid once and the subscription every month. Two things the numbers do not show also decide: whether the paid assistant does the task as well as the pilot, and whether the free quota survives.

Every formula maps to a column. The minutes column gives the minutes per run; tool separates manual, template and jarvis runs (saving per run = mean minutes where tool = manual − mean minutes where tool = jarvis, for the same people); routine and staff_id group the rows; date counts runs per day (× 20 = runs per month). The hourly value, the price and the quota are given numbers; set-up hours, review minutes and the price per request are stated assumptions until Phase 2 measures them.

Concept Formula EconEngine method Guard
Cost of a routine minutes ÷ 60 × hourly value × runs routine_cost(mean_minutes, hourly_value, runs_per_month) refuses negative minutes or runs
Opportunity cost hours × rate of the next-best use opportunity_cost(hours, next_best_rate) —
Marginal benefit net minutes saved ÷ 60 × hourly value × runs marginal_benefit(saved_minutes, hourly_value, runs_per_month) —
Total cost FC (fixed cost) + VC (variable cost) total_cost(fixed_cost, variable_cost) —
Average cost TC (total cost) ÷ runs average_cost(total_cost, runs) runs = 0 → ValueError
Break-even hours monthly price ÷ hourly value break_even_hours(monthly_price, hourly_value) hourly value ≤ 0 → ValueError
Payback months set-up ÷ monthly net saving payback_months(fixed_cost, monthly_saving) saving ≤ 0 → math.inf

Limits. These numbers rest on 14 days, 5 people, 15 pilot runs and stated assumptions: strong enough to rank routines and answer the owner with an order of magnitude, not to promise the second decimal. The decision candidate of Brick 3 (about 120 words) follows the four-part pattern — finding, evidence, decision, risk — and names one routine to automate first, one later and one to leave alone. A decision candidate without its risks is a sales pitch; with them, it is consulting.

Exam angle Compute break-even hours (per seat and for all seats), payback months (and recognise the math.inf case), and a make-or-buy comparison at two horizons; say what the formulas leave out.

Chapter 4

Statistics Refresher: Letting the Time Log Speak

0:35–0:50

Class 4 module · 4 sub-chapters · tick Reviewed when you can answer the exam-angle box without looking.

4.1

Central tendency

The data of the day. The teaching copy of the file has 420 rows: 14 working days (September 14 to October 1, 2026) × 5 staff × 6 routines. The tool column has three values: manual; template (the daily report written with a template from day 8, September 23); jarvis (the pilot assistant that triages e-mail for S1, S2 and S3 from day 10, September 25). Rule of the day: describe one process at a time — filter by routine and by tool before computing anything; a list that mixes manual and jarvis runs describes no process that exists.

Notation. n is the number of observations; x₁, x₂, …, xₙ the values; Σx their sum.

A measure of central tendency is one number that represents the centre of a set of values.

Formula mean x̄ = Σx ÷ n · median = middle value of the sorted data (odd n: position (n + 1) ÷ 2; even n: average of positions n ÷ 2 and n ÷ 2 + 1)

Mean. Uses every value — its strength and its weakness: one very large value changes it. Python: sum(values) / len(values) or statistics.mean(values).

Median. Sorting always comes first. The median depends on the order of the values, not on how far the extreme ones are: it is resistant (robust) to outliers. An outlier is an observation unusually far from the other values, defined by a rule stated in advance (4.3).

Worked week (S2, e-mail triage): Monday 105, Tuesday 36, Wednesday 33, Thursday 38, Friday 34. Σx = 246, n = 5 → mean 49.2 minutes. Sorted: 33, 34, 36, 38, 105 → median 36. Remove Monday: mean 35.25, median (34 + 36) ÷ 2 = 35. The median moved by one minute; the mean moved by almost fourteen. Monday is long because the inbox holds a whole weekend of mail (a backlog).

Mode. The value that occurs most often; the natural centre for discrete counts such as interruptions. S2's interruptions 5, 1, 0, 2, 1 → mode 1. For measured times the mode is often of little use; among the 55 manual e-mail runs three values tie (29, 32 and 37 minutes, five runs each). Two modes = bimodal, more = multimodal. Decide the tie rule in advance: statistics.mode returns the first mode met in the data; statistics.multimode returns all of them; JARVIS's StatsEngine.mode returns the list of tied values, sorted.

Range. Largest minus smallest: 105 − 33 = 72 minutes. Quick, but decided by the two most extreme runs only; it describes spread, not centre.

Which number is "typical"? Report the median when there are a few extreme values or a long tail; report the mean when values are roughly symmetric, and whenever the number will be multiplied (a monthly total is mean × number of runs, because Σx = n × x̄ exactly); report both, with the reason, when they differ by more than a few percent.

Routine (manual runs) n Mean Median
email_triage 55 35.15 35
standup_notes 70 9.91 10
scheduling 70 15.70 15
invoice_check 70 20.84 21
social_post 70 21.31 21.5
daily_report 35 26.83 27

In the full log the routines are close to symmetric, so mean and median agree within one minute. Decision written for the owner: "Typical e-mail slot: 35 minutes (median of 55 manual runs; the mean, 35.15, agrees). Mondays run longer."

Exam angle Compute mean, median, mode and range of five or six daily values, recompute without the extreme day, and justify which value you report.

4.2

Dispersion

Same centre, different reliability. Set A = 8, 10, 9, 12, 11 and set B = 4, 16, 6, 15, 9 both have a mean of 10. A planner can rely on A's 10 minutes; B's runs range from 4 to 16. Dispersion (spread, variability) measures how far values typically lie from their centre. For JARVIS it matters twice: a variable routine is hard to schedule, and its estimated saving is less certain.

Deviations always add up to zero. The deviation of a value is xᵢ − x̄. For A: −2, 0, −1, +2, +1 → sum 0. Their average says nothing about spread, so deviations are squared.

Formula s² = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1) · s = √s² · CV (Coefficient of Variation) = s ÷ x̄ (× 100 %)

Worked set A. Squared deviations 4, 0, 1, 4, 1 → sum of squares 10 → s² = 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5 min² → s = √2.5 ≈ 1.58 minutes (a run typically lies about 1.6 minutes from the mean). Set B: deviations −6, +6, −4, +5, −1 → sum of squares 114 → s² = 28.5 → s ≈ 5.34 minutes, more than three times A's spread with the same mean.

Why n − 1? A population is the complete set of values we want to describe; a sample is the part we observed (the studio's 14 days are a sample of all its working days). Deviations measured from the sample's own mean are, by construction, as small as possible; dividing by n would underestimate the population variance on average, and dividing by n − 1 corrects this. n − 1 is the number of degrees of freedom: once the mean is fixed, only n − 1 deviations can vary freely. In Python, statistics.variance and statistics.stdev divide by n − 1 (sample); statistics.pvariance and statistics.pstdev divide by n (population). For A: stdev 1.581, pstdev 1.414. Spreadsheets: STDEV.S versus STDEV.P. JARVIS uses n − 1.

Coefficient of variation. The SD (Standard Deviation) grows with the size of the values (6 minutes is moderate for a 35-minute routine, very large for a 10-minute one). The CV (Coefficient of Variation) has no unit, so it compares routines of different length (A: 15.8 %; B: 53.4 %). It is meaningful only for data measured from a true zero, with a mean clearly above zero.

Routine (manual) n Mean (min) SD (Standard Deviation), min CV (Coefficient of Variation)
email_triage 55 35.15 6.35 18.1 %
standup_notes 70 9.91 2.62 26.4 %
scheduling 70 15.70 3.10 19.8 %
invoice_check 70 20.84 3.36 16.1 %
social_post 70 21.31 4.12 19.3 %
daily_report 35 26.83 4.42 16.5 %

E-mail triage has the largest SD (Standard Deviation); stand-up notes have the smallest SD (Standard Deviation) but the largest CV (Coefficient of Variation). Both are correct. To plan a buffer in minutes, use the SD (Standard Deviation): e-mail needs the largest buffer. To compare how predictable two processes are, use the CV (Coefficient of Variation): stand-up notes are the least predictable in relative terms, because each interruption adds about 2 minutes to a routine that normally takes under 10.

Describe one process at a time. The SD (Standard Deviation) of all e-mail runs, manual and jarvis mixed, is 10.54 minutes (CV (Coefficient of Variation) 34.5 %), larger than either group alone (6.35 and 2.46): the difference between the two groups' means is counted as if it were variation within one process.

Planning slot. A common compromise is a slot of ⌈mean + 1 SD (Standard Deviation)⌉: for e-mail, ⌈35.15 + 6.35⌉ = 42 minutes, which would have covered 48 of the 55 manual runs (87.3 %).

Hand-computation drill (S5, scheduling): 14, 17, 12, 16, 16 → mean 15; deviations −1, +2, −3, +1, +1; sum of squares 16; s² = 16 ÷ 4 = 4; s = 2.00; CV (Coefficient of Variation) = 13.3 %; pstdev would give 1.79.

Exam angle Compute s² and s with n − 1 for five values, then the CV (Coefficient of Variation); explain why pstdev gives a smaller number; say which routine needs the largest buffer and which is the least predictable.

4.3

Distributions and outliers

Frequency table and histogram. The distribution of a variable describes which values occur and how often. A frequency table divides the range into bins of equal width that do not overlap and cover every value (boundary convention here: lower limit included, upper excluded, 25 ≤ x < 30). Relative frequency = count ÷ n.

Bin (minutes) 25–29 30–34 35–39 40–44 45–49 50–54 Total
Runs 13 14 14 10 3 1 55
Relative frequency 23.6 % 25.5 % 25.5 % 18.2 % 5.5 % 1.8 % 100 %

A histogram draws the table: bars touch because the axis is a continuous numeric scale (a bar chart shows separate categories and its bars can be placed in any order). Bin width changes the picture: too wide hides the shape, too narrow shows random ups and downs; for about 50 values start with 6 to 10 bins and check that the shape survives one wider and one narrower version. Brick 4 accepts a text histogram (one # per run); matplotlib.pyplot.hist draws the graphic version later.

Shape. Symmetric: halves roughly mirror each other, mean ≈ median. Right-skewed (positively skewed): a long tail toward large values, mean > median — typical of durations, which have a floor but no ceiling (backlogs, difficult requests, interruptions). Left-skewed: the long tail on the small side. Bimodal: two peaks — adding the 15 jarvis runs (10 to 19 minutes) to the 55 manual runs produces two peaks, the visible sign that two processes were mixed.

Quartiles and IQR (Interquartile Range), inclusive method. Q1 (first quartile) has about 25 % of the sorted values below it, Q2 (second quartile) is the median, Q3 (third quartile) has about 75 % below it. Course method: sort; number positions 0 to n − 1; compute p × (n − 1) for p = 0.25 or 0.75; interpolate between neighbours when the position is not whole. This is statistics.quantiles(values, n=4, method="inclusive"), QUARTILE.INC and NumPy's default; Python's default method="exclusive" gives slightly different values, so always state the method.

E-mail runs, n = 55: Q1 (first quartile) position 0.25 × 54 = 13.5 → between 30 and 31 → Q1 (first quartile) = 30.5; Q3 (third quartile) position 40.5 → between 39 and 40 → Q3 (third quartile) = 39.5; IQR (Interquartile Range) = Q3 (third quartile) − Q1 (first quartile) = 9 minutes (the middle half of the runs lies in a 9-minute window). Like the median, the IQR (Interquartile Range) is resistant.

Box plot. A box from Q1 (first quartile) to Q3 (third quartile), a line at the median, whiskers to the most extreme values that are not outliers, and points beyond the fences drawn separately: centre, spread and symmetry in one line.

Two outlier rules — chosen before looking.

Formula fences = Q1 (first quartile) − 1.5 × IQR (Interquartile Range) and Q3 (third quartile) + 1.5 × IQR (Interquartile Range) · second rule: mean ± 2 × SD (Standard Deviation)

  • 1.5 × IQR (Interquartile Range) rule (Tukey's fences): 30.5 − 13.5 = 17 and 39.5 + 13.5 = 53 → no manual e-mail run is outside [17, 53], so nothing is flagged.
  • Mean ± 2 SD (Standard Deviation): 35.15 ± 2 × 6.35 → [22.44, 47.85] → two runs flagged: 48 minutes (S3, Monday, September 14, the first day of the log) and 51 minutes (S5, Friday, September 18, three interruptions).

The rules disagree and both were applied correctly: quartiles are barely affected by the extreme values, while the mean and SD (Standard Deviation) are pulled by them; the ± 2 SD (Standard Deviation) rule also flags about 5 % of perfectly regular bell-shaped data. Write the rule and its reason in one sentence.

What to do with a flagged run. A flagged value is a question, not a mistake. Check it against the log first (the 51-minute run had three interruptions; the 48-minute run is a Monday after a weekend). Then keep it (default — it is a real run), correct it only when it is a proven data-entry error (510 typed for 51) and record the correction in the bug log, or report results with and without it when it changes a conclusion. Never delete a value silently: removing the 51-minute run would make e-mail look cheaper than it is and understate the 1 640 $ monthly cost.

Exam angle Build a frequency table, describe the shape, compute inclusive quartiles, the IQR (Interquartile Range) and the fences, flag outliers with a stated rule, and say what you do with a flagged run.

4.4

Relationships, groups and the limits of 14 days

Scatter plot. One point per run for two numeric variables; x is the explanatory variable (interruptions), y the response variable (minutes). Read three properties: direction (rising = positive, falling = negative), form (straight line, curve, no pattern) and strength (how closely points follow the form). When x is a discrete count, a small random horizontal shift called jitter keeps overlapping points visible.

Pearson's r. Measures the direction and strength of the linear relationship, always between −1 and +1, with no unit; swapping x and y does not change it. Python: statistics.correlation(xs, ys) (since Python 3.10).

Formula r = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ) ÷ √[Σ(xᵢ − x̄)² × Σ(yᵢ − ȳ)²]

A run above average on both variables (or below on both) adds a positive product; above on one and below on the other adds a negative product. r = +1: all points on a rising line; r = −1: on a falling line; r near 0: no linear relationship (a curved one may still exist).

|r| Wording in the report
below 0.10 negligible
0.10 to 0.29 weak
0.30 to 0.69 moderate
0.70 and above strong

Always give the sign, the value, n and the period: "r = +0.21 between interruptions and minutes, 55 manual e-mail runs, September 14 – October 1, 2026."

Pair (x, y) Routine n r Reading
interruptions, minutes standup_notes 70 +0.883 strong positive
interruptions, minutes email_triage 55 +0.215 weak positive
start hour, minutes email_triage 55 −0.093 negligible

r measures how closely points follow a straight line, not how many minutes an interruption costs. The trend lines give about 2.2 minutes per interruption for stand-up notes and 1.4 for e-mail (ŷ ≈ 32.9 + 1.42x). A stand-up note normally takes 6 to 10 minutes, so an interruption is a large share and the points line up closely; e-mail varies by about ± 6 minutes for many other reasons, so interruptions explain only a small part. The method that fits the line (least squares) is the topic of Class 7.

Before and after a change. The daily-report template (day 8) splits the log into two groups:

Group Days n Mean (min) SD (Standard Deviation), min Median
before — manual 1–7 35 26.83 4.42 27
after — template 8–14 35 16.83 3.06 17

Difference of the means: −10.00 minutes per run (−37.3 %). Always give n and the SD (Standard Deviation) next to a mean: a 10-minute difference with SDs (Standard Deviations) of 3 to 4 and 35 runs per group is a clear separation; the same difference with SDs (Standard Deviations) of 15 and four runs per group would be very uncertain.

The comparison group. For the e-mail pilot (jarvis for S1–S3 from day 10), S4 and S5 stayed manual:

Group Days 1–9 Days 10–14 Change
S1–S3 (pilot) 35.85 min (n = 27, manual) 13.73 min (n = 15, jarvis) −22.12 min
S4–S5 (comparison) 34.67 min (n = 18, manual) 34.10 min (n = 10, manual) −0.57 min

The comparison group barely changed, so the drop of the pilot group cannot be explained by the calendar alone (for example a quieter last week for everyone). The difference of the changes, (−22.12) − (−0.57) = −21.55 minutes per run, is the estimated effect of the assistant (the design is called difference-in-differences (https://learn.mru.org/lessons/introduction-differences-differencesVirusTotal), reviewed again in 10.4).

What 14 days and five people can and cannot show.

  • Correlation is not causation. A confounding variable can influence both x and y: Mondays bring more mail and more interruptions (manual Monday runs average 37.6 minutes, other days 34.5).
  • Sample size. At most 70 runs per routine; the jarvis result rests on 15 runs by three people over five days. Results suggest; they do not prove.
  • Scope. Five people of one studio during three September weeks are not "consultancies in general". Write the scope next to every conclusion.
  • Measurement. Staff logged their own minutes (rounding to 5, forgotten short runs); jarvis runs are timed by the assistant — a different measurement process.
  • Novelty. A new tool is often used with extra care at first; the effect can shrink later.

Writing the interpretation: number, then limit. Sentence 1 gives the number with n and the period; sentence 2 gives the main limit. "From day 8, daily-report runs took 10.0 minutes less on average (26.8 → 16.8 minutes; 35 runs in each group; SD (Standard Deviation) 4.4 and 3.1). This is a before/after comparison over two weeks in one studio, so it cannot separate the effect of the template from other changes made at the same time."

Exam angle Read the sign and strength of r and name a possible confounder; compute a before/after difference and the difference of the changes with a comparison group; write the two-sentence interpretation.

Chapter 5

Python and OOP (Object-Oriented Programming) Refresher + Design: Blueprint Before Bricks

0:50–1:05

Class 5 module · 4 sub-chapters · tick Reviewed when you can answer the exam-angle box without looking.

5.1

Classes, objects and the dataclass

Why one row needs a class. csv gives nine pieces of text per row ('2026-09-14', 'S1', 'email_triage', …, '36', …). Text cannot be added, compared as dates, or protected against −19 minutes. JARVIS has two engines, a store, a reporter and several tools that use the same rows, so the row is defined once, as a class, in jarvis/models.py.

Core vocabulary.

Term Meaning
Class a named definition grouping data (attributes) and operations on that data (methods) — TimeEntry
Object (instance) one concrete value built from a class, with its own attribute values — first = TimeEntry(...)
Method a function defined in a class; Python passes the object as the first parameter, self
__init__ the special method called to initialise a new object with the constructor arguments
Special (dunder) method a method named with double underscores (__init__, __repr__, __str__, __eq__) that Python calls for built-in operations
Decorator a callable applied with @name above a definition, which returns a modified version
Invariant a condition true for every object during its whole life (minutes ≥ 0 for every TimeEntry)

The @dataclass decorator (module dataclasses, Python 3.7, PEP (Python Enhancement Proposal) 557) reads the annotated fields and writes the repetitive methods.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import date

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class TimeEntry:
    """One timed run of one routine by one staff member."""
    date: date
    staff_id: str
    routine: str
    category: str
    start_hour: int
    minutes: int
    interruptions: int
    tool: str
    done: bool
Written by @dataclass(frozen=True) Effect
__init__ takes the nine fields in class-body order and stores them
__repr__ TimeEntry(date=datetime.date(2026, 9, 14), staff_id='S1', …)
__eq__ compares two entries field by field
__setattr__, __delattr__ (frozen) raise FrozenInstanceError on any change after creation
__hash__ (frozen with eq) lets an entry live in a set or be a dictionary key

Type hints are not checked. minutes: int declares a field and documents its intended type, but Python does not check it at creation: TimeEntry(..., interruptions="1", ...) is accepted and the text "1" stays in the object. That is why the loader converts every value before building the object.

Validation in __post_init__. The generated __init__ calls __post_init__ after storing the fields; it is the place for checks from the data dictionary:

    def __post_init__(self) -> None:
        if self.minutes < 0:
            raise ValueError(f"minutes must be >= 0, got {self.minutes}")
        if not 0 <= self.start_hour <= 23:
            raise ValueError(f"start_hour must be 0-23, got {self.start_hour}")
        if self.tool not in ALLOWED_TOOLS:    # {"manual", "template", "jarvis"}
            raise ValueError(f"unknown tool {self.tool!r}")

If a check fails, no object exists and the caller receives a ValueError whose message names the field and the value. With frozen=True the checks establish an invariant: the engines never meet a negative duration.

Methods and properties. cost(self, hourly_value) returns self.minutes / 60 * hourly_value (36 minutes at 28 $/h → 16.80 $); the hourly value is a parameter, not a number hidden inside the method. A property (@property) is read like an attribute and computed when read: first.hours returns 0.6. A property cannot disagree with the data it is computed from — the reason hours is a property, not a tenth field.

Encapsulation in Python. Encapsulation keeps data and the code that uses it in one class and controls access. Python has no private keyword: a single leading underscore (_tools) is a convention meaning "internal" (PEP (Python Enhancement Proposal) 8's weak internal-use indicator — not enforced); two leading underscores (__secret) trigger name mangling (_ClassName__secret) to avoid clashes in subclasses — not a protection mechanism; a property without a setter refuses assignment; frozen=True refuses every field assignment (first.hours = 2 raises FrozenInstanceError, a subclass of AttributeError). In UML (Unified Modeling Language), internal members carry − and public ones +.

__repr__ versus __str__. repr(obj) should return an unambiguous text for developers (ideally the expression that recreates the object; the dataclass writes it). str(obj) and print(obj) call __str__, a readable text for people (2026-09-14 S1 email_triage: 36 min (manual)); without __str__, Python uses __repr__.

Exam angle Predict what happens when a TimeEntry is created with bad values or modified after creation, explain why hours is a property, and explain encapsulation on code like this.

5.2

Collections and CSV (Comma-Separated Values) parsing

Four collections, four jobs.

Type Ordered Changeable Duplicates Job in JARVIS
list yes yes allowed entries: the 420 TimeEntry objects in file order
dict insertion order yes keys unique one CSV (Comma-Separated Values) row: {"date": "2026-09-14", …}
set no yes no ALLOWED_TOOLS, staff codes — fast membership test
tuple yes no allowed one skipped line: (4, "invalid literal for int() …")

ALLOWED_TOOLS is a set because the only question asked is "is this tool in it?", answered in constant average time; a skipped line is a tuple because the pair (line number, reason) is a fixed record.

Paths: pathlib, never a hard-coded path. C:\Users\ana\Desktop\boreal.csv works on one computer only — not on a teammate's Mac, the Linux runner of GitHub Actions (https://docs.github.com/en/actionsVirusTotal) or the projector computer ("a fresh clone that runs in under two minutes"). The rubric lists hard-coded paths under Developing for Lab Proficiency.

from pathlib import Path
HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent   # folder of this .py file
DATA = HERE.parent / "data"              # / joins with the right separator
csv_path = DATA / "boreal_routines_2026.csv"

Opening the file correctly: with path.open(newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f: — with makes the file a context manager (closed at the end of the block, even after an error); newline="" is required by the csv documentation so the module handles line endings; encoding="utf-8" reads "Boréal" correctly on every operating system.

csv.DictReader. Reads the header and returns each following line as a dict of strings (it never guesses types). reader.fieldnames lists the columns — a missing required column stops the program with a clear message (a wrong file is not a bad row). A line with more values than the header keeps the extras in a list under the key None (restkey); a line with fewer values gets None for the missing keys (restval); completely empty lines are skipped.

Converting text, and what fails. The loader follows the EAFP (Easier to Ask for Forgiveness than Permission) style: it tries the conversion and handles the exception, instead of checking every condition first, which is the opposite LBYL (Look Before You Leap) style.

Text Conversion Result
"36" int() 36
" 36 " int() 36 (spaces accepted)
"17.0" int() ValueError
"" int() ValueError
None int() TypeError
"2026-09-14" date.fromisoformat() date(2026, 9, 14)
"2026/09/14" date.fromisoformat() ValueError
"1" == "1" True

The yyyy-mm-dd format is the calendar date of ISO (International Organization for Standardization) 8601 (https://www.iso.org/iso-8601-date-and-time-format.htmlVirusTotal). int("17.0") fails because int() accepts only the text of a whole number; int(float("17.0")) would hide the problem and would also turn "17.9" into 17 silently, so the loader rejects the value.

try/except: report the row, never crash.

for line_no, row in enumerate(reader, start=2):   # line 1 is the header
    try:
        entries.append(self._parse_row(row))
    except (ValueError, TypeError) as err:
        self.skipped.append((line_no, str(err)))

Only the two exceptions a bad row can produce are caught; FileNotFoundError still stops the program, because it signals a setup problem, not a data problem. On the damaged 12-row sample the loader returns 8 objects and 4 skipped lines; on the full dataset, 420 and 0.

Grouping and counting. defaultdict(list) creates an empty list the first time a key is used, so minutes_by_routine[entry.routine].append(entry.minutes) needs no if key not in d test (6 keys × 70 values). Counter(entry.tool for entry in entries) gives 370 manual, 35 template, 15 jarvis.

Exam angle Choose the right collection for a job, predict the result of a conversion, explain each argument of open(...), and count how many rows a loader keeps and skips.

5.3

Responsibilities, classes and UML (Unified Modeling Language)

Responsibility and the SRP (Single Responsibility Principle). A responsibility is something a class must know or do. Give each requirement to exactly one class. The Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) says a class should have one responsibility — in Robert C. Martin's words, one reason to change. Consequences: high cohesion (every member serves the same responsibility) and low coupling (a change in one class rarely forces a change in another). A CRC (Class–Responsibility–Collaborator) card, introduced by Kent Beck and Ward Cunningham (https://c2.com/doc/oopsla89/paper.htmlVirusTotal) at OOPSLA (Object-Oriented Programming, Systems, Languages and Applications) in 1989, tests a design on paper: name, responsibilities, collaborators; more than three or four items usually means mixed purposes — split the class.

The ten core classes of JARVIS.

Class Module One responsibility
TimeEntry models.py holds one timed run and computes its cost
Task models.py holds one to-do item
DataLoader loader.py turns a routines CSV (Comma-Separated Values) into TimeEntry objects and reports bad rows
Store store.py owns data/jarvis.db: save, query, export
StatsEngine stats_engine.py computes the statistics of a list of minutes
EconEngine econ_engine.py prices the time: cost, break-even, payback
Tool (abstract) tools/base.py defines one action the assistant can perform
Provider (abstract) providers.py turns a text request into an Intent
Agent agent.py runs the loop request → intent → tool → result → log
Reporter reporter.py writes the console report, the charts and the dashboard

Six small classes complete the reference design: Intent, LogTimeTool, AddTaskTool, DailyReportTool, OfflineProvider, ApiProvider. Brick 5 asks for 8 to 10 classes in 6 to 7 modules in version 1. In the class example a draft gave "publish a dashboard with aggregated numbers only" to the Agent; the check found the Agent with two requirements, and the requirement moved to the Reporter.

UML (Unified Modeling Language). The Unified Modeling Language is the standard graphical language for software models, maintained by the OMG (Object Management Group) (https://www.omg.org/spec/UML/VirusTotal); current formal version 2.5.1 (December 2017). A class box has three compartments: name; attributes (visibility name: type); operations (visibility name(parameter: type): return type).

Symbol Meaning Python form
+ public plain name
− private one leading underscore (convention)
# protected also one leading underscore
~ package no equivalent
italic or {abstract} abstract class or operation ABC and @abstractmethod
{readOnly} read-only attribute property without setter

Relationships.

Relationship Drawing JARVIS example
Association solid line (arrowhead = navigability) Agent → Store ("logs runs in")
Aggregation hollow diamond at the whole; part can exist without the whole Agent ◇— Tool (tools created in main() and passed in)
Composition filled diamond at the whole; part belongs to one whole and is deleted with it if Agent.__init__ created self._provider = OfflineProvider() itself
Dependency dashed arrow; temporary use (parameter, local, return value) DataLoader ⇢ TimeEntry ("creates")
Generalization solid line, hollow triangle at the parent LogTimeTool —▷ Tool

JARVIS avoids composition for the provider on purpose, so that a test or the ApiProvider can be passed in instead.

Multiplicity. 1 exactly one; 0..1 zero or one; * (= 0..*) any number, zero included; 1..* at least one. Agent "1" ◇— "1..*" Tool reads "one agent holds one or more tools"; Store "1" — "0..*" TimeEntry reads "one store keeps zero or more entries" (an empty database is valid).

Drawing tools accepted for Brick 5: draw.io (https://www.drawio.com/VirusTotal), PlantUML (https://plantuml.com/class-diagramVirusTotal) (a text file docs/uml.puml versioned in Git with the code) or a clean photographed drawing. The class diagram is the design slide of the Alpha demo, your Design Card for the Mid-Term and section 4 of the report.

Exam angle Read a relationship and its multiplicity aloud, give one requirement to the right class, and explain why a class with two reasons to change should be split.

5.4

Abstract base classes, polymorphism and clean code
