Inheritance and overriding. In class LogTimeTool(Tool):, Tool is the superclass and LogTimeTool the subclass; the subclass receives name, description and run, and overrides run with its own version. Test: "a LogTimeTool is a Tool" is true; "an Agent is a Tool" is false — an agent has tools (aggregation).

Abstract base classes.

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class Tool(ABC):
    """One action the assistant can perform; subclasses implement run()."""
    name: str = ""
    @abstractmethod
    def run(self, args: dict, store) -> str:
        """Perform the action and return a reply for the user."""

class Provider(ABC):
    """Turns a text request into an Intent; subclasses implement parse()."""
    @abstractmethod
    def parse(self, text: str) -> "Intent":
        """Return the Intent of the request."""

An abstract base class (ABC) declares methods its subclasses must implement and cannot be instantiated itself (module abc, PEP (Python Enhancement Proposal) 3119). Tool() raises TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class Tool without an implementation for abstract method 'run'; so does a subclass that forgets run() (the planned SummarizeTool). The value of the mechanism is the moment of the error: at object creation, on the developer's computer, not during a demo. A concrete class implements every abstract method (LogTimeTool, OfflineProvider).

Polymorphism and dependency injection.

class Agent:
    def __init__(self, provider: Provider, tools: list[Tool], store) -> None:
        self._provider = provider
        self._tools = {tool.name: tool for tool in tools}
        self._store = store

    def handle(self, text: str) -> str:
        intent = self._provider.parse(text)        # any Provider subclass
        tool = self._tools.get(intent.name)
        if tool is None:
            return f"sorry, no tool for {text!r}"
        return tool.run(intent.args, self._store)  # any Tool subclass

Polymorphism: one call, tool.run(...), executes LogTimeTool.run, AddTaskTool.run or DailyReportTool.run depending on the object — no if intent.name == ...: elif ... chain. Adding a tool = one subclass + one provider rule + one object in main(); the Agent class does not change. Replacing OfflineProvider with ApiProvider = one argument in main(). This works because of dependency injection: the agent receives its provider, tools and store as constructor parameters instead of creating them, so a test can pass a fake provider or an in-memory store. The rubric's Exemplary Tech Implementation level asks for advanced object-oriented programming, with abstract base classes and polymorphism used effectively; Developing describes a procedural style instead of OOP (Object-Oriented Programming).

Regular expressions. re.compile(r"log\s+(\d+)\s*min\s+(\w+)") matches "log 25 min email_triage" and captures 25 and email_triage — the core of the OfflineProvider.

Clean-code habits that cost or earn marks. A code smell (Martin Fowler (https://martinfowler.com/bliki/CodeSmell.htmlVirusTotal)) is a surface sign that usually points to a deeper problem.

Habit Rule in JARVIS
Follow PEP (Python Enhancement Proposal) 8 4 spaces; at most 79 characters per code line and 72 for comments and docstrings; snake_case functions and variables, CapWords classes, UPPER_CASE constants
Type hints on public functions (PEP (Python Enhancement Proposal) 484) def load(self, path: Path) -> list[TimeEntry]:
A docstring on every module, class and public method (PEP (Python Enhancement Proposal) 257) one sentence stating the responsibility
Small functions, one job if the docstring needs "and", split the function
Meaningful names minutes_manual, line_no — not x1, l, tmp
No secret in the code os.environ.get("JARVIS_API_KEY"), a git-ignored .env, a repository secret; a key committed once is replaced the same day
No hard-coded path Path(__file__).resolve().parent
No mutable default argument seen=None, then seen = [] if seen is None else seen
Catch only expected exceptions except (ValueError, TypeError), never a bare except:
A design that pytest (https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/VirusTotal) can test inputs as parameters, results returned, dependencies injected

The mutable default argument, precisely. A default value is evaluated once, when def runs, not at each call. In def add(item, seen=[]), every call that omits seen shares the same list, so values from an earlier call appear in the next one — invisible in a single test.

Activity 4 smells (ten lines): an API (Application Programming Interface) key written in the code; a hard-coded Windows path as a default; a mutable default rows=[]; meaningless names l, x1, x2; a file opened without with; splitting lines on commas instead of using csv; and the crash on the very first line, where int(x1[5]) meets the header text "minutes" and raises ValueError.

Exam angle Explain why Tool is abstract and what happens when it is instantiated, point to the polymorphic call in a loop, and name and fix three smells in a short function.

Chapter 6

Development I: The Engines and the Store Come Alive

0:50–1:05

Class 6 module · 4 sub-chapters · tick Reviewed when you can answer the exam-angle box without looking.

6.1

Mean and median in code

Engine, static method, oracle. An engine is the part of a program that performs the calculations and nothing else: no screen, no file, no network — numbers in, numbers out. StatsEngine holds the statistics of Chapter 4 and EconEngine the formulas of Chapter 3, written as static methods (@staticmethod): they belong to the class but need no object and no self, because the result depends only on the arguments. Rule of the hour: the engine is yours, the library is the oracle. A test oracle is an independent, trusted source of the correct answer — here the statistics module. The engine must never call it, for three reasons: the Mid-Term asks you to write and explain these methods yourself; a method you wrote can be read line by line when a number looks wrong; a check is only a check when the two sides are independent. The oracle lives in the validation table (6.4) and in the tests (Chapter 10).

mean with its guard.

@staticmethod
def mean(xs: list[float]) -> float:
    if not xs:
        raise ValueError("mean of an empty list is undefined")
    return sum(xs) / len(xs)

/ always returns a float (the mean of 36, 41, 48, 34, 39 is 39.6). The guard matters more than the formula: an empty list is falsy, so not xs is True exactly when there are no values. Without the guard, len(xs) is 0 and the division raises ZeroDivisionError — a message about division, when the real problem is missing data. ValueError is the standard exception for "right type, impossible value", the type the tests and the Mid-Term expect. Why raise instead of returning 0 or None? A mean of 0 would silently flow into a cost (0 × 28 $/h = 0 $); an exception cannot be ignored.

median on a sorted copy.

@staticmethod
def median(xs: list[float]) -> float:
    if not xs:
        raise ValueError("median of an empty list is undefined")
    ordered = sorted(xs)              # a new list; xs keeps its order
    n = len(ordered)
    mid = n // 2
    if n % 2 == 1:
        return ordered[mid]
    return (ordered[mid - 1] + ordered[mid]) / 2

sorted(xs) builds a new list and leaves xs unchanged; xs.sort() reorders xs in place and returns None. The engine must use sorted(): the list belongs to the caller, and a method that quietly reorders its argument has a side effect. For the 55 e-mail runs, mid = 27 and ordered[27] (the 28th value) is 35. The trap [4, 9, 1, 7]: sorted copy [1, 4, 7, 9] → (4 + 7) ÷ 2 = 5.5; the same two positions without sorting give (9 + 1) ÷ 2 = 5.0 — a wrong number with no error message.

value_range and a naming rule. max(xs) - min(xs) (e-mail: 51 − 25 = 26). The method is called value_range, not range, because range is a built-in; reusing the name would shadow it. The engine provides both mean and median; the Reporter prints both.

First validation rows. The program prints the engine's value next to the oracle's and the word match, comparing with math.isclose, not == (6.2).

Exam angle Write mean and median from memory with their guards, explain sorted versus .sort(), and find the bug in a median that forgets to sort.

6.2

Mode, variance, standard deviation and outliers in code

mode with Counter and a documented tie rule.

counts = Counter(xs)
top = counts.most_common(1)[0][1]          # highest count
return sorted(v for v, c in counts.items() if c == top)

For the 55 manual e-mail runs the highest count is 5, shared by 29, 32 and 37. A tie is information, not an error: JARVIS returns all tied values, sorted — [29, 32, 37] — and says so in the docstring. The module disagrees on purpose: statistics.mode returns only the first value met (37 here, file order), statistics.multimode returns all in order of first appearance ([37, 32, 29]); the engine is compared with sorted(statistics.multimode(xs)).

variance and std_dev with n − 1.

m = StatsEngine.mean(xs)
return sum((x - m) ** 2 for x in xs) / (len(xs) - 1)

The guard differs from the mean's: if len(xs) < 2: raise ValueError("variance needs at least two values"), because with one value n − 1 is zero. std_dev is math.sqrt(StatsEngine.variance(xs)). The expression inside sum(...) is a generator expression: values are produced one by one without building a list. The n − 1 corrects the bias of measuring deviations from the sample mean (Bessel's correction); statistics.stdev (n − 1) is the oracle, statistics.pstdev (n) is the workshop bug. Set A [8, 10, 9, 12, 11]: variance 2.5, s = 1.581; with n: 2.0 and 1.414 — "close enough to pass a quick look, wrong enough to fail a test".

cv. s ÷ x̄, returned as a ratio (0.181) and printed as a percentage with :.1% (18.1 %); the guard refuses a mean of zero. Ranking by CV (Coefficient of Variation) answers RQ1 (Research Question 1)'s "most variable": stand-up notes 26.4 %, scheduling 19.8 %, social posts 19.3 %, e-mail 18.1 %, daily report (manual) 16.5 %, invoice checks 16.1 %.

The floating-point trap. Python's float follows IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 754 (https://standards.ieee.org/ieee/754/6210/VirusTotal): a binary fraction with 53 significant bits. Most decimal fractions are stored approximately: 0.1 + 0.2 gives 0.30000000000000004, so 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is False — arithmetic in base 2, not a bug. Never compare two float results with ==; use math.isclose(a, b) (relative tolerance 10⁻⁹ by default; add abs_tol= when a value can be zero). The engine's SD (Standard Deviation) of the 55 runs is 6.352072224780001 and statistics.stdev gives 6.3520722247800006: == is False, math.isclose is True.

Quartiles, IQR (Interquartile Range) and fences in code. Inclusive method: quartile p at position (n − 1) × p of the sorted copy, interpolated (= statistics.quantiles(xs, n=4, method="inclusive")). E-mail: Q1 (first quartile) 30.5, median 35, Q3 (third quartile) 39.5, IQR (Interquartile Range) 9, fences 17 and 53 → no outlier; mean ± 2 × s = [22.44, 47.85] flags 48 and 51. The engine makes the rule explicit with parameters: outliers(xs, k=1.5) and outliers_sd(xs, z=2.0), both returning the flagged values in their original order so the Reporter can say on which day they happened.

Exam angle Write mode with Counter and state the tie rule, write variance with n − 1 and its guard, and explain why math.isclose replaces ==.

6.3

EconEngine and the Store

Parameters, not constants. The three given numbers (28 $/h, 20 $ per user per month, the free quota — 3 000 requests and 0.02 $ beyond it in the teaching assumptions) never appear inside the engine; they are parameters, so the same code answers "what if the hourly value were 32 $?". Methods: routine_cost, opportunity_cost, fixed_cost(setup_hours, hourly_value) (40 h → 1 120 $), variable_cost(requests, free_quota, price_per_request) = max(0, requests − quota) × price (3 500 against 3 000 at 0.02 $ → 10 $), total_cost (1 120 + 10 = 1 130 $), average_cost (1 130 ÷ 100 runs = 11.30 $ per run), marginal_benefit (20.1 × 100 × 28 ÷ 60 → 938 $). Each refuses negative minutes, hours, runs or requests with a ValueError.

Two strategies for a breaking input.

Method Input that breaks it Strategy Why
break_even_hours(monthly_price, hourly_value) hourly value ≤ 0 raise ValueError(f"hourly value must be > 0, got {hourly_value}") an impossible input
payback_months(fixed_cost, monthly_saving) saving ≤ 0 return math.inf, documented a legitimate extreme result: "never recovered"

math.inf prints as inf and is larger than any number (inf > 12 is True). Rule: refuse an impossible input with an exception; return a legitimate extreme result as a documented value. average_cost refuses zero runs: an average over no runs does not exist.

SQLite (https://www.sqlite.org/VirusTotal): one file, one table, one language. A database is a structured store of data with rules about what may enter it. SQLite is a database engine embedded in the program: no server, no installation, the whole database is one file, and Python ships the sqlite3 module. A table has rows and typed columns with constraints: PRIMARY KEY (a unique integer id), NOT NULL (no row without date, staff, routine or minutes), CHECK (minutes >= 0), DEFAULT 'manual', and UNIQUE (date, staff_id, routine, start_hour) (refuses the same run twice — and also a second genuine run of the same routine by the same person in the same hour). SQL (Structured Query Language): CREATE TABLE, INSERT, SELECT, GROUP BY. SELECT routine, tool, COUNT(*), AVG(minutes) FROM entries GROUP BY routine, tool collapses 420 rows into 8 rows (one per routine-and-tool pair); COUNT and AVG are aggregate functions.

The Store: open, use, close — every time. The Store is the only class that speaks SQL (Structured Query Language). Its constructor runs the schema with executescript(SCHEMA) (CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS makes it safe to repeat). Every method uses:

with closing(sqlite3.connect(self.path)) as con, con:
    con.execute("SELECT minutes FROM entries WHERE routine = ? AND tool = ?",
                (routine, tool))

closing(...) guarantees con.close(); the inner con manages the transaction: committed if the block ends normally, rolled back if an exception escapes. Closing does not commit — rows written outside with con: (or without con.commit()) are lost, and a pending write transaction makes other connections fail with database is locked. Values travel through ? placeholders, separately from the SQL (Structured Query Language) text, so they can never change its meaning; gluing them in with an f-string breaks on an apostrophe and lets user input become a command. executemany(sql, rows) runs one INSERT per tuple inside a single transaction (420 rows in milliseconds).

Idempotent import, export, VACUUM. INSERT OR IGNORE skips a row that violates a constraint (a UNIQUE duplicate — but also, silently, a CHECK or NOT NULL failure). With the UNIQUE key, the import is idempotent: running it twice gives the same result (420 rows after import #1 and #2). import_csv returns the table's row count, so compare before and after. Without the key, every import adds 420 rows (about 30 kilobytes) and the file passes 1 MB (megabyte) after a few weeks. export_csv writes data/export/entries.csv (a text file shows a readable diff on GitHub; a .db file shows nothing). VACUUM rebuilds the file and reclaims empty pages; it fails inside a pending transaction, so it runs on a connection with isolation_level=None (autocommit). After vacuum the demo file weighs 53 248 bytes, about 5 % of the limit.

Exam angle Explain raise-versus-math.inf, write a parameterised query with ?, explain why INSERT OR IGNORE + UNIQUE makes an import idempotent, and say what GROUP BY routine, tool returns.

6.4

Grouping, validation and the tiny-database rule

Grouping in one pass. Three defaultdict(list) objects filled in one loop give the runs per routine (6 keys), per staff member (5) and per day (14). Trap: reading a missing key, by_routine["emal_triage"], does not raise — it creates an empty group, and len(by_routine) becomes 7; test with in first. SQL (Structured Query Language) GROUP BY does the same grouping inside the database; the homework asks for one of the two (a small Grouper class or Store queries), not both. Note: StatsEngine.mean(by_routine["email_triage"]) over all 70 runs (pilot included) gives 30.56 minutes — filter to manual runs when the question asks for the current practice.

The validation table: the Phase 1 scripts are the oracle. One row per method — method · engine value · script value · match? — with at least 8 green rows at the Brick 6 checkpoint. The comparison is math.isclose with an absolute tolerance of half a unit of the last printed digit (0.5 × 10⁻ᵈᵉᶜⁱᵐᵃˡˢ: 0.005 for two decimals, 0.05 for one, 0.0005 for three). With a uniform 0.005, the CV (Coefficient of Variation) row would turn red (18.074 against a script value printed as 18.1) only because of rounding.

Chasing a red row, in this order: rounding (tolerance, decimals) → formula (n or n − 1? inclusive or exclusive quartiles?) → rows counted (runs per month? pilot rows?). Real case: the monthly bill over all rows was 5 607.33 $ against the script's 5 821.45 $; no tolerance covers 214 $; the cause was a rule — Brick 3 priced the current practice and left out the 15 pilot runs (tool != "jarvis"). Once the engine applies the same rule, the row turns green, and the rule is written in one place where a test will protect it. The validation table is your first unit test.

f-strings and format specs — [fill][align][width][,][.precision][type]:

Spec Effect Example
{name:<14} left-aligned in 14 characters email_triage
{value:>10.2f} right-aligned in 10, 2 decimals, fixed point 35.15
{runs:>4} integer right-aligned in 4 55
{ratio:.1%} × 100, one decimal, percent sign 18.1%
{cost:,.2f} thousands separator, 2 decimals 5,821.45

The same widths in the header and the rows put numbers in columns the eye can compare.

The tiny-database rule and the one-writer discipline. data/jarvis.db is committed to GitHub and shared by the team and, from December, by the scheduled job:

  • Stay under 1 MB (megabyte): the 420 entries weigh about 50 KB (kilobyte), and the UNIQUE key and INSERT OR IGNORE prevent repeated imports.
  • VACUUM before every commit.
  • One writer at a time: git pull before you run the assistant, git commit right after. If a push is rejected, git pull --rebase; if Git reports a conflict on the .db, take GitHub's version (git checkout origin/main -- data/jarvis.db, then git add and git rebase --continue) and run your command again. Never merge two database files by hand.
  • Export for readable diffs (python -m jarvis export).
  • No secrets, no raw personal logs, no message contents in any repository; the public dashboard shows aggregated numbers only. The scheduled bot's commit message carries [skip ci] so its own commit never triggers the test workflow.

This is a non-functional requirement of Brick 2 made concrete, and the Exemplary Lab Proficiency level of the rubric ("reproducible setup; database committed and updated by the workflow").

Exam angle Explain the defaultdict read trap, derive the tolerance from the printed decimals, chase a red validation row in the right order, and predict the output of an f-string format spec.

Chapter 10

Development III: Testing, Error Resolution, the API (Application Programming Interface) Provider and the Road to the Report

1:05–1:15

Class 10 module · 4 sub-chapters · tick Reviewed when you can answer the exam-angle box without looking.

10.1

Tests with pytest, edge cases and the oracle

Why automated tests. The Class 6 validation table was correct but manual and done once. From Phase 3 the code changes every week (new tools, an API (Application Programming Interface) provider, a workflow), and any change can silently break a method that worked yesterday. A unit test is a short function that calls one unit (for example StatsEngine.median) with a known input and compares the result with the expected value. An automated test suite is the collection of all unit tests, run by one command in a few seconds. In software testing, a regression is a defect in behaviour that used to work and stopped working after a change — a different meaning from the statistical regression of Class 7 (fitting a line). Detecting regressions is the main purpose of a suite.

pytest (https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/VirusTotal) in five rules.

  1. Install it in the virtual environment (python -m pip install pytest) and pin the version in requirements.txt (for example pytest==9.2.0, as printed by pip freeze), so every computer and GitHub Actions (https://docs.github.com/en/actionsVirusTotal) install the same version.
  2. Put tests in tests/, in files named test_*.py.
  3. Name every test function test_... and describe the behaviour: test_median_of_even_count_averages_the_two_middles.
  4. Check with the plain assert statement; when it is false, pytest prints both values.
  5. Run from the repository root with python -m pytest -q (the python -m form adds the current folder to sys.path, so import jarvis works).

Reading the output. One character per test: . passed, F failed (an assert was false or the test raised an unexpected exception), E error (the problem happened outside the test body, for example in a fixture). Last line: for example 8 passed in 0.04s. Exit codes: 0 all passed, 1 at least one failed, 5 no test found; GitHub Actions reads this number to mark a commit green or red.

The shape of one test: prepare, call, check.

def test_median_of_even_count_averages_the_two_middles():
    xs = [4, 9, 1, 7]                         # 1. prepare
    result = StatsEngine.median(xs)           # 2. call
    assert result == pytest.approx(5.5)       # 3. check

The expected value must come from outside the code under test (a hand computation, the Brick 4 sheet, an independent library). Tests are short (about 3 to 8 lines) and independent — any test can be run alone (python -m pytest -q -k median). If the median forgot to sort, it would return 5.0 and this test would fail.

Floats and exceptions. pytest.approx compares with a tolerance (by default the larger of a relative 1e-6 and an absolute 1e-12) — the pytest version of math.isclose. pytest.raises requires an exception:

with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="hourly value must be > 0"):
    EconEngine.break_even_hours(20, 0)

match performs a regular-expression search on the message. A legitimate extreme value is not an error: assert EconEngine.payback_months(1120, 0) == math.inf.

Edge cases and the oracle. An edge case is an input at the limit of a method's valid domain; methods rarely fail on typical data. For JARVIS: an empty list (mean, median, SD (Standard Deviation) raise ValueError); one element (mean and median return it; the sample SD (Standard Deviation) needs two); even and odd counts for the median; all values equal (SD (Standard Deviation) = 0, CV (Coefficient of Variation) = 0, fences collapse); a zero hourly value (break-even raises) and a zero saving (payback is math.inf). The oracle test: assert StatsEngine.std_dev(xs) == pytest.approx(statistics.stdev(xs)); the Brick 4 hand computation is a second oracle (S5 scheduling 14, 17, 12, 16, 16 → variance 4, SD (Standard Deviation) 2.00). The engine itself still never calls statistics.

Test first: red, green, refactor. Test-Driven Development (TDD): red — write one failing test for the next behaviour; green — write the simplest code that passes, run the whole suite; refactor — improve names and structure while every test stays green. The loop is mandatory for every bug: first a test that reproduces it (red), then the fix (green). In the workshop, ci.yml makes GitHub Actions install the pinned requirements and run python -m pytest -q on every push — continuous integration (CI); a red run marks the commit.

Exam angle · introductory Read a pytest progress line and exit code, put the three steps of a test in order, and recognise an edge case.

10.2

Tracebacks, the debugger, validation and the bug log

Exceptions and the traceback. When an operation cannot be completed, Python creates an exception (an object of a class such as ValueError or KeyError) at the line where the problem occurred; if no try/except handles it, the program stops and prints a traceback. A running program keeps a call stack with one frame per call that has started and not returned; the traceback lists the frames from the oldest (top) to the most recent (bottom), hence Traceback (most recent call last):. Each frame shows file, line, function and source; the last line names the exception and its message. Since Python 3.11 the failing expression is underlined with ^ and ~ (PEP (Python Enhancement Proposal) 657).

Read it from the bottom — four steps.

  1. Read the last line: type and message (ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '' — int() received the empty string).
  2. Read the frame just above: the statement that raised.
  3. Move up to the first frame in your own files (jarvis/…, analysis/…, your tests); frames inside Python or site-packages almost never contain the defect.
  4. Ask where the wrong value came from — data file → loader → parser → engine — until you find the first place that should have rejected it.
Exception Typical cause in JARVIS Where to fix it
ValueError int(""), int("17.0"), date.fromisoformat("2026/09/14") validate the field in the loader or parser
KeyError row["minute"] (misspelt column); unknown intent in the tool table check the header; clear reply for unknown intents
TypeError None + 1; text where a number is expected convert types at the boundary
AttributeError: 'NoneType' … a function returned None (fetchone() found no row, re.match() no match) test for None right after the call
FileNotFoundError relative path run from another folder build paths with pathlib
ZeroDivisionError mean of an empty group without a guard guard: raise ValueError with a message
sqlite3.OperationalError: no such table schema not created; wrong path created an empty file create the schema at start-up; check the path
json.JSONDecodeError an API (Application Programming Interface) answer that is not JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) catch it and fall back to the offline provider

The debugger. A debugger stops at a breakpoint before executing that line, shows every variable in every frame and executes one line at a time — the same frames as a traceback, but while the program is still running. breakpoint() (built in since Python 3.7, PEP (Python Enhancement Proposal) 553) opens pdb: n next line, s step into a call, c continue to the next breakpoint, p raw print an expression, l list source, w where (call stack), q quit. In VS Code (Visual Studio Code): red dot left of the line number, Run and Debug (F5), step over F10, into F11, out Shift+F11. Remove every breakpoint() before committing: a forgotten one stops the scheduled workflow, which has no keyboard.

Input validation at the boundary. Data from outside (a CSV (Comma-Separated Values) row, a typed command, an API (Application Programming Interface) answer) is checked for type, range and format at the boundary — the first function that receives it (loader, parser, provider). A good message names the place, the field, the rule and the value: line 4: minutes must be a whole number >= 0, got ''. After a rejection: one bad row in a batch → skip, count, report at the end (one typing error must not stop the morning brief); a bad configuration (no database file, no tests/ folder) → stop immediately with a clear message. The check is written as a guard clause: test the bad case first and leave the function before the normal path.

The bug log and the debugging loop. docs/buglog.md has one row per defect: ID (identifier) · date · symptom · cause · fix (with commit) · test · status. The symptom ("the morning brief stopped at 06:30") differs from the root cause ("the loader converted minutes with int() without checking for an empty cell"); fixing the symptom leaves the cause in place. A bug is closed only when a test reproduces it — red before the fix, green after; "fixed, but no test" stays open. The loop: reproduce → read the traceback → isolate (smallest failing input, debugger) → fix the cause at the boundary → prove (red then green) → log (commit the fix, the test and the log together).

Exam angle · introductory Say which line of a traceback you read first, explain what 'NoneType' object has no attribute means, and say when a bug-log entry may be closed.

10.3

The ApiProvider, the key and the scheduled workflow

One contract, two implementations. Provider has one method, parse(text) -> Intent. OfflineProvider uses regular expressions and a keyword table: deterministic, therefore testable. ApiProvider is a second subclass with the same method: it sends the text to a large language model (LLM) offered as a web service and asks for the intent and its arguments as JSON (JavaScript Object Notation). The Agent does not change: polymorphism.

One HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) request, four parts.

Part In the ApiProvider
method POST — send data to be processed
URL (Uniform Resource Locator) the provider's base URL (Uniform Resource Locator) followed by /chat/completions
headers Authorization: Bearer <key> and Content-Type: application/json
body a JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) object: model name, temperature 0, two messages (system instructions and the staff member's text)

Status codes to recognise: 200 success; 401 key refused; 429 Too Many Requests (rate limit exceeded, often with a Retry-After header); 5xx an error on the provider's server. "OpenAI-compatible" means the provider accepts the Chat Completions request format, so one class works with several providers by changing the base URL (Uniform Resource Locator) and model name (Groq (https://console.groq.com/docs/openaiVirusTotal): https://api.groq.com/openai/v1; Gemini API (Application Programming Interface) (https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/openaiVirusTotal): https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/openai/). The model's text is at data["choices"][0]["message"]["content"], decoded with json.loads. Temperature 0 reduces variation but does not make the model deterministic — one more reason tests and the Mid-Term use the offline provider. With the standard library: urllib.request.Request(...) and urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=10); status ≥ 400 raises HTTPError, no network raises URLError, no answer in time raises TimeoutError.

The fallback rule. Any failure returns the OfflineProvider's answer: no key (no request sent at all), HTTPError (401, 429, 5xx), URLError, TimeoutError, json.JSONDecodeError, KeyError or ValueError (missing fields, unknown intent). Every run is logged with provider = "api" or "offline". A fallback is a planned, tested path, not an error; it implements the Brick 2 NFR (Non-Functional Requirement) "works with no key and no network". Free tiers limit requests per minute (RPM), requests per day (RPD) and tokens per minute (TPM); a token is a piece of a word, the unit in which models count text. Exceeding any limit returns 429. Limits change, so read the provider's page the week you connect and record the numbers with the date: they are inputs to the break-even model. GitHub Models (https://docs.github.com/en/github-modelsVirusTotal) was fully retired on July 30, 2026: use Groq or the Gemini API (Application Programming Interface).

The key never enters the repository. An API (Application Programming Interface) key identifies your account; anyone who has it can spend your quota. Never in code, a committed file, a screenshot or the report. On your computer it lives in an environment variable (os.environ.get("JARVIS_API_KEY"), which returns None when unset), set in the terminal or in a git-ignored .env. On GitHub it is a repository secret (Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions), passed to one step with env: JARVIS_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.JARVIS_API_KEY }}; secrets are not passed to workflows triggered by pull requests from forks. A key committed once stays in the Git history: create a new key and delete the old one the same day (rotating the key).

jarvis.yml, line by line. A workflow is a YAML (YAML Ain't Markup Language) file in .github/workflows/ that tells GitHub Actions (https://docs.github.com/en/actionsVirusTotal) when to run a job on a fresh virtual machine (a runner).

  • When: schedule: - cron: '30 11 * * 1-5' — five fields (minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week): minute 30 of hour 11, Monday to Friday. GitHub evaluates schedules in UTC (Coordinated Universal Time), so the run starts at 06:30 in Montréal in winter (EST (Eastern Standard Time), UTC (Coordinated Universal Time)−5) and 07:30 in summer (EDT (Eastern Daylight Time), UTC (Coordinated Universal Time)−4). Scheduled runs may start late when GitHub is busy (another reason for minute 30); the shortest interval is 5 minutes. workflow_dispatch: adds a Run workflow button for testing.
  • Rights: permissions: contents: write lets the built-in GITHUB_TOKEN push a commit; without it the final push is rejected.
  • What: checkout → setup-python 3.12 → pip install -r requirements.txt → python -m jarvis brief (the step that receives the secret) → python -m jarvis report.
  • Commit-back: author github-actions[bot]; stage data/ and docs/; git diff --cached --quiet || git commit -m 'jarvis: morning brief [skip ci]' (|| commits only when something is staged, so a quiet day does not fail on an empty commit); git push.
  • No loop: [skip ci] tells GitHub to skip push-triggered workflows for that commit, and events caused by GITHUB_TOKEN do not create new runs (except workflow_dispatch and repository_dispatch) — two independent protections.
  • Keep it alive: in a public repository GitHub disables scheduled workflows after 60 days without activity; the bot's daily commit counts as activity. The one-writer rule still applies.

The dashboard on GitHub Pages (https://docs.github.com/en/pages/getting-started-with-github-pages/configuring-a-publishing-source-for-your-github-pages-siteVirusTotal). python -m jarvis report writes docs/dashboard.html; Pages can publish the docs/ folder (Settings → Pages → branch main, folder /docs). On GitHub Free, Pages works only for public repositories (private ones need GitHub Pro, part of the free Student Developer Pack), or the team copies only the dashboard to a separate public repository. The dashboard shows aggregated numbers only.

Exam angle · introductory Name the four parts of an HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) request, state the fallback rule, explain where the key lives, and translate the cron line into a local time.

10.4

From results to a decision, the report and the sprints

Result, discussion, conclusion. A result is a number or table with its evidence (data, method, n) and its limits. A discussion interprets results for the reader (what they mean for the owner, whether they match expectations, what could make them wrong). A conclusion answers one research question in one or two sentences using only results already presented — no new data or analysis.

Which chart answers which question.

Question type Chart JARVIS example
compare categories bar chart, bars sorted, axis from zero monthly cost per routine, for RQ1 (Research Question 1)
change over time line chart, time on the horizontal axis mean e-mail minutes per day, pilot and comparison group
relationship between two numeric variables scatter plot with the fitted line interruptions and minutes of stand-up notes
effect of a change before/after bars for changed and comparison groups e-mail triage before and after the pilot, for RQ3 (Research Question 3)

Four rules: one message per chart; axis titles with units; a numbered caption (APA (American Psychological Association): Figure 3 plus a short italic title); a sentence in the text that cites it ("As Figure 3 shows, …"). A chart the text never mentions is removed. Public charts use aggregated numbers only.

The numbers behind the decision.

RQ (Research Question) Result Evidence
RQ1 (Research Question 1) e-mail triage is the most expensive routine: 1 640.12 $ per month, 28.2 % of 5 821.45 $ mean minutes × 100 runs × 28 $/h ÷ 60
RQ1 (Research Question 1) stand-up notes vary the most: CV (Coefficient of Variation) 26.4 % sample SD (Standard Deviation) ÷ mean of manual runs
RQ2 (Research Question 2) an hour is worth 28 $; the paid tier breaks even at 0.714 h = 43 min per user per month; set-up pays back in 1.23 months Chapter 3 formulas
RQ3 (Research Question 3) pilot S1–S3: 35.85 → 13.73 min (−22.12); comparison S4–S5: 34.67 → 34.10 (−0.57) 14 days, n = 27 → 15 and 18 → 10 runs

The comparison group's change estimates what would have happened without the assistant. Difference of the changes: (−22.12) − (−0.57) = −21.55 minutes per run — the design economists call difference-in-differences (DiD) (https://learn.mru.org/lessons/introduction-differences-differencesVirusTotal). Expected impact: 21.55 − 2.00 minutes of review = 19.55 minutes per run; × 100 runs = 1 955 minutes = 32.6 hours per month; × 28 $/h ≈ 912 $ per month.

The six-part recommendation. Class 7's four parts plus impact and alternatives: Finding (assistant-triaged e-mail took 21.55 minutes less per run than the comparison group's change) · Evidence (14 working days; pilot 27 runs before, 15 after; comparison 18 and 10) · Decision (automate e-mail triage first, for all five staff, on the free tier with the offline fallback) · Impact (about 32.6 hours and 912 $ per month after a 2-minute review) · Risk (14 days and five people; a possible novelty effect; the free tier's daily quota — the fallback keeps the brief running; no message text stored) · Alternatives (the paid tier is justified only if it saves more than 43 minutes per user per month beyond the free tier; doing nothing keeps about 1 640 $ per month of manual triage). A decision without a number is an opinion; a number without a decision is not yet a recommendation.

The technical report (at least 8 pages including figures): Title · Abstract (at most 150 words, written last) · 1 Introduction and Problem · 2 Requirements · 3 Method · 4 Design · 5 Implementation · 6 Testing · 7 Results · 8 Discussion and Recommendation · 9 Conclusion · References (APA (American Psychological Association) 7 (https://apastyle.apa.org/VirusTotal)) · Appendices (testing log, code-review evidence, Actions run history, data sheets). Nothing is written from zero:

Brick Report section
1 Kick-off Pack title page, team, first problem statement
2 Requirements and Research Proposal §1, §2, References
3 Economic Analysis Script §3 Method (economics), Appendix
4 Statistical Analysis Script §3 Method (statistics)
5 Design Pack + Loader §4 Design
6 Alpha Engines + Store §5 Implementation
7 Alpha Demo + Agent v0 §5 Implementation, §7 Results (first)
Mid-Term (corrected Part A) §7 Results, §4 Design
9 Tests + Report Skeleton §6 Testing, whole skeleton
10 Sprint 1 §6 Testing, Appendix (bug log, code review)
11 Sprint 2 §7 Results, §8 Discussion and Recommendation
12 Sprint 3 all sections (full draft)

Academic honesty and generative AI (Artificial Intelligence). Cite textbooks, articles, documentation pages, reused code (address and licence), datasets and generative AI (Artificial Intelligence). Since September 2025 the APA (American Psychological Association) Style team (https://apastyle.apa.org/blog/cite-generative-ai-referencesVirusTotal) recommends referencing a specific AI (Artificial Intelligence) chat: Company. (Year, Month Day). Title of the chat [Generative AI (Artificial Intelligence) chat]. Tool or model. URL (Uniform Resource Locator) of the chat. When AI (Artificial Intelligence) only helped find sources, cite the sources it found. Describe in §3 Method how and where AI (Artificial Intelligence) assistance was used.

What the Final grades and the three sprints. Five rubric dimensions: Methodology · Tech Implementation · Analytical Rigor · Lab Proficiency · Communication; suggested split of the 40 %: report 15 · working assistant and codebase 15 · demonstration and presentation 10. Sprints are supervised work sessions (no new lecture; a Sprint Brief posted the Wednesday before; a Q&A (Questions and Answers) board; a checkpoint submission at 2:45):

Sprint Date Goal Brick · tag
Sprint 1 Fri Dec 4 tests, error resolution and going live Brick 10 · Thu Dec 10 · beta-0.2
Sprint 2 Fri Dec 11 results, charts and conclusions Brick 11 · Thu Dec 17 · beta-0.3
Sprint 3 Fri Dec 18 report draft and peer review Brick 12 · Sun Dec 20 · rc-1.0

Then: winter break (December 21 – January 8), Final Review (January 15), submission (Thursday, January 21, 23:59, tag v1.0-final), Product Defense (Friday, January 22).

Exam angle · introductory Tell a result from a conclusion, pick the chart for a question, compute a difference of the changes and the monthly impact, and list the six parts of the recommendation.

Part B

Twenty case studies with model answers

1:25–2:05

Each case is a twin of an exam question: new numbers, the same method. Solve it on paper with your two cards only, then open the model answer.

Case 1

Léa's grade path

Chapter 1 · 1.3 Course map, grading and the Brick system
Situation

Léa is a student of CS (Computer Science) 251. At the end of the semester her record shows nine Bricks graded Complete, two graded Partial and one Missing. She scores 72/100 on the Mid-Term and 88/100 on the Product Defense.

Tasks
  1. Compute her points for the continuous assessment, the Mid-Term and the Final.
  2. Compute her final percentage and read her letter grade on the course scale.
  3. Recompute the grade if the missing Brick had been submitted complete. What changes?
  4. Explain why a missing Brick must still be submitted after its due date.
Model answer
  1. Continuous assessment: 9 × 2.5 + 2 × 1.25 + 1 × 0 = 22.5 + 2.5 + 0 = 25.0 points (out of 30). Mid-Term: 72 × 0.30 = 21.6 points. Final: 88 × 0.40 = 35.2 points.
  2. Total: 25.0 + 21.6 + 35.2 = 81.8 % → band 80–82 → B−.
  3. With the twelfth Brick complete: 27.5 + 21.6 + 35.2 = 84.3 % → band 83–86 → B. One Brick (2.5 points) moves her a full letter step.
  4. The Bricks assemble into JARVIS and into the technical report, and the Mid-Term is written on the same basis (Bricks 1 to 7). A missing Brick scores 0, but the work is still needed for the exam, for the report sections it feeds, and for the team's product; the late policy is announced on the LMS (Learning Management System).
Case 2

From a complaint to research questions at Atelier Lumen

Chapter 2 · 2.1 From a business problem to a research problem
Situation

Atelier Lumen is a fictional four-person architecture office in Québec City. The owner writes: "Timesheets take forever, the weekly client update is always late, and a vendor offers a scheduling assistant at 15 $ per user per month. Before I sign, I want to know what to automate first." The office could log its routines for 14 working days in a file with the same nine columns as Boréal Studio's. The given hourly value is 32 $ per hour.

Tasks
  1. Write a problem statement of at most 150 words that names the situation, the decision and the evidence.
  2. Divide the problem into three sub-problems, one per course.
  3. Write one research question per sub-problem and check it with the four checks.
  4. Two colleagues propose "Is the assistant worth it?" and "How can the office become more efficient?". Reject each one by naming the check it fails.
Model answer
  1. Model problem statement (about 80 words): "Atelier Lumen, a four-person architecture office in Québec City, spends part of every working day on recurring routines such as timesheets and the weekly client update. The owner must decide which routine to automate first and whether an assistant at 15 $ per user per month is justified. This project measures how long each routine takes over 14 working days, prices that time at 32 $ per hour, and compares the time an assistant saves with its cost, in order to recommend what to automate first."
  2. Sub-problems: Microeconomics — what does each routine cost per month at 32 $/h, and what does each option (do nothing, free tool, paid tier) cost? Statistics — how long does each routine take, and how much does it vary? Python and OOP (Object-Oriented Programming) — how can an assistant run one routine and measure the minutes it saves?
  3. Research questions: RQ1 (Research Question 1), Statistics: "Which routines take the most minutes per run, and which vary the most?" RQ2 (Research Question 2), Microeconomics: "What does each routine cost per month at 32 $ per hour, and how many saved hours per user per month make the 15 $ tier worth paying?" RQ3 (Research Question 3), integration: "Which routine should the assistant automate first, how many minutes per run does it save, and with what risk?" Each is open (not yes/no), names something measurable (minutes, dollars, hours), belongs to one sub-problem and can be answered with 14 days of data before the deadline.
  4. "Is the assistant worth it?" fails check 1 (it can be answered yes or no) and check 2 ("worth it" names nothing measurable). "How can the office become more efficient?" is open but fails check 2: "efficient" has no unit in the data. Its measurable version is RQ1 (Research Question 1) or RQ2 (Research Question 2).
Case 3

Six interview statements become requirements

Chapter 2 · 2.2 Requirements analysis
Situation

After a 20-minute interview, a team wrote six statements about its assistant:

  1. "The assistant shall export the weekly hours per routine to a CSV (Comma-Separated Values) file."
  2. "The assistant shall start in under 3 seconds on the lab computer."
  3. "The app should be user-friendly."
  4. "The assistant shall keep working when the network is down."
  5. "The assistant shall add a task with a due date from one command."
  6. "The assistant shall store no message text."
Tasks
  1. Classify each statement as functional or non-functional.
  2. Which statement cannot be verified as written? Rewrite it as one or two verifiable requirements.
  3. Write a user story for statement 5 and two acceptance criteria in Given / When / Then form.
  4. Explain the difference between "shall" and "should".
Model answer
  1. Functional (behaviours): 1 (export) and 5 (add a task). Non-functional (qualities or constraints): 2 (performance), 3 (usability), 4 (works without network — the offline rule), 6 (a privacy constraint on how data is stored).
  2. Statement 3 cannot be verified: "user-friendly" has no threshold, and "should" marks a wish. Verifiable rewrites: "A new user shall add a first task within 5 minutes, using only the README" and "Every error message shall show the expected command format."
  3. Story: "As a staff member, I want to add a task with a due date in one command, so that I do not forget deadlines." Criterion 1: Given an empty task list, when I type add task call the accountant due 2026-11-25, then one task is stored with that title and due date 2026-11-25. Criterion 2: Given an empty task list, when I type add task call the accountant due tomorrowish, then nothing is stored and the reply shows the expected date format yyyy-mm-dd.
  4. In ISO/IEC/IEEE (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission / Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 29148, shall marks a binding requirement that must be met and tested; should marks a goal or a wish. A statement with "should" and no threshold is not yet a requirement.
Case 4

Scoring four objectives against the team's capacity

Chapter 2 · 2.3 Scope, SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) objectives and project selection
Situation

A team of two students works 4 hours per week each (2 h in the workshop, 2 h at home). It drafts four objectives:

# Objective as drafted Hours estimated Serves Due
A Make the dashboard beautiful. — — —
B Compute the coefficient of variation of minutes per routine for the 14-day log by October 22. 6 RQ1 (Research Question 1) Oct 22 (2 weeks away)
C Add voice commands and calendar synchronisation by December 18. 150 RQ3 (Research Question 3) Dec 18 (11 weeks away)
D Compute the break-even hours of the paid tier by October 15. 5 RQ2 (Research Question 2) Oct 15 (1 week away)

The team also wrote four sentences: (i) "The free API (Application Programming Interface) quota will not change before January." (ii) "The project is written in Python only." (iii) "The fourteen logged days are typical working days." (iv) "The database file stays under 1 MB (megabyte)."

Tasks
  1. Compute the team's capacity before each due date.
  2. Score each objective letter by letter (S, M, A, R, T) and give a verdict.
  3. Rewrite the objectives that fail.
  4. Classify sentences (i) to (iv) as assumptions or constraints.
Model answer
  1. Capacity = 2 members × 4 h = 8 h per week: 16 h before October 22; 8 h before October 15; 88 h before December 18.
  2. A fails all five letters: no deliverable, no measure, no estimate, no research question, no date → rewrite. B is Specific (CV (Coefficient of Variation) per routine), Measurable (a number per routine), Achievable (6 h ≤ 16 h), Relevant to RQ1 (Research Question 1) and Time-bound → SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound). C is Specific, Measurable, Relevant and Time-bound but fails Achievable twice: voice and calendar services are outside the course constraints and delimitations (and real calendars expose personal data), and 150 h > 88 h → rewrite. D passes all five (5 h ≤ 8 h; RQ2 (Research Question 2); dated) → SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound).
  3. A → "By November 6, the console report prints the mean, SD (Standard Deviation) and monthly cost of each routine in aligned columns." C → "By November 6, JARVIS adds a task with a due date from one typed command, offline." Both pass the January test: they can be demonstrated on January 22.
  4. (i) assumption (treated as true without proof; if the quota changes, the break-even model changes — record the quota with its date); (ii) constraint; (iii) assumption; (iv) constraint (the tiny-database rule).
Case 5

Building a reference list with CRAAP (Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose) and APA (American Psychological Association) 7

Chapter 2 · 2.4 References and experts
Situation

A team considers five sources for Brick 2:

  1. The OpenStax (https://openstax.org/VirusTotal) textbook Introductory statistics (2nd edition), by Barbara Illowsky and Susan Dean, 2023.
  2. A vendor's landing page titled "Our bot saves you 10 hours a week!", with no author and a "Buy now" button.
  3. The Python documentation (https://docs.python.org/3/VirusTotal) page csv — CSV (Comma-Separated Values) File Reading and Writing, which has no date and is updated regularly; the team read it on November 14, 2026.
  4. An undated forum post signed "codeguy99" claiming that the median is always better than the mean.
  5. Leedy and Ormrod (https://www.pearson.com/en-us/subject-catalog/p/practical-research-planning-and-design/P200000001398VirusTotal), Practical research: Planning and design, 12th edition, Pearson Education, 2019.
Tasks
  1. Apply the CRAAP (Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose) test to each source and give a verdict.
  2. Write the APA (American Psychological Association) 7 reference of every kept source and sort the list.
  3. Write the in-text citation of each kept source.
  4. What should the team do with a useful idea that appears only in a rejected source?
Model answer
  1. Source 1 passes all five questions → keep. Source 2 may be Relevant but fails Authority (no author), Accuracy (no evidence) and Purpose (it sells) → reject. Source 3 is current (maintained), relevant, authoritative (the Python Software Foundation (https://www.python.org/psf/VirusTotal)), accurate and informative → keep, with a retrieval date. Source 4 fails Currency (no date), Authority (anonymous) and Accuracy (an absolute claim without evidence, and false: the choice depends on the shape of the data) → reject. Source 5 passes → keep.

  2. Sorted alphabetically by first author:

    • Illowsky, B., & Dean, S. (2023). Introductory statistics (2nd ed.). OpenStax. https://openstax.org/details/books/introductory-statistics-2e
    • Leedy, P. D., & Ormrod, J. E. (2019). Practical research: Planning and design (12th ed.). Pearson Education.
    • Python Software Foundation. (n.d.). csv — CSV (Comma-Separated Values) File Reading and Writing. Python documentation. Retrieved November 14, 2026, from https://docs.python.org/3/library/csv.html 3. (Illowsky & Dean, 2023) · (Leedy & Ormrod, 2019) · (Python Software Foundation, n.d.). 4. Look for a credible source (a textbook, an official documentation page, a peer-reviewed article) that supports the idea, read it, and cite that source instead. Brick 2 also needs at least five sources, so a fifth credible one must be added.
Case 6

Eight rows checked against the data dictionary

Chapter 2 · 2.5 The data dictionary and personal data
Situation

Before the loader exists, eight rows arrive by e-mail (five of the nine columns shown):

Row date staff_id routine start_hour minutes
1 2026-09-15 S2 scheduling 10 14
2 2026-09-15 S3 invoice_check 14 (empty)
3 15/09/2026 S1 social_post 11 20
4 2026-09-15 S4 standup_notes 9 −3
5 2026-09-15 S5 Daily_Report 16 25
6 2026-09-15 S2 scheduling 10 14
7 2026-09-15 Marc Tremblay email_triage 8 30
8 2026-09-15 S3 email_triage 25 30

A teammate also proposes done = bool(row["done"]) in the loader.

Tasks
  1. Classify the problem of each row by the four checks (completeness, validity, consistency, uniqueness) or as a privacy risk.
  2. Give the Python type and the conversion of date, minutes and done.
  3. What is wrong with the teammate's line?
  4. Are the codes S1–S5 anonymized or de-identified? What does that mean for the repository?
Model answer
  1. Row 1: correct. Row 2: completeness (missing minutes). Row 3: validity (date not in yyyy-mm-dd). Row 4: validity (negative duration). Row 5: consistency (not on the agreed list — the dictionary says daily_report in lowercase). Row 6: uniqueness (repeats row 1 — same date, staff, routine and start hour). Row 7: privacy risk (a real name where a code is expected; the loader must accept only S1–S5). Row 8: validity (hour 25 outside 0–23).
  2. date → datetime.date, date.fromisoformat("2026-09-15"); minutes → int, int("14"); done → bool, row["done"] == "1".
  3. bool("0") is True, because every non-empty text is true in Python, so unfinished runs would be counted as done. The comparison row["done"] == "1" is the correct conversion.
  4. De-identified: a code replaces the name, but the person can still be linked back (the team knows who S3 is). De-identified data remains personal information, so the raw logs stay in the private repository, the codes table is never committed, and public pages show aggregated numbers only.
Case 7

The monthly cost of the invoice check

Chapter 3 · 3.1 Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost
Situation

In a twin of the studio file, a manual invoice check takes 21 minutes per run. Each of the five staff members runs it once per working day; a month has 20 working days. The loaded hourly value is 28 $/h. A consultant's hour could be billed to a client at 65 $/h.

Tasks
  1. Compute the runs per month, the hours per month and the monthly cost of the routine.
  2. Compute the opportunity cost of the same hours at the billable rate.
  3. Explain why both numbers are correct and which question each one answers.
  4. Why must the hourly value be a parameter of routine_cost() rather than a number written inside it?
Model answer
  1. Runs per month = 5 × 20 = 100. Hours = 21 × 100 ÷ 60 = 35 h per month. Cost = 21 ÷ 60 × 28 × 100 = 980 $ per month.
  2. Opportunity cost = 35 h × 65 $/h = 2 275 $ per month of client work given up.
  3. 980 $ is the explicit (loaded) cost: what the hours cost the studio in salary and overhead. 2 275 $ is the opportunity cost: the value of the next-best use of the same hours. The first answers "what do we pay for this routine?"; the second answers "what do we give up by doing it by hand?". An opportunity cost is always relative to a named alternative.
  4. The hourly value is an input that can change (28 $, 32 $, 65 $ answer different questions). As a parameter, the same method answers "what if" questions without editing code, and the assumption stays visible instead of hidden in a formula.
Case 8

Which of three routines should JARVIS automate first?

Chapter 3 · 3.2 Marginal analysis
Situation

Three candidates run 100 times per month each. The hourly value is 28 $/h; set-up hours are valued at 28 $/h and spread over a 12-month horizon; all requests stay inside the free quota.

Candidate Net minutes saved per run Set-up hours
A — scheduling 4 18
B — daily report 8 30
C — invoice check the tool saves 4 min, but a person must review each flagged invoice for 6 min 20
Tasks
  1. Compute MB (marginal benefit), MC (marginal cost) and the net benefit of each candidate.
  2. Apply the MB (marginal benefit) ≥ MC (marginal cost) rule and rank the candidates that pass.
  3. If all candidates passed, why would the ranking still matter?
  4. Automation of B can be pushed one level further (sending reports without review) with an extra MB (marginal benefit) of 60 $/month and an extra MC (marginal cost) of 75 $/month. Decide.
Model answer
  1. A: MB (marginal benefit) = 4 ÷ 60 × 28 × 100 = 186.67 $; MC (marginal cost) = 18 × 28 ÷ 12 = 42.00 $; net = 144.67 $/month. B: MB (marginal benefit) = 8 ÷ 60 × 28 × 100 = 373.33 $; MC (marginal cost) = 30 × 28 ÷ 12 = 70.00 $; net = 303.33 $/month. C: net minutes = 4 − 6 = −2 → MB (marginal benefit) = −93.33 $; MC (marginal cost) = 20 × 28 ÷ 12 = 46.67 $; net = −140.00 $/month.
  2. A and B pass (MB (marginal benefit) ≥ MC (marginal cost)); C fails and stays manual for now. Ranking by net benefit: 1. B (daily report), 2. A (scheduling).
  3. Because of diminishing returns and limited capacity: each additional tool returns less, while it costs the same effort. With fifteen Fridays, the team builds the largest net benefit first; three tools that work beat ten that do not.
  4. Judge the level on its own increment: 60 $ < 75 $ → stop at the previous level. Sending without review also carries a risk the numbers do not show (a report sent with an error).
Case 9

Free tier or paid tier as the volume grows — and a sunk-cost trap

Chapter 3 · 3.3 Fixed, variable, total, average and marginal cost; the sunk cost
Situation

For a twin studio, the free tier has a quota of 2 000 requests per month and costs 0.03 $ per request beyond it. The paid tier costs 90 $ per month for three seats, whatever the volume. One routine run uses 3 requests. The team has already spent 30 hours (840 $ at 28 $/h) building its tool. The tool's measured benefit is 600 $ per month, and it needs 1 hour of maintenance (28 $) per month.

Tasks
  1. Compute the total cost of each option at 1 500, 4 000 and 6 000 requests per month.
  2. Compute the average cost per run of each option at 4 000 requests.
  3. Find the volume at which the two options cost the same, and state the marginal cost per request inside and beyond the quota.
  4. A teammate says: "600 − 28 − 840 = −268 $: the tool loses money, stop it." Correct the reasoning.
Model answer
  1. Free: 1 500 → 0 $ (inside the quota); 4 000 → (4 000 − 2 000) × 0.03 = 60 $; 6 000 → 4 000 × 0.03 = 120 $. Paid: 90 $ at every volume.
  2. 4 000 requests = 1 333 runs. Free: 60 ÷ 1 333 ≈ 0.045 $ per run. Paid: 90 ÷ 1 333 ≈ 0.068 $ per run.
  3. Equal cost when (requests − 2 000) × 0.03 = 90 → requests = 2 000 + 90 ÷ 0.03 = 5 000 requests per month. Below 5 000 the free tier costs less; above, the paid tier does. Marginal cost per request: 0 $ inside the quota, 0.03 $ beyond it (the kink of the total cost curve is at 2 000).
  4. The 840 $ is a sunk cost: it is spent whether the tool continues or stops, so it must not enter the decision. Looking forward: continue = 600 − 28 = +572 $ per month; stop = 0 $. The tool should continue. The set-up belongs in the payback computation (840 ÷ 572 ≈ 1.47 months), not in the monthly decision.
Case 10

Break-even, payback and make-or-buy for a four-person office

Chapter 3 · 3.4 Break-even, payback and make-or-buy
Situation

A four-person office values staff time at 30 $/h. A paid assistant costs 25 $ per user per month. A pilot shows 15 net minutes saved per run, with 20 runs per user per month. Building the office's own tool takes 36 hours of set-up (valued at 30 $/h) and 1 hour of maintenance per month.

Tasks
  1. Compute the break-even hours of one paid seat and of the four seats.
  2. Compare the hours the pilot saves per user per month with the break-even.
  3. Compute the set-up cost, the monthly net saving of the built tool for the office and the payback in months.
  4. Compare build and buy over 12 and 24 months; find the horizon at which they cost the same.
  5. What do break_even_hours(25, 0) and payback_months(1080, 0) return in the course engine, and why?
Model answer
  1. One seat: 25 ÷ 30 = 0.833 h = 50 minutes per user per month. Four seats: 100 ÷ 30 = 3.33 h per month.
  2. Saved per user: 15 × 20 ÷ 60 = 5 h per month — six times the break-even. Any assistant that performs like the pilot pays for its seat; the choice depends on fit and risk.
  3. Set-up = 36 × 30 = 1 080 $. Benefit for the office: 4 × 20 = 80 runs × 15 ÷ 60 × 30 = 600 $ per month; minus maintenance 30 $ → 570 $ per month net. Payback = 1 080 ÷ 570 ≈ 1.89 months.
  4. 12 months: build = 1 080 + 30 × 12 = 1 440 $; buy = 100 × 12 = 1 200 $ → buy is cheaper. 24 months: build = 1 080 + 720 = 1 800 $; buy = 2 400 $ → build is cheaper. Equal when 1 080 + 30m = 100m → m = 1 080 ÷ 70 ≈ 15.4 months.
  5. break_even_hours(25, 0) raises ValueError ("hourly value must be > 0"): an hourly value of zero is an impossible input. payback_months(1080, 0) returns math.inf: a tool that saves nothing is a real possibility, and "never recovered" is the honest, documented answer.
Case 11

A typical e-mail morning with a Monday backlog

Chapter 4 · 4.1 Central tendency
Situation

S4's e-mail triage minutes for one week: Monday 92, Tuesday 34, Wednesday 31, Thursday 36, Friday 32. The interruptions of the same runs were 4, 2, 0, 2, 1.

Tasks
  1. Compute the mean, the median and the range of the minutes.
  2. Recompute the mean and the median without Monday. Which one moved more, and why?
  3. Compute the mode of the interruptions.
  4. Which value should the owner write in her planning sheet as the typical slot? Which value should a monthly cost use?
Model answer
  1. Σx = 225, n = 5 → mean = 45.0 min. Sorted: 31, 32, 34, 36, 92 → median = 34 min. Range = 92 − 31 = 61 min.
  2. Without Monday: mean = 133 ÷ 4 = 33.25 min; median = (32 + 34) ÷ 2 = 33 min. The mean moved by 11.75 minutes, the median by 1 minute: the median is resistant to one extreme value because it depends on order, not on distance; the mean uses every value.
  3. Interruptions 4, 2, 0, 2, 1 → the value 2 occurs twice → mode = 2.
  4. For the typical day, the median (34 min), because one backlog day pulls the mean up; report the mean beside it with the reason. A monthly total multiplies the per-run value by the number of runs, and Σx = n × x̄ exactly, so the cost uses the mean — after checking with the median that the mean is not driven by a few long days.
Case 12

Two routines, two spreads, two rankings

Chapter 4 · 4.2 Dispersion
Situation

Five runs of two routines (minutes):

  • social posts: 18, 22, 20, 25, 15
  • stand-up notes: 8, 12, 9, 14, 7
Tasks
  1. Compute the mean, the deviations, the sum of squares, the sample variance and the sample standard deviation of each routine.
  2. Compute the coefficient of variation of each routine.
  3. Which routine needs the larger time buffer, and which is less predictable? Why can both answers be right?
  4. Propose a planning slot equal to ⌈mean + 1 SD (Standard Deviation)⌉ for each routine.
  5. What would statistics.pstdev give for the social posts, and why is it smaller?
Model answer
  1. Social posts: mean 20; deviations −2, +2, 0, +5, −5; sum of squares 4 + 4 + 0 + 25 + 25 = 58; s² = 58 ÷ 4 = 14.5; s = 3.81 min. Stand-up notes: mean 10; deviations −2, +2, −1, +4, −3; sum of squares 4 + 4 + 1 + 16 + 9 = 34; s² = 34 ÷ 4 = 8.5; s = 2.92 min.
  2. CV (Coefficient of Variation) social = 3.81 ÷ 20 = 19.0 %; CV (Coefficient of Variation) stand-up = 2.92 ÷ 10 = 29.2 %.
  3. Social posts have the larger SD (Standard Deviation) → the larger buffer in minutes. Stand-up notes have the larger CV (Coefficient of Variation) → the less predictable process relative to its length. The SD (Standard Deviation) answers "how many minutes of buffer?"; the CV (Coefficient of Variation) answers "how predictable compared with its size?".
  4. Social posts: ⌈20 + 3.81⌉ = 24 min. Stand-up notes: ⌈10 + 2.92⌉ = 13 min.
  5. pstdev divides by n: √(58 ÷ 5) = 3.41 min. It is the population formula; the studio's runs are a sample, so the course uses n − 1 (stdev), which corrects the underestimate caused by measuring deviations from the sample's own mean.
Case 13

Eleven daily reports and one unusual run

Chapter 4 · 4.3 Distributions and outliers
Situation

Eleven manual daily-report runs, already sorted (minutes): 22, 25, 26, 27, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31, 33, 48. Their mean is 29.64 and their sample SD (Standard Deviation) is 6.79.

Tasks
  1. Build a frequency table with 5-minute bins starting at 20 (lower limit included) and describe the shape.
  2. Compute Q1 (first quartile), the median and Q3 (third quartile) with the inclusive method, then the IQR (Interquartile Range).
  3. Compute the 1.5 × IQR (Interquartile Range) fences and the mean ± 2 SD (Standard Deviation) interval. Which runs does each rule flag?
  4. The 48-minute run happened on the day a client changed the brief. What should the team do with it?
Model answer
  1. Bins: 20–24: 1 · 25–29: 6 · 30–34: 3 · 35–39: 0 · 40–44: 0 · 45–49: 1 (total 11). Most runs lie between 25 and 34, with one run far out on the right: a right-skewed shape, and the mean (29.64) is above the median.
  2. Positions (n − 1) × p with n − 1 = 10: Q1 (first quartile) at 2.5 → between 26 and 27 → Q1 (first quartile) = 26.5; median at 5 → 28; Q3 (third quartile) at 7.5 → between 30 and 31 → Q3 (third quartile) = 30.5. IQR (Interquartile Range) = 30.5 − 26.5 = 4 min.
  3. Fences: 26.5 − 1.5 × 4 = 20.5 and 30.5 + 6 = 36.5 → 48 is flagged. Mean ± 2 SD (Standard Deviation): 29.64 ± 13.58 → [16.06, 43.21] → 48 is flagged too. Here the two rules agree; on the e-mail data of the class they did not, which is why the rule must be stated before looking.
  4. A flagged value is a question, not a mistake. The log explains it (a changed brief), so it is a real run: keep it (the default), and report the result with and without it if it changes a conclusion. Correct it only if it were a proven typing error, recorded in the bug log. Never delete it silently: that would make the routine look cheaper and more predictable than it is.
Case 14

Reading correlations and measuring a pilot with a comparison group

Chapter 4 · 4.4 Relationships, groups and the limits of 14 days
Situation

A twin studio reports three correlations (manual runs, 14 working days): interruptions and minutes for scheduling, r = +0.62 (n = 70); interruptions and minutes for invoice checks, r = +0.08 (n = 70); start hour and minutes for social posts, r = −0.35 (n = 70). It also tested a new invoice tool with S1 and S2 from day 10, while S3 to S5 stayed manual:

Group Days 1–9 Days 10–14
S1–S2 (pilot) 22.4 min (n = 18) 14.9 min (n = 10)
S3–S5 (comparison) 21.8 min (n = 27) 21.2 min (n = 15)

A person still spends 1 minute checking each assisted run; the routine runs 100 times per month; staff time is worth 28 $/h.

Tasks
  1. Interpret each correlation with its sign and strength, using the course convention.
  2. Compute the change of each group and the difference of the changes.
  3. Compute the expected impact in hours and dollars per month.
  4. Write the two-sentence interpretation (number, then limit) of the pilot.
Model answer
  1. +0.62: moderate positive — runs with more interruptions tend to take longer. +0.08: negligible — no linear relationship in this sample. −0.35: moderate negative — later starts tend to go with shorter runs. None of them proves a cause; a confounder such as the day of the week can influence both variables.
  2. Pilot: 14.9 − 22.4 = −7.5 min. Comparison: 21.2 − 21.8 = −0.6 min. Difference of the changes: (−7.5) − (−0.6) = −6.9 min per run (the estimated effect of the tool).
  3. Net saving = 6.9 − 1.0 = 5.9 min per run → × 100 = 590 min = 9.83 h per month → × 28 $/h ≈ 275 $ per month.
  4. "From day 10, the two pilot staff members' invoice checks took 6.9 minutes less per run than the change observed in the comparison group (22.4 → 14.9 minutes, n = 18 → 10; comparison 21.8 → 21.2, n = 27 → 15). The result rests on 10 assisted runs by two people over five days, so it may include a novelty effect and should be confirmed with a longer log."
Case 15

TimeEntry under pressure

Chapter 5 · 5.1 Classes, objects and the dataclass
Situation

The team's model is the frozen dataclass TimeEntry of the course (nine fields) with a __post_init__ that refuses negative minutes, a start hour outside 0–23 and a tool outside {"manual", "template", "jarvis"}, a property hours and a method cost(self, hourly_value). A teammate runs the following lines one after the other:

e = TimeEntry(date(2026, 9, 14), "S1", "email_triage", "communication", 9, 36, 1, "manual", True)
print(e.hours, e.cost(28.0))
bad = TimeEntry(date(2026, 9, 14), "S2", "invoice_check", "finance", 14, -19, 0, "manual", True)
e.minutes = 40
odd = TimeEntry(date(2026, 9, 14), "S3", "scheduling", "planning", 10, 15, "1", "manual", True)
Tasks
  1. What does line 2 print?
  2. What happens on line 3, and why?
  3. What happens on line 4?
  4. Line 5 passes "1" (text) for interruptions. What happens, and what does it teach about type hints?
  5. Why is hours a property and not a tenth field?
Model answer
  1. 0.6 16.8 — 36 ÷ 60 = 0.6 hours; 0.6 × 28 = 16.80 dollars.
  2. __post_init__ raises ValueError: minutes must be >= 0, got -19. The creation is interrupted, so no object named bad exists.
  3. FrozenInstanceError: frozen=True makes every field read-only after creation, which protects the invariant.
  4. The object is created: __post_init__ does not check interruptions, and Python does not enforce type hints at creation, so the text "1" stays in the object. This is why the loader converts every value to its type before building a TimeEntry.
  5. A property is computed from minutes each time it is read, so it can never disagree with the data; a stored tenth field could become inconsistent. Read like an attribute (e.hours), it keeps the interface simple.
Case 16

A damaged export goes through the loader

Chapter 5 · 5.2 Collections and CSV (Comma-Separated Values) parsing
Situation

The loader reads a file with a header line and six data lines with csv.DictReader and the loop for line_no, row in enumerate(reader, start=2):, converting with int(), date.fromisoformat() and == "1", catching (ValueError, TypeError) and building TimeEntry objects:

Line Problem in the line
2 none
3 minutes written "17.0"
4 date written "2026/09/16"
5 the line stops after the routine name (fewer values than the header)
6 tool written "jarvs"
7 none
Tasks
  1. How many TimeEntry objects are loaded and which line numbers are skipped? Give the exception for each skipped line.
  2. Why does the loop start counting at 2?
  3. Why are only ValueError and TypeError caught? What happens if the file does not exist?
  4. Explain newline="" and encoding="utf-8" in the open call, and why the path is built with pathlib.
Model answer
  1. 2 objects (lines 2 and 7) and 4 skipped lines: line 3 — ValueError (int("17.0")); line 4 — ValueError (invalid ISO (International Organization for Standardization) format); line 5 — TypeError (missing values arrive as None, and int(None) fails); line 6 — ValueError raised by TimeEntry.__post_init__ ("unknown tool 'jarvs'"). Each skip is stored as a tuple (line number, reason).
  2. Line 1 of the file is the header, so the first data record is line 2; the report then gives the real line number to the person who must correct the cell.
  3. These are the two exceptions a bad row can produce. A FileNotFoundError is a setup problem, not a data problem, so it is not caught and stops the program with a clear message.
  4. newline="" is required by the csv documentation so that the module handles line endings itself; encoding="utf-8" reads "Boréal" correctly on every operating system. pathlib builds the path from the location of the program, so it works on every teammate's computer, on the GitHub runner and on the defense computer — a hard-coded path works on one machine only.
Case 17

Fixing a draft design of JARVIS

Chapter 5 · 5.3 Responsibilities, classes and UML (Unified Modeling Language)Chapter 5 · 5.4 Abstract base classes, polymorphism and clean code
Situation

A team's first class diagram gives these responsibilities:

  • Agent: runs the loop request → intent → tool → result → log, and publishes the dashboard;
  • Store: saves entries and computes the mean minutes per routine;
  • Agent.__init__ contains self._provider = OfflineProvider().

The diagram also shows: Agent "1" o-- "1..*" Tool, Agent --> Store, DataLoader ..> TimeEntry, LogTimeTool --|> Tool. A planned class SummarizeTool(Tool) has a name but no run() method yet.

Tasks
  1. Which responsibilities break the Single Responsibility Principle, and where should they go?
  2. Name each of the four relationships and read the first one aloud with its multiplicity.
  3. What relationship does self._provider = OfflineProvider() create, and why does the course avoid it?
  4. What happens when SummarizeTool() is created, and why is that useful?
  5. Point to the polymorphic call in the agent loop.
Model answer
  1. The Agent has two reasons to change (the loop and the dashboard): publishing the dashboard moves to the Reporter. The Store both saves and computes statistics: the mean moves to StatsEngine; the Store only saves, queries and exports.
  2. o-- = aggregation ("one agent holds one or more tools"; the tools exist independently and are passed in); --> = association with navigability (the agent knows the store); ..> = dependency (the loader creates entries and returns them without keeping them); --|> = generalization (a LogTimeTool is a Tool).
  3. The agent creates the provider and owns it for its whole life: a composition. The course passes the provider in through the constructor (dependency injection) so that a test can use a fake provider and the ApiProvider of Class 10 can replace the offline one by changing one argument in main().
  4. Python raises TypeError ("Can't instantiate abstract class SummarizeTool without an implementation for abstract method 'run'"). The error appears at creation time, on the developer's computer, instead of during a demo when the first request needs run().
  5. reply = tool.run(intent.args, self._store) — the same call runs LogTimeTool.run, AddTaskTool.run or DailyReportTool.run depending on the object (and self._provider.parse(text) is polymorphic over the providers).
Case 18

Code review of a ten-line summary function

Chapter 5 · 5.4 Abstract base classes, polymorphism and clean codeChapter 6 · 6.1 Mean and median in codeChapter 6 · 6.2 Mode, variance, standard deviation and outliers in code
Situation

A teammate submits this function for the Reporter:

import statistics

def summary(xs, seen=[]):
    xs.sort()
    n = len(xs)
    mid = n // 2
    med = xs[mid]
    sd = statistics.pstdev(xs)
    seen.append(med)
    return med, sd, seen
Tasks
  1. List every defect you can find (correctness, course rules and clean-code habits).
  2. What does summary([4, 9, 1, 7]) return for the median, and what should it return?
  3. Rewrite the median and the standard deviation as engine code that follows the course rules.
Model answer
  1. (a) Mutable default argument seen=[]: the list is created once and shared by every call. (b) xs.sort() reorders the caller's list (a side effect); use sorted(xs). (c) The median is wrong for an even count (it takes one value instead of averaging the two middles). (d) statistics.pstdev divides by n; the course uses the sample SD (Standard Deviation) with n − 1. (e) The engine calls statistics, which is reserved for the oracle (validation table and tests). (f) No guard: an empty list raises an unhelpful error (IndexError). (g) No type hints, no docstring, and a function that does three jobs.
  2. The sorted list is [1, 4, 7, 9]; mid = 2 → xs[2] = 7. The correct median is (4 + 7) ÷ 2 = 5.5.
  3. Corrected engine code (the guards, sorted() and n − 1 follow the course rules):
@staticmethod
def median(xs: list[float]) -> float:
    """Middle value of a sorted copy; mean of the two middles for even n."""
    if not xs:
        raise ValueError("median of an empty list is undefined")
    ordered = sorted(xs)
    n = len(ordered)
    mid = n // 2
    if n % 2 == 1:
        return ordered[mid]
    return (ordered[mid - 1] + ordered[mid]) / 2

@staticmethod
def std_dev(xs: list[float]) -> float:
    """Sample standard deviation (n - 1)."""
    if len(xs) < 2:
        raise ValueError("variance needs at least two values")
    m = sum(xs) / len(xs)
    return math.sqrt(sum((x - m) ** 2 for x in xs) / (len(xs) - 1))
Case 19

The database that kept growing

Chapter 6 · 6.3 EconEngine and the StoreChapter 6 · 6.4 Grouping, validation and the tiny-database rule
Situation

A teammate's Store.import_csv() runs a plain INSERT for every row of the CSV (Comma-Separated Values) each time the assistant starts, and builds queries like f"SELECT AVG(minutes) FROM entries WHERE routine = '{routine}'". After three weeks data/jarvis.db weighs 1.4 MB (megabyte). Another teammate wrote rows inside with closing(sqlite3.connect(path)) as con: only, without the inner con context manager or con.commit(). Yesterday a git push of the database was rejected.

Tasks
  1. Why does the file grow, and how do the schema and the import fix it? What property does the import gain?
  2. What is wrong with the f-string query? Rewrite it.
  3. What happens to the rows of the second teammate, and why?
  4. What must the team do about the rejected push?
  5. What does SELECT routine, tool, COUNT(*), AVG(minutes) FROM entries GROUP BY routine, tool return on the 420-row teaching file?
Model answer
  1. Every start inserts the 420 rows again (about 30 KB (kilobyte) each time), so the file passes the 1 MB (megabyte) limit. Fix: the constraint UNIQUE (date, staff_id, routine, start_hour) in the schema plus INSERT OR IGNORE: duplicates are skipped and the import becomes idempotent (running it twice gives the same table: 420 rows). Then run VACUUM to rebuild the file at its real size before committing.
  2. Values glued into SQL (Structured Query Language) text can change the query's meaning: a routine name with an apostrophe breaks it, and user input could become a command. Use a placeholder: con.execute("SELECT AVG(minutes) FROM entries WHERE routine = ?", (routine,)).
  3. They are lost: closing a connection does not commit. The first INSERT opened a transaction that was never committed; the stacked form with closing(sqlite3.connect(path)) as con, con: commits when the block ends normally (or call con.commit()).
