A pending write transaction would also make other connections fail with database is locked.
  4. Someone committed first: run git pull --rebase; if Git reports a conflict on data/jarvis.db, take GitHub's version (git checkout origin/main -- data/jarvis.db, git add data/jarvis.db, git rebase --continue) and run the assistant command again so the new rows are written on top. Never merge two database files by hand; in future, pull before running and commit right after (one writer at a time).
  5. Eight rows, one per routine-and-tool pair (six routines; e-mail has manual and jarvis runs, the daily report has manual and template runs), each with its run count and average minutes.
Case 20

The morning brief crashed: test it, fix it, recommend

Chapter 10 · 10.1 Tests with pytest, edge cases and the oracleChapter 10 · 10.2 Tracebacks, the debugger, validation and the bug logChapter 10 · 10.4 From results to a decision, the report and the sprints
Situation

The scheduled morning brief stopped with this traceback (shortened):

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "jarvis/__main__.py", line 74, in main
    brief = make_brief(store, path)
  File "jarvis/brief.py", line 68, in make_brief
    entries = load_entries(path)
  File "jarvis/loader.py", line 52, in load_entries
    rows.append(parse_row(row))
  File "jarvis/loader.py", line 40, in parse_row
    minutes = int(raw)
              ^^^^^^^^
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: ''

After the fix, python -m pytest -q prints ..F..... and the team's numbers are: pilot 35.85 → 13.73 minutes per run; comparison 34.67 → 34.10; 2 minutes of review; 100 runs per month; 28 $/h.

Tasks
  1. Read the traceback with the four-step procedure: what failed, where, and where should the bug be fixed?
  2. Write the bug-log entry (symptom, cause, fix, test, status) and the test that closes it.
  3. What does ..F..... mean, and what exit code does pytest return?
  4. Compute the difference of the changes and the monthly impact, and write the six-part recommendation in short form.
Model answer
  1. Last line: int() received an empty string (an empty minutes cell). The frame just above shows jarvis/loader.py, line 40, minutes = int(raw) (the carets confirm that the failing value is raw). The value came from the data file through load_entries (line 52) into parse_row: the loader is the boundary, the first function that should have rejected it. Fix there: validate the field and skip the row with a clear message, counting it, so one bad cell no longer stops the brief.
  2. Symptom: the morning brief stopped at 06:30. Cause: the loader converted minutes with int() without handling an empty cell. Fix: validation in parse_row (commit reference). Test: a row with an empty minutes is skipped and reported, not a crash. Status: closed only once the test is red before the fix and green after. Test: with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="minutes"): around parse_row given a row whose minutes is "" (or a loader test asserting that one row is skipped and counted).
  3. Eight tests: the third failed (F), seven passed (.). Because at least one failed, the exit code is 1, and GitHub Actions (https://docs.github.com/en/actionsVirusTotal) marks the commit red.
  4. Changes: pilot −22.12, comparison −0.57 → difference −21.55 min per run. Net saving 21.55 − 2.00 = 19.55 min × 100 = 1 955 min = 32.6 h per month ≈ 912 $ per month. Finding: the assistant cut e-mail triage by 21.55 minutes per run beyond the comparison group's change. Evidence: 14 working days; pilot 27 → 15 runs, comparison 18 → 10. Decision: automate e-mail triage first, for all staff, on the free tier with the offline fallback. Impact: about 32.6 h and 912 $ per month. Risk: small sample, possible novelty effect, the free tier's daily quota; no message text stored. Alternatives: the paid tier only if it saves more than 43 minutes per user per month beyond the free tier; doing nothing keeps about 1 640 $ per month of manual triage.

Questions on Chapter 1 — Welcome: One Real Problem, Three Courses, One Team

Multiple-choice question 1one right answer
Chapter 1 · 1.1 Welcome, routines and the one rule

Which of the following tasks is a routine in the sense used in CS (Computer Science) 251?

Answer: c) Triaging the studio's mailbox every morning

Why: A routine repeats on a regular schedule and follows more or less the same steps each time. Registering, the exam and an installation happen once: they are events, not routines.

Multiple-choice question 2one right answer
Chapter 1 · 1.1 Welcome, routines and the one rule

What does CS (Computer Science) 251 add in terms of theory?

Answer: d) No new theory: it integrates three courses already taken on one real business problem

Why: The one rule of the course is "no new theory": everything comes from Principles of Microeconomics, Introduction to OOP (Object-Oriented Programming) in Python and Statistics. What is new is their integration on one problem.

Multiple-choice question 3one right answer
Chapter 1 · 1.2 What an integrative project is

In the consulting habit followed by every Brick, what comes immediately after stating the problem?

Answer: a) The evidence: data collected and analysed with methods you can defend

Why: The order is problem, evidence, recommendation. Evidence is what makes the solution research-based; the recommendation and its risk come only after the data has been analysed.

Multiple-choice question 4one right answer
Chapter 1 · 1.2 What an integrative project is

Which of the three integrated courses supplies the idea of break-even?

Answer: c) Principles of Microeconomics

Why: Opportunity cost, marginal benefit and cost, fixed and variable cost, break-even and payback come from Principles of Microeconomics. Statistics describes the data and Python computes and automates.

Multiple-choice question 5one right answer
Chapter 1 · 1.3 Course map, grading and the Brick system

How much is one Brick worth in the final grade when it is graded Complete?

Answer: b) 2.5 %

Why: Twelve Bricks make the 30 % continuous assessment, so one Brick is worth 30 ÷ 12 = 2.5 %. A Partial Brick earns 1.25 and a Missing Brick 0.

Multiple-choice question 6one right answer
Chapter 1 · 1.3 Course map, grading and the Brick system

A student has all twelve Bricks complete (30 points), scores 70/100 on the Mid-Term and 80/100 on the Final. What is the letter grade?

Answer: b) B

Why: 30 + 70 × 0.30 + 80 × 0.40 = 30 + 21 + 32 = 83 %, which falls in the 83–86 band of the course scale: B.

Multiple-choice question 7one right answer
Chapter 1 · 1.4 The client, the dataset and the toolbox

Which column of boreal_routines_2026.csv records how a run was done (manual, template or jarvis)?

Answer: b) tool

Why: The tool column takes the values manual, template and jarvis. It separates the current practice from the report template (day 8) and the assistant pilot (day 10).

Multiple-choice question 8one right answer
Chapter 1 · 1.4 The client, the dataset and the toolbox

What must JARVIS do when there is no API (Application Programming Interface) key and no network?

Answer: d) Keep working with the offline provider, which uses rules and regular expressions

Why: The offline fallback rule says JARVIS runs with no key and no network; the API (Application Programming Interface) provider is an upgrade that drops into the same loop, never a dependency. Tests, demos and the exam never depend on the internet.

Questions on Chapter 2 — The Problem Before the Code: Requirements and the Research Process

Which sentence is a problem statement rather than a complaint?

Answer: d) "The owner must decide which routine to automate first; the project measures the minutes of each routine, prices them at 28 $/h and compares the savings with the cost of a paid tier."

Why: A problem statement names the situation, the decision to support and the evidence to collect. The other sentences describe a difficulty, a wish or an opinion, with no decision and no evidence.

Multiple-choice question 10one right answer

According to Leedy and Ormrod, which statement about sub-problems is correct?

Answer: a) Together they add up to the whole problem, no more and no less

Why: Good sub-problems are researchable units, tied to the interpretation of data, few (two to six) and together equal to the whole problem. Planning decisions are pseudo-sub-problems.

Multiple-choice question 11one right answer
Chapter 2 · 2.1 From a business problem to a research problem

Which candidate research question passes the four checks of the course?

Answer: d) "How many minutes per run does assistant-triaged e-mail save compared with manual triage during the 14 logged days?"

Why: The accepted question is open, names something measurable (minutes per run), belongs to one sub-problem and can be answered with the log. The others are a yes/no question, a question with nothing measurable in the data, and a planning decision.

Multiple-choice question 12one right answer

Which statement is a non-functional requirement of JARVIS?

Answer: d) JARVIS shall work with no **API** (Application Programming Interface) key and no network.

Why: A non-functional requirement describes a quality or a constraint on how the system performs its functions. Computing a cost, recording a run and adding a task are behaviours: functional requirements.

Multiple-choice question 13one right answer
Chapter 2 · 2.2 Requirements analysis

Why is "JARVIS should be fast" not yet a verifiable requirement?

Answer: b) It has no threshold that a test could check, and "should" marks a wish rather than a binding requirement

Why: A requirement must be verifiable: "under one second on the lab computer" can be checked with a stopwatch, "fast" cannot. In ISO/IEC/IEEE (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission / Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 29148, "shall" is binding and "should" is a goal.

Questions on Chapter 3 — Microeconomics Refresher: What Is an Hour Worth?

Multiple-choice question 21one right answer
Chapter 3 · 3.1 Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost

A routine takes 30 minutes per run and runs 100 times a month. At 28 $/h, what is its monthly cost?

Answer: b) 1 400 $

Why: Cost = 30 ÷ 60 × 28 × 100 = 1 400 $. Forgetting the division by 60 gives 84 000 $; using a 65 $ billable rate gives 3 250 $, which is an opportunity cost, not the loaded cost.

Multiple-choice question 22one right answer
Chapter 3 · 3.1 Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost

What is the opportunity cost of an hour of staff time?

Answer: d) The value of the next-best use of that hour, the best alternative given up

Why: Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative given up. The salary is an explicit cost, a non-recoverable cost is sunk, and the extra cost of one more unit is the marginal cost.

Multiple-choice question 23one right answer
Chapter 3 · 3.1 Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost

What does the loaded hourly cost of 28 $/h include?

Answer: a) The salary for the hour plus the employer's overhead for it

Why: A loaded cost adds the employer's overhead (contributions, vacation pay, equipment, office) to the salary: it is what the hour costs the business.

Multiple-choice question 24one right answer
Chapter 3 · 3.2 Marginal analysis

Automating a routine saves 10 net minutes per run, the routine runs 100 times a month and staff time is worth 28 $/h. What is the MB (marginal benefit) per month?

Answer: b) 466.67 $

Why: MB (marginal benefit) = 10 ÷ 60 × 28 × 100 = 466.67 $. Using 20 runs gives 93.33 $; a 65 $ rate gives 1 083.33 $; forgetting the division by 60 gives 28 000 $.

Multiple-choice question 25one right answer
Chapter 3 · 3.2 Marginal analysis

A tool needs 24 hours of set-up valued at 28 $/h, spread over a 12-month horizon, and all its requests stay inside the free quota. What is its MC (marginal cost) per month?

Answer: c) 56.00 $

Why: MC (marginal cost) = paid requests × price + set-up ÷ horizon = 0 + (24 × 28) ÷ 12 = 672 ÷ 12 = 56 $ per month. 672 $ is the whole set-up without the horizon.

Multiple-choice question 26one right answer
Chapter 3 · 3.2 Marginal analysis

What is the decision rule of marginal analysis for automating one more routine?

Answer: a) Automate while the marginal benefit is at least equal to the marginal cost

Why: The rule is MB (marginal benefit) ≥ MC (marginal cost), and candidates that pass are ranked by MB (marginal benefit) − MC (marginal cost). A large total cost does not guarantee a positive net benefit (the invoice check is the counter-example).

Multiple-choice question 27one right answer
Chapter 3 · 3.2 Marginal analysis

What do diminishing returns mean for the team's automation plan?

Answer: b) Each additional tool brings less benefit than the previous one

Why: As more of an activity is done, each additional unit brings less. The first tool saves the most, the fifth very little, which is why three working tools beat ten unfinished ones.

Multiple-choice question 28one right answer
Chapter 3 · 3.3 Fixed, variable, total, average and marginal cost; the sunk cost

With respect to which quantity is the paid tier (20 $ per user per month) a fixed cost?

Answer: d) The number of requests sent during the month

Why: The subscription does not change with the number of requests in the period, so it is fixed with respect to requests. It grows with users or seats and with months, so it is variable with respect to those quantities.

Multiple-choice question 29one right answer
Chapter 3 · 3.3 Fixed, variable, total, average and marginal cost; the sunk cost

What is the marginal cost of one more request when the studio is still inside the free quota?

Answer: c) 0 $

Why: Inside the quota, one more request does not change the total cost, so its marginal cost is zero. The price per request applies only beyond the quota, where the total cost curve has its kink.

Multiple-choice question 30one right answer
Chapter 3 · 3.3 Fixed, variable, total, average and marginal cost; the sunk cost

What is the rule about a sunk cost?

Answer: c) It must not influence the decision, because it is the same under every alternative

Why: A sunk cost is already spent and no decision can recover it, so it cancels out between alternatives. The decision to continue compares future benefits with future costs.

Multiple-choice question 31one right answer
Chapter 3 · 3.4 Break-even, payback and make-or-buy

A paid seat costs 20 $ per user per month and staff time is worth 28 $/h. What are the break-even hours per user per month?

Answer: a) 0.714 h, about 43 minutes

Why: Break-even hours = monthly price ÷ hourly value = 20 ÷ 28 = 0.714 h ≈ 43 minutes. 3.57 h is the break-even of five seats (100 ÷ 28); 1.4 h inverts the division.

Multiple-choice question 32one right answer
Chapter 3 · 3.4 Break-even, payback and make-or-buy

A tool costs 1 200 $ to set up. It brings 450 $ of benefit per month and needs 50 $ of maintenance per month. What is the payback period?

Answer: c) 3.00 months

Why: Payback = set-up ÷ monthly net saving = 1 200 ÷ (450 − 50) = 1 200 ÷ 400 = 3 months. Using the gross benefit gives 2.67 months; inverting the division gives 0.33.

Multiple-choice question 33one right answer
Chapter 3 · 3.4 Break-even, payback and make-or-buy

What does EconEngine.payback_months() return when the monthly net saving is zero or negative?

Answer: a) It returns `math.inf`, documented as "never recovered"

Why: A tool that saves nothing is a real possibility, not an impossible input, so the honest answer is a documented value: math.inf. Impossible inputs, such as a zero hourly value in break-even, raise ValueError.

Questions on Chapter 4 — Statistics Refresher: Letting the Time Log Speak

Multiple-choice question 34one right answer
Chapter 4 · 4.1 Central tendency

What is the median of 12, 9, 15, 30, 10 minutes?

Answer: b) 12

Why: Sorted: 9, 10, 12, 15, 30; with n = 5 the median is the third value, 12. 15.2 is the mean, pulled up by the 30-minute run.

Multiple-choice question 35one right answer
Chapter 4 · 4.1 Central tendency

Which measure of central tendency is resistant to one extreme value?

Answer: a) The median

Why: The median depends on the order of the values, not on their distance from the centre, so one very long run barely moves it. The mean and the range are both pulled by an extreme value.

Multiple-choice question 36one right answer
Chapter 4 · 4.1 Central tendency

The interruptions of six runs are 0, 2, 1, 2, 3, 2. What is the mode?

Answer: c) 2

Why: The value 2 occurs three times, more than any other value. 1.67 is the mean, not the mode.

Multiple-choice question 37one right answer
Chapter 4 · 4.1 Central tendency

Which measure should a monthly cost use when it multiplies minutes per run by the number of runs?

Answer: c) The mean, because the total equals n × x̄ exactly

Why: Σx = n × x̄, so a total built from the mean is exact. The median is checked beside it to make sure a few long days do not drive the mean.

Multiple-choice question 38one right answer
Chapter 4 · 4.2 Dispersion

What is the sample variance of 6, 8 and 10?

Answer: c) 4

Why: Mean 8; deviations −2, 0, +2; sum of squares 8; s² = 8 ÷ (3 − 1) = 4. Dividing by n gives 2.67 (the population variance); 2 is the standard deviation; 8 is the sum of squares.

Multiple-choice question 39one right answer
Chapter 4 · 4.2 Dispersion

Why does the sample variance divide by n − 1?

Answer: c) Because deviations are measured from the sample's own mean, which makes them too small on average; n − 1 corrects that bias

Why: The sample mean minimises the sum of squared deviations, so dividing by n underestimates the population variance on average. n − 1 is the number of degrees of freedom.

Multiple-choice question 40one right answer
Chapter 4 · 4.2 Dispersion

Routine X has a mean of 40 minutes and an SD (Standard Deviation) of 6; routine Y has a mean of 10 minutes and an SD (Standard Deviation) of 3. Which routine is less predictable relative to its length?

Answer: d) Y, because its **CV** (Coefficient of Variation) is larger (30 % against 15 %)

Why: CV (Coefficient of Variation) = s ÷ x̄: 6 ÷ 40 = 15 % and 3 ÷ 10 = 30 %. The CV (Coefficient of Variation) has no unit and compares routines of different length; the SD (Standard Deviation) answers a different question, the buffer in minutes.

Multiple-choice question 41one right answer
Chapter 4 · 4.2 Dispersion

Which statement about statistics.stdev and statistics.pstdev is correct?

Answer: d) stdev divides by n − 1 (sample) and pstdev divides by n (population)

Why: stdev is the sample standard deviation and is the oracle of the engine; pstdev is the population version and gives a smaller number on the same data. The studio's 14 days are a sample.

Multiple-choice question 42one right answer
Chapter 4 · 4.3 Distributions and outliers

What distinguishes a histogram from a bar chart?

Answer: a) Its bars touch, because the horizontal axis is a continuous numeric scale

Why: A histogram draws a frequency table of a numeric variable, so neighbouring bins touch. A bar chart shows categories such as routines, separated, in any order.

Multiple-choice question 43one right answer
Chapter 4 · 4.3 Distributions and outliers

What characterises a right-skewed distribution of durations?

Answer: d) A long tail toward large values, with the mean larger than the median

Why: Durations have a floor but no ceiling, so a few long runs form a tail on the right and pull the mean above the median. Two peaks describe a bimodal shape; mirrored halves describe symmetry.

Multiple-choice question 44one right answer
Chapter 4 · 4.3 Distributions and outliers

For a routine, Q1 (first quartile) = 20 and Q3 (third quartile) = 28 minutes. What are the 1.5 × IQR (Interquartile Range) fences?

Answer: a) 8 and 40 minutes

Why: IQR (Interquartile Range) = 28 − 20 = 8; 1.5 × 8 = 12; fences = 20 − 12 = 8 and 28 + 12 = 40. 12 and 36 use 1 × IQR (Interquartile Range); 20 and 28 are the edges of the box.

Multiple-choice question 45one right answer
Chapter 4 · 4.4 Relationships, groups and the limits of 14 days

What does a Pearson correlation of r = −0.85 indicate?

Answer: a) A strong negative linear relationship

Why: The sign gives the direction and the absolute value 0.85 is above 0.70, the course threshold for "strong". r describes association, never causation.

Multiple-choice question 46one right answer
Chapter 4 · 4.4 Relationships, groups and the limits of 14 days

Why does the e-mail pilot analysis use a comparison group (S4 and S5)?

Answer: d) To separate the effect of the assistant from changes that affected everybody in the same period

Why: The comparison group did not receive the assistant, so its change (−0.57 min) estimates what the calendar alone did. The difference of the changes isolates the effect of the tool.

Questions on Chapter 5 — Python and OOP (Object-Oriented Programming) Refresher + Design: Blueprint Before Bricks

Multiple-choice question 47one right answer
Chapter 5 · 5.1 Classes, objects and the dataclass

Which methods does the @dataclass decorator write automatically?

Answer: d) `__init__`, `__repr__` and `__eq__`, from the annotated fields

Why: @dataclass generates __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ (plus __hash__ and the blocking __setattr__ when frozen). __post_init__ is written by you, and type hints are not checked at creation.

Multiple-choice question 48one right answer
Chapter 5 · 5.1 Classes, objects and the dataclass

What does frozen=True do to a TimeEntry?

Answer: a) Any assignment to a field after creation raises `FrozenInstanceError`

Why: A frozen dataclass refuses to change or delete fields after creation, which, with the checks of __post_init__, establishes an invariant for every object.

Multiple-choice question 49one right answer
Chapter 5 · 5.1 Classes, objects and the dataclass

What does a single leading underscore, as in self._tools, mean in Python?

Answer: c) A convention meaning "internal": other modules should not use it, but Python does not block access

Why: One underscore is an agreement between programmers (PEP (Python Enhancement Proposal) 8's weak internal-use indicator). Name mangling is triggered by two leading underscores and is meant to avoid clashes in subclasses.

Multiple-choice question 50one right answer
Chapter 5 · 5.2 Collections and CSV (Comma-Separated Values) parsing

Which collection should hold ALLOWED_TOOLS = manual, template, jarvis?

Answer: a) A set, because the only question is membership and a set answers it fast with no duplicates

Why: The loader only asks "is this tool allowed?". A set answers in constant average time and cannot contain the same tool twice.

Multiple-choice question 51one right answer
Chapter 5 · 5.2 Collections and CSV (Comma-Separated Values) parsing

What does csv.DictReader return for each data line of the file?

Answer: b) A dict that maps the column names of the header to text values

Why: The reader never guesses types: every value is a string, including "36". The loader converts each value before building a TimeEntry.

Multiple-choice question 52one right answer
Chapter 5 · 5.2 Collections and CSV (Comma-Separated Values) parsing

What happens when the loader evaluates int("17.0")?

Answer: b) It raises `ValueError`

Why: int() accepts only the text of a whole number; "17.0" is the text of a decimal number. TypeError is what int(None) raises for a missing field.

Multiple-choice question 53one right answer
Chapter 5 · 5.2 Collections and CSV (Comma-Separated Values) parsing

Why does DataLoader.load catch only ValueError and TypeError?

Answer: a) These are the errors a bad row produces; other errors, such as `FileNotFoundError`, signal a setup problem and should stop the program

Why: A bad value is skipped and reported; a missing file means the program is set up wrongly and must stop with a clear message. Catching everything would hide real bugs.

Multiple-choice question 54one right answer
Chapter 5 · 5.3 Responsibilities, classes and UML (Unified Modeling Language)

What does the Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) say?

Answer: c) A class should have one responsibility, that is, one reason to change

Why: In Robert C. Martin's wording, a class should have one reason to change. It produces high cohesion and low coupling.

Multiple-choice question 55one right answer
Chapter 5 · 5.3 Responsibilities, classes and UML (Unified Modeling Language)

In a UML (Unified Modeling Language) class diagram, what does a hollow diamond at one end of a line show?

Answer: b) Aggregation: a whole–part link in which the part can exist without the whole

Why: A hollow diamond is aggregation (Agent ◇— Tool: the tools exist before the agent). Composition uses a filled diamond, generalization a hollow triangle and dependency a dashed arrow.

Multiple-choice question 56one right answer
Chapter 5 · 5.4 Abstract base classes, polymorphism and clean code

Tool inherits from ABC (Abstract Base Class) and declares run() with @abstractmethod. What happens on Tool()?

Answer: d) Python raises `TypeError`: an abstract class cannot be instantiated

Why: A class with an unimplemented abstract method cannot be instantiated, so the error appears at creation time, on the developer's computer, rather than during a demo.

Multiple-choice question 57one right answer
Chapter 5 · 5.4 Abstract base classes, polymorphism and clean code

What is the problem with def add(item, seen=[])?

Answer: c) The default list is created once, when def runs, and is shared by every call that omits seen

Why: Default values are evaluated once. Every call without seen appends to the same list, so values from earlier calls leak into later ones. The fix is seen=None, then seen = [] if seen is None else seen.

Questions on Chapter 6 — Development I: The Engines and the Store Come Alive

Multiple-choice question 58one right answer
Chapter 6 · 6.1 Mean and median in code

Why must StatsEngine never call the statistics module inside its own methods?

Answer: c) Because the module is the independent oracle: a check is a check only when both sides are independent

Why: The engine is yours and the library is the oracle used in the validation table and the tests. The Mid-Term also asks you to write and explain the methods yourself.

Multiple-choice question 59one right answer
Chapter 6 · 6.1 Mean and median in code

What is the difference between sorted(xs) and xs.sort()?

Answer: d) `sorted(xs)` returns a new sorted list and leaves xs unchanged; `xs.sort()` reorders xs in place and returns None

Why: The engine uses sorted() because the list belongs to the caller; reordering it would be a side effect that can break later before/after comparisons.

Multiple-choice question 60one right answer
Chapter 6 · 6.1 Mean and median in code

Why is the engine method called value_range and not range?

Answer: b) To avoid shadowing Python's built-in function range

Why: range is a built-in used in for loops; a method with the same name would hide it inside the class and confuse readers.

Multiple-choice question 61one right answer
Chapter 6 · 6.2 Mode, variance, standard deviation and outliers in code

What does StatsEngine.mode return when several values share the highest count?

Answer: d) The list of all tied values, sorted, as written in its docstring

Why: The JARVIS convention returns every tied value, sorted (for the e-mail runs, [29, 32, 37]), so nothing is lost and the answer does not depend on row order.

Multiple-choice question 62one right answer
Chapter 6 · 6.2 Mode, variance, standard deviation and outliers in code

What does 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 evaluate to in Python, and what should be used instead?

Answer: a) False; use `math.isclose` for floating-point results

Why: Floats are binary fractions (IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 754 (https://standards.ieee.org/ieee/754/6210/VirusTotal)), so 0.1 + 0.2 gives 0.30000000000000004. Two correct float results can differ in their last digit, so they are compared with a tolerance.

Multiple-choice question 63one right answer
Chapter 6 · 6.2 Mode, variance, standard deviation and outliers in code

What is the guard of StatsEngine.variance?

Answer: b) It raises `ValueError` when the list has fewer than two values

Why: With one value, n − 1 is zero, so the sample variance is undefined. The guard if len(xs) < 2 raises ValueError before any division.

Multiple-choice question 64one right answer
Chapter 6 · 6.3 EconEngine and the Store

Why does the Store pass values to SQL (Structured Query Language) with ? placeholders?

Answer: a) Because values travel separately from the **SQL** (Structured Query Language) text and can never change the meaning of the query

Why: Gluing values into the query text breaks on an apostrophe and lets user input become a command. Placeholders keep data and instructions apart.

Multiple-choice question 65one right answer
Chapter 6 · 6.3 EconEngine and the Store

What does INSERT OR IGNORE combined with UNIQUE (date, staff_id, routine, start_hour) give the CSV (Comma-Separated Values) import?

Answer: c) The import becomes idempotent: running it twice leaves the same 420 rows

Why: A row that repeats the UNIQUE key is skipped instead of raising an error, so repeated imports add nothing. VACUUM, not INSERT OR IGNORE, rebuilds the file.

Multiple-choice question 66one right answer
Chapter 6 · 6.3 EconEngine and the Store

Rows were inserted inside with closing(sqlite3.connect(path)) as con: only, with no commit. What happens to them?

Answer: d) They are lost, because closing a connection does not commit

Why: The first INSERT opens a transaction; only a commit writes it to the file. The stacked form with closing(...) as con, con: commits when the block ends normally.

Multiple-choice question 67one right answer
Chapter 6 · 6.4 Grouping, validation and the tiny-database rule

An oracle value was printed with one decimal (for example 18.1). Which absolute tolerance does the validation table use?

Answer: b) 0.05

Why: The tolerance is half a unit of the last printed digit: 0.5 × 10⁻¹ = 0.05. A uniform 0.005 would turn the row red only because of the script's rounding.

Questions on Chapter 10 — Development III: Testing, Error Resolution, the API (Application Programming Interface) Provider and the Road to the Report

Multiple-choice question 68one right answer
Chapter 10 · 10.1 Tests with pytest, edge cases and the oracle

In the pytest progress line, what does the character F mean?

Answer: b) A test failed: an assert was false or the test raised an unexpected exception

Why: The progress line shows . for passed, F for failed and E for an error outside the test body (for example in a fixture).

Multiple-choice question 69one right answer
Chapter 10 · 10.1 Tests with pytest, edge cases and the oracle

Which exit code does pytest return when every test passed?

Answer: a) 0

Why: 0 means all tests passed, 1 that at least one failed and 5 that no test was found. GitHub Actions (https://docs.github.com/en/actionsVirusTotal) reads this number to mark the commit green or red.

Multiple-choice question 70one right answer
Chapter 10 · 10.1 Tests with pytest, edge cases and the oracle

In which order are the three steps of a good test written?

Answer: a) Prepare the input, call the method once, check the result

Why: Prepare (arrange), call (act), check (assert). The expected value must come from outside the code under test, such as a hand computation or the oracle.

Multiple-choice question 71one right answer
Chapter 10 · 10.2 Tracebacks, the debugger, validation and the bug log

Which line of a traceback do you read first?

Answer: b) The last line, which names the exception type and its message

Why: The four-step procedure starts at the bottom: the last line says what went wrong; then the frame above it, then the first frame in your own files, then where the wrong value came from.

Multiple-choice question 72one right answer
Chapter 10 · 10.2 Tracebacks, the debugger, validation and the bug log

When may a bug-log entry be marked closed?

Answer: c) When a test reproduces the bug: red before the fix and green after it

Why: Without a test, a later change can bring the defect back unnoticed (a regression). "Fixed, but no test" stays open.

Multiple-choice question 73one right answer
Chapter 10 · 10.3 The ApiProvider, the key and the scheduled workflow

Where does the API (Application Programming Interface) key of JARVIS live?

Answer: c) In an environment variable on your computer and in a repository secret on GitHub

Why: The key is read with os.environ.get("JARVIS_API_KEY"); the .env file is git-ignored, and GitHub passes the repository secret to one workflow step. A key committed once must be rotated the same day.

Multiple-choice question 74one right answer
Chapter 10 · 10.3 The ApiProvider, the key and the scheduled workflow

Which HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) status code means that the provider's rate limit was exceeded?

Answer: c) 429

Why: 429 is Too Many Requests, often with a Retry-After header. 200 is success, 401 means the key was refused and 5xx codes are server errors; all failures fall back to the offline provider.

Multiple-choice question 75one right answer
Chapter 10 · 10.4 From results to a decision, the report and the sprints

What is a conclusion in the technical report?

Answer: d) One or two sentences that answer one research question using only results already presented

Why: A result is a number with its evidence and limits; a discussion interprets results; a conclusion answers a research question and introduces nothing new.

Questions on Chapter 3 — Microeconomics Refresher: What Is an Hour Worth?

Multiple-select question 15select 2
Chapter 3 · 3.2 Marginal analysis

Which items are parts of the MC (marginal cost) per month of automating a routine?

Answers: b) Paid requests beyond the free quota multiplied by the price per request; e) The set-up cost divided by the planning horizon in months

Why: MC (marginal cost) = paid requests × price + set-up ÷ horizon. Minutes saved and review minutes enter the marginal benefit; the routine bill and the opportunity cost answer other questions.

Six candidates have these monthly values, written as marginal benefit / marginal cost: A 300 $ / 50 $; B 120 $ / 130 $; C 90 $ / 40 $; D −20 $ / 30 $; E 200 $ / 200 $; F 60 $ / 80 $. Which candidates pass the rule MB (marginal benefit) ≥ MC (marginal cost)?

Answers: a) A; c) C; e) E

Why: A (300 ≥ 50), C (90 ≥ 40) and E (200 ≥ 200, equality passes) satisfy MB (marginal benefit) ≥ MC (marginal cost). B, D and F have MB (marginal benefit) below MC (marginal cost). Ranked by net benefit: A (250 $), C (50 $), E (0 $).

Why: A subscription and a one-time set-up do not change with the number of requests. Requests beyond the quota and staff minutes grow with the quantity: they are variable.

Why: 20 ÷ 28 = 0.714 h per user. The set-up belongs to payback, which is the formula in the fourth option; 3.57 h is the break-even of all five seats together.

Why: Build = 1 120 + 28 × 12 = 1 456 $; buy = 100 × 12 = 1 200 $, so buying is cheaper at 12 months. At 24 months the order reverses (1 792 $ against 2 400 $).

For the run times 5, 7, 7, 9 and 22 minutes, which statements are correct?

Answers: a) The median is 7 minutes; b) The mean is 10 minutes; f) The mode is 7 minutes

Why: Sum 50 ÷ 5 = 10; the sorted middle value is 7; 7 occurs twice. The range is 22 − 5 = 17. The mean is pulled up by the 22-minute run.

Multiple-select question 22select 2
Chapter 4 · 4.1 Central tendency

When should the median be reported as the typical run?

Answers: d) When the data contain a few extreme values; f) When the distribution has a long tail on one side

Why: The median resists extreme values and long tails. A total uses the mean (Σx = n × x̄); for symmetric data the mean is preferred and both agree.

Multiple-select question 23select 3
Chapter 4 · 4.2 Dispersion

For the values 2, 4 and 6, which statements are correct?

Answers: a) The mean is 4; e) The sample variance is 4; f) The sample standard deviation is 2

Why: Deviations −2, 0, +2; sum of squares 8; s² = 8 ÷ 2 = 4; s = 2. 2.67 and 1.63 divide by n (population); the CV (Coefficient of Variation) is 2 ÷ 4 = 50 %.

Multiple-select question 24select 3
Chapter 4 · 4.2 Dispersion

Which statements about the standard deviation and the coefficient of variation are true?

Answers: c) The **CV** (Coefficient of Variation) compares the variability of routines of different length; d) The **SD** (Standard Deviation) is expressed in the unit of the data; f) The **CV** (Coefficient of Variation) has no unit

Why: The SD (Standard Deviation) is in minutes; dividing it by the mean removes the unit, so the CV (Coefficient of Variation) can compare a 10-minute and a 35-minute routine. Deviations always add up to zero.

Which statements describe a right-skewed distribution?

Answers: c) It has a long tail toward large values; e) Its mean is larger than its median

Why: In a right skew a few large values pull the mean above the median. Two peaks describe a bimodal shape; mirrored halves describe symmetry; a tail on the small side is a left skew.

For the 55 manual e-mail runs, Q1 (first quartile) = 30.5 and Q3 (third quartile) = 39.5 minutes. Which statements are correct?

Why: IQR (Interquartile Range) = 39.5 − 30.5 = 9; 1.5 × 9 = 13.5; fences 30.5 − 13.5 = 17 and 39.5 + 13.5 = 53. No manual run lies outside them.

Multiple-select question 27select 3
Chapter 4 · 4.4 Relationships, groups and the limits of 14 days

Which are limits of conclusions drawn from a 14-day log of five people?

Answers: a) A correlation can come from a confounding variable, such as the day of the week; b) The jarvis result rests on a small sample of runs and people; d) The data describe one studio during three weeks, not consultancies in general

Why: Correlation is not causation, the sample is small and the scope is narrow (measurement and novelty are two more limits). r and the median can be computed on these data, and a comparison group strengthens a result without proving it.

Answers: c) It has no unit; e) It always lies between −1 and +1; f) Swapping x and y does not change it

Why: r measures the direction and strength of a linear relationship. Minutes per interruption is the slope of the trend line; r near 0 can hide a curved relationship; r needs two numeric variables.

Part E

30 short essay questions with model answers

2:35–2:55

Write five to eight sentences with the course vocabulary and at least one number or example from Boréal Studio. Your drafts are kept in this browser only. Then open the model answer and read why it earns full marks.

Essay 1
Chapter 1 · 1.2 What an integrative project is

Explain what an integrative project is in CS (Computer Science) 251, and why none of the three integrated courses can answer the owner's question alone.

0 words

Model answer

An integrative project is a sustained period of independent study and research, combined with work in a team, that starts from a real business problem and seeks a research-based solution integrating knowledge from previous courses, in the way a consultant works for a client; it adds no new theory. Boréal Studio's question splits into three sub-problems. Microeconomics prices the time (opportunity cost, marginal benefit and cost, break-even), Statistics describes what the time log shows (mean, median, standard deviation, correlation, before/after), and Python builds the tool that automates a routine and measures the saving. Economics without data is a guess, statistics without a tool is a spreadsheet nobody maintains, and a program without economics may automate the wrong routine. Only the intersection of the three gives a decision the owner can act on.

Why this is the right answer

The answer quotes the elements of the official definition (independent research and team work, real problem, research-based solution, integration, consulting, no new theory) and shows, sub-problem by sub-problem, why each course is necessary but not sufficient.

Essay 2
Chapter 1 · 1.4 The client, the dataset and the toolbox

Describe the five stages of the JARVIS loop using the request "log 25 min email_triage", and explain the offline fallback rule.

0 words

Model answer

(1) Request: a staff member types "log 25 min email_triage". (2) Intent: a provider turns the sentence into a structured intent, the name log_time with the arguments minutes = 25 and routine = email_triage; the first provider is offline and uses rules and a regular expression. (3) Tool: the agent looks up log_time in its table of tools and selects LogTimeTool. (4) Result: the tool runs and adds an entry to the tiny database data/jarvis.db. (5) Log: the run is recorded with its timestamp, request, intent, tool, provider, success and duration in milliseconds; this log becomes JARVIS's own dataset. The offline fallback rule says that JARVIS must run with no API (Application Programming Interface) key and no network. Tests, demos and the Mid-Term never depend on the internet; the API (Application Programming Interface) provider connected later is an upgrade that drops into the same loop, never a dependency.

Why this is the right answer

It names the five stages in the right order with the concrete values of the example, and states the rule together with its consequence for tests, demos and the exam.

Essay 3
Chapter 1 · 1.1 Welcome, routines and the one ruleChapter 2 · 2.5 The data dictionary and personal data

Explain why a personal time log is personal information, and list the rules that protect it in the course.

0 words

Model answer

Personal information is information about an identifiable individual (the PIPEDA (Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act) definition; Québec's private-sector act uses a similar one). A time log records when a person worked, on what, for how long and how often they were interrupted, so it describes an identifiable person. Codes such as S1 to S5 only de-identify the data: the team can still link a code to a person, so the data stays personal. The course rules are: keep the log in the private team repository; record routine names, minutes and timestamps only; never record other people's names or message contents; ignore personal logs in Git where required (data/timelog_*.csv in .gitignore); never place raw logs on a public page; and publish only aggregated numbers per routine, because with five staff a chart per person would identify the person.

Why this is the right answer

The answer gives the legal definition, applies it to the content of a log, explains why codes are de-identification and not anonymization, and lists the concrete mitigations of the course.

Essay 4
Chapter 2 · 2.1 From a business problem to a research problem

A three-person bakery, Boulangerie Saint-Laurent, says: "Taking phone orders eats our afternoons, and an ordering app costs 18 $ per user per month." Write a problem statement, one sub-problem and one research question, and justify that the question passes the four checks.

0 words

Model answer

Problem statement: "Boulangerie Saint-Laurent, a three-person bakery, spends part of every afternoon on recurring routines, phone orders in particular. The owners must decide which routine to automate first and whether an ordering app at 18 $ per user per month is justified. This project will log how long each routine takes over 14 working days, price that time at the bakery's hourly value, and compare the time an assistant or the app could save with its cost, in order to recommend what to automate first." Sub-problem (Microeconomics): what does each routine cost per month, and what does each option cost? Research question: "How many minutes per month does phone-order taking cost the bakery, and how many saved hours per user per month would make the 18 $ app worth paying?" It is open (not yes/no), names measurable quantities (minutes, hours, dollars), belongs to one sub-problem (economics) and can be answered with 14 days of data before the deadline.

Why this is the right answer

The statement names the situation, the decision and the evidence in fewer than 150 words, the sub-problem is tied to one course and to data, and the four checks are applied explicitly.

Essay 5
Chapter 2 · 2.1 From a business problem to a research problem

Explain the four checks of a research question and apply them to "Is automation good for the studio?".

0 words

Model answer

A research question must be (1) an open question that cannot be answered by yes or no; (2) measurable, naming something in the data or the given numbers such as minutes, interruptions, runs or dollars; (3) tied to one sub-problem; and (4) answerable with the project's data by January 22. "Is automation good for the studio?" fails check 1, because it is answered by yes or no, and check 2, because "good" has no unit in the data. It does not belong clearly to one sub-problem either. An acceptable rewrite is: "How many minutes per run does assistant-triaged e-mail save compared with manual triage, and what is that saving worth per month at 28 $ per hour?", which is open, measurable and answerable with the log.

Why this is the right answer

The four checks are stated precisely, each one is applied to the question with a reason, and the answer ends with a rewrite that passes, which shows understanding beyond the definition.

Essay 6
Chapter 2 · 2.2 Requirements analysis

Distinguish functional from non-functional requirements with two examples each from JARVIS, and explain why a non-functional requirement needs a threshold.

0 words

Model answer

A functional requirement describes a behaviour: given an input or an event, the system produces an output or changes its data. Examples: "JARVIS shall record a routine run from one command" and "JARVIS shall compute the monthly cost of each routine at 28 $/h". A non-functional requirement describes a quality or a constraint on how the system performs its functions. Examples: "JARVIS shall work with no API (Application Programming Interface) key and no network" and "the database file shall stay under 1 MB (megabyte)". A requirement must be verifiable by a test, an inspection or a measurement. "JARVIS shall be fast" cannot be checked, because nobody can say when it is met; "JARVIS shall answer a log command in under one second on the lab computer" can be checked with a stopwatch. Without a threshold, a non-functional requirement can never be tested or declared met.

Why this is the right answer

The definitions use the "what does it do / how well, under which limits" distinction, the examples are the course's own, and the threshold argument is linked to verifiability.

Essay 7
Chapter 2 · 2.2 Requirements analysis

Write two user stories for JARVIS, one for the owner and one for a staff member, each with one acceptance criterion in Given / When / Then form, and say what makes them testable.

0 words

Model answer

Story 1: "As the owner, I want to see the monthly cost of each routine, so that I can decide what to automate first." Criterion: Given the 14-day data, when I run python -m jarvis report, then each routine shows its monthly cost in dollars. Story 2: "As a staff member, I want to log a routine with one command, so that recording my time takes seconds." Criterion: Given an empty log, when I type log 25 min email_triage, then one entry is stored with routine email_triage and minutes 25. They are testable because each criterion fixes a starting state, one action and an observable result that a program can compare with an expected value; in Class 10 each criterion becomes one pytest (https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/VirusTotal) test.

Why this is the right answer

Both stories follow the role–goal–benefit template, the criteria follow Given / When / Then with concrete values, and the explanation links testability to an observable, checkable result, which is the T of INVEST (Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable).

Essay 8
Chapter 2 · 2.3 Scope, SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) objectives and project selection

Explain the difference between an assumption and a constraint, give two examples of each for JARVIS, and say how each is treated later in the project.

0 words

Model answer

An assumption is a statement the team treats as true for planning, without proof; it must be written down because the results change if it is false. Examples: 28 $ per hour is a fair loaded cost for the studio; the fourteen logged days are typical working days (others: staff logged honestly; the pilot saving continues). A constraint is a limit the project cannot change. Examples: the Product Defense takes place on January 22, 2027, after fifteen Fridays; the project is written in Python only (others: teams of two or three, free API (Application Programming Interface) tiers with changing quotas, a database under 1 MB (megabyte), no personal data in public repositories). Assumptions are tested and discussed, for instance in the risk part of the Sprint 2 recommendation; constraints are respected, and every objective must fit inside them.

Why this is the right answer

The definitions are precise, the examples come from the course lists, and the answer states the different treatment (discussed versus respected) that makes the distinction useful.

Essay 9
Chapter 2 · 2.4 References and experts

Explain the two purposes of citation, describe the CRAAP (Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose) test, and explain how AI (Artificial Intelligence) assistance is cited in CS (Computer Science) 251.

0 words

Model answer

A citation lets the reader verify a claim and gives credit to the work you build on; the reference at the end describes the source precisely enough to find it. In CS (Computer Science) 251 four kinds of material are cited: books and articles, documentation pages, reused code and AI (Artificial Intelligence) assistance. The CRAAP (Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose) test judges a source with five questions: Currency (when was it published or updated?), Relevance (does it answer my question?), Authority (who wrote it and what qualifies them?), Accuracy (is there evidence that can be checked?) and Purpose (does it inform, sell or persuade?). AI (Artificial Intelligence) assistance is cited in APA (American Psychological Association) 7 (https://apastyle.apa.org/VirusTotal) style; since September 2025 the APA (American Psychological Association) Style team (https://apastyle.apa.org/blog/cite-generative-ai-referencesVirusTotal) recommends referencing the specific chat as Company. (Year, Month Day). Title of the chat [Generative AI (Artificial Intelligence) chat]. Tool or model. URL (Uniform Resource Locator) of the chat, and the report's Method section describes how and where AI (Artificial Intelligence) was used. When AI (Artificial Intelligence) only helped find sources, the sources it found are cited instead.

Why this is the right answer

The answer covers verification and credit, names the five CRAAP (Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose) questions correctly and gives the course rule for AI (Artificial Intelligence), including the description in the Method section.

Essay 10
Chapter 3 · 3.1 Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost

Explain opportunity cost and use it to show why "free" software still costs something.

0 words

Model answer

The opportunity cost of using a resource in one way is the value of its next-best use, the best alternative given up. For Boréal Studio the scarce resource is staff time. An hour of manual e-mail triage costs 28 $ in loaded salary and overhead, but if that hour could have been billed to a client at 65 $, the triage gives up 65 $ of revenue. A free assistant has no price, yet installing it, learning it, setting it up and checking its output take hours, and those hours have a next-best use. That is why Brick 3 values the team's set-up hours at the hourly value: they are costly not because someone paid for them, but because they could have been used otherwise. Opportunity cost is always relative to a named alternative, so the analysis must state which alternative it uses.

Why this is the right answer

The definition is exact, the studio numbers illustrate the difference between explicit cost and opportunity cost, and the free-software argument follows directly from the definition.

Essay 11
Chapter 3 · 3.2 Marginal analysis

Explain the MB (marginal benefit) ≥ MC (marginal cost) rule and diminishing returns, using the levels of e-mail triage automation.

0 words

Model answer

Marginal analysis compares the extra benefit and the extra cost of one more unit. The MB (marginal benefit) of automating a routine is the value of the net minutes saved per month; the MC (marginal cost) is the cost of paid requests beyond the quota plus the monthly share of the set-up. The rule is: undertake the unit while MB (marginal benefit) ≥ MC (marginal cost), and stop at the first unit that fails. Diminishing returns mean that each additional unit brings less than the previous one. E-mail triage can be automated in levels, each judged on its own increment: sorting and labelling the mailbox brings 700 $ against 46.67 $, so it is added; drafting replies brings 233.33 $ against 58.33 $, so it is added; sending replies without review brings only 93.33 $ against 105 $, so the team stops there. The last level also carries a risk the numbers do not show, an e-mail sent by mistake.

Why this is the right answer

The answer defines both quantities, states the rule with its stopping condition, and applies it level by level with the course numbers, which demonstrates diminishing returns rather than just naming them.

Essay 12
Chapter 3 · 3.3 Fixed, variable, total, average and marginal cost; the sunk cost

Explain the sunk-cost error using the e-mail pilot example, and say where the set-up cost does belong.

0 words

Model answer

A sunk cost is a cost already incurred that no present or future decision can recover, so it must not influence a decision. The team spent 40 hours (1 120 $) building the e-mail tool. In the first month the benefit is 938 $ and the running cost 28 $. Subtracting the set-up gives −210 $ and the conclusion "the pilot loses money, stop it". The arithmetic is right but the logic is wrong: stopping does not return the 1 120 $, it only forfeits the net saving. Looking forward, the choice is +910 $ per month if the pilot continues against 0 $ if it stops, and the set-up appears in neither column. The set-up belongs in two places only: before the decision to build, as a monthly share in the marginal cost; after it, in the payback period, which says how long recovery takes, not whether to continue.

Why this is the right answer

The answer defines the sunk cost, reproduces the wrong computation, explains why it is wrong and gives the correct forward-looking comparison and the two legitimate places of the set-up.

Essay 13
Chapter 3 · 3.4 Break-even, payback and make-or-buy

Explain the difference between break-even hours and the payback period: what each measures, its formula, a course example, and where the set-up cost appears.

0 words

Model answer

Break-even hours measure how many hours a paid option must save each month to pay for itself: break-even hours = monthly price ÷ hourly value. For a 20 $ seat at 28 $ per hour, 20 ÷ 28 = 0.714 h, about 43 minutes per user per month; the pilot saves about 6.7 hours per user, so a seat that performs like the pilot pays for itself many times. The set-up cost does not appear in this formula. The payback period measures how many months the net savings take to recover a one-time set-up: payback months = set-up cost ÷ monthly net saving. With 1 120 $ of set-up and 910.86 $ of monthly net saving, payback is 1.23 months. When the saving is zero or negative, the set-up is never recovered and the engine returns math.inf. Payback ignores what happens after recovery, so it is reported next to the monthly saving.

Why this is the right answer

Both formulas, units and course numbers are correct, and the answer states explicitly that the set-up enters payback and not break-even, which is the distinction the question tests.

Essay 14
Chapter 3 · 3.4 Break-even, payback and make-or-buy

Explain why the make-or-buy decision depends on the horizon, with the course numbers for 12 and 24 months, and name two factors the numbers do not show.

0 words

Model answer

Building JARVIS costs a one-time set-up plus maintenance every month; buying a paid assistant costs a subscription every month and no set-up. Because the set-up is paid once and the subscription is paid repeatedly, the cheaper option changes with the length of the period. Over 12 months: build = 1 120 + 28 × 12 = 1 456 $, buy = 100 × 12 = 1 200 $, so buying costs less. Over 24 months: build = 1 120 + 28 × 24 = 1 792 $, buy = 100 × 24 = 2 400 $, so building costs less. Two factors the numbers do not show also decide: whether the paid assistant performs the task as well as the pilot did, and whether the free quota on which the built tool relies survives. A decision candidate must state both, with the horizon used.

Why this is the right answer

The answer explains the mechanism (one-time against recurring cost), computes both horizons correctly and names the two qualitative factors given in the course.

Essay 15
Chapter 4 · 4.1 Central tendency

Using S2's week (105, 36, 33, 38, 34 minutes), explain when the median should be reported instead of the mean, and when the mean must be used.

0 words

Model answer

The mean of the week is 246 ÷ 5 = 49.2 minutes; the sorted values are 33, 34, 36, 38, 105, so the median is 36 minutes. Four runs took between 33 and 38 minutes, yet the mean is longer than every run except Monday's, because the weekend backlog makes Monday very long. Without Monday the mean drops to 35.25 while the median moves only to 35: the median is resistant to one extreme value because it depends on order, not distance. The median is therefore the honest typical day when there are a few extreme values or a long tail. The mean must be used whenever the number will be multiplied, for example in a monthly cost, because the total of the runs equals n × x̄ exactly. When the two differ by more than a few percent, both are reported with the reason.

Why this is the right answer

The computations are correct, the effect of the extreme value is shown numerically, and the answer gives the course's decision rule, including the multiplication argument for the mean.

Essay 16
Chapter 4 · 4.2 Dispersion

Explain why the sample variance divides by n − 1, and how this appears in Python and in JARVIS.

0 words

Model answer

The studio's 14 days are a sample of all its working days, not the whole population. Deviations are measured from the sample mean, and the sample mean is, by construction, the point that makes the sum of squared deviations as small as possible. Measured from the true population mean, the same values would give a larger sum, so dividing the sample sum by n underestimates the population variance on average. Dividing by n − 1 corrects this bias. n − 1 is the number of degrees of freedom: once the mean is fixed, only n − 1 deviations can vary freely, because all n of them must add up to zero. In Python, statistics.variance and statistics.stdev divide by n − 1, while statistics.pvariance and statistics.pstdev divide by n; for set A (8, 10, 9, 12, 11), stdev gives 1.581 and pstdev 1.414. JARVIS's StatsEngine uses n − 1, refuses fewer than two values, and is validated against statistics.stdev.

Why this is the right answer

The answer gives the sample/population argument, the bias explanation and the degrees-of-freedom interpretation, and connects the theory to the exact Python functions and engine behaviour.

Essay 17
Chapter 4 · 4.2 Dispersion

Explain why the standard deviation and the coefficient of variation can rank the studio's routines differently, using e-mail triage and stand-up notes.

0 words

Model answer

The standard deviation measures spread in the unit of the data, minutes, so it tends to grow with the size of the values. The coefficient of variation divides the SD (Standard Deviation) by the mean, so it has no unit and compares routines of different length. E-mail triage has the largest SD (Standard Deviation), 6.35 minutes on a mean of 35.15 (a CV (Coefficient of Variation) of 18.1 %), while stand-up notes have the smallest SD (Standard Deviation), 2.62 minutes, but the largest CV (Coefficient of Variation), 26.4 % on a mean of 9.91. Both facts are correct because they answer different questions. To plan a buffer in the calendar, the SD (Standard Deviation) in minutes matters, and e-mail triage needs the largest buffer. To compare how predictable two processes are, the CV (Coefficient of Variation) matters, and stand-up notes are the least predictable relative to their length; each interruption adds about 2 minutes to a routine that normally takes under 10.

Why this is the right answer

The answer defines both measures, uses the correct course values and explains which management question each measure answers.

Essay 18
Chapter 4 · 4.3 Distributions and outliers

Explain the two outlier rules of the course, why they can disagree on the same data, and what must be done with a flagged run.

0 words

Model answer

The 1.5 × IQR (Interquartile Range) rule flags values below Q1 (first quartile) − 1.5 × IQR (Interquartile Range) or above Q3 (third quartile) + 1.5 × IQR (Interquartile Range). For the 55 manual e-mail runs, Q1 (first quartile) = 30.5 and Q3 (third quartile) = 39.5, so the fences are 17 and 53 and no run is flagged. The mean ± 2 SD (Standard Deviation) rule flags values more than two standard deviations from the mean: 35.15 ± 2 × 6.35 gives [22.44, 47.85], and two runs (48 and 51 minutes) are flagged. The rules disagree because quartiles are barely affected by the extreme values being judged, while the mean and the SD (Standard Deviation) are pulled by them; the second rule also flags about 5 % of perfectly regular bell-shaped data. The rule must be chosen and written before looking at the results. A flagged run is a question, not a mistake: check it against the log, keep it by default, correct it only if it is a proven typing error recorded in the bug log, and report results with and without it if it changes a conclusion. It is never deleted silently.

Why this is the right answer

Both rules are applied with the course numbers, the reason for the disagreement is explained statistically, and the treatment of flagged runs follows the course's three options.

Essay 19
Chapter 4 · 4.4 Relationships, groups and the limits of 14 days

Explain why correlation is not causation and how a comparison group strengthens the e-mail pilot result; then write the two-sentence interpretation of the pilot.

0 words

Model answer

Pearson's r measures how closely two variables follow a straight line, not whether one causes the other. A confounding variable can influence both: on Mondays there is more mail and more interruptions, so part of the association between interruptions and minutes may come from the day of the week. For the pilot, comparing the participants before and after day 10 could also reflect a quieter last week for everybody. The comparison group S4–S5, who stayed manual, changed by only −0.57 minutes, while the pilot group changed by −22.12 minutes, so the difference of the changes, −21.55 minutes per run, estimates the effect of the assistant more credibly. Interpretation: "From day 10, assistant-triaged e-mail took 21.55 minutes less per run than the change seen in the comparison group (35.85 → 13.73 minutes, n = 27 → 15; comparison 34.67 → 34.10, n = 18 → 10). The result rests on 15 assisted runs by three people over five days, so it may include a novelty effect and should be confirmed with a longer log."

Why this is the right answer

The answer explains confounding with a course example, shows how the comparison group removes the period effect, computes the difference of the changes and writes the interpretation in the required "number, then limit" form.

Essay 20
Chapter 5 · 5.1 Classes, objects and the dataclass

Explain encapsulation in Python using the TimeEntry class.

0 words

Model answer

Encapsulation keeps data and the code that uses it in one class and controls how that data can be read or changed from outside. TimeEntry holds the nine fields of one run together with the operations on them, such as cost(hourly_value) and the property hours. It controls access in several ways. __post_init__ checks the values at creation (minutes ≥ 0, start hour 0–23, tool in the allowed set), so no invalid object can exist. frozen=True refuses any change after creation, which keeps that invariant true for the whole life of the object. The property hours is computed from minutes when it is read, so it cannot disagree with the data, and without a setter it cannot be assigned. Python has no private keyword: a single leading underscore marks a member as internal by convention, and two underscores trigger name mangling to avoid clashes in subclasses. In UML (Unified Modeling Language), internal members are marked − and public ones +.

Why this is the right answer

The definition is correct and each mechanism of TimeEntry is explained as a way of controlling access, including the Python conventions and their limits.

Essay 21
Chapter 5 · 5.2 Collections and CSV (Comma-Separated Values) parsing

Explain how DataLoader reads boreal_routines_2026.csv into a list of TimeEntry objects without crashing on a bad row.

0 words

Model answer

The path is built with pathlib from the location of the program, so it works on every computer. The file is opened with with path.open(newline="", encoding="utf-8"), which closes it automatically, lets the csv module handle line endings and reads accented characters correctly. csv.DictReader returns each data line as a dict of strings keyed by the header names, and the loader first checks that the nine required columns are present. For each record, numbered from 2 because line 1 is the header, the loader converts the text with int(), date.fromisoformat() and == "1", and builds a TimeEntry, whose __post_init__ checks the values. The loop wraps this in try/except (ValueError, TypeError): a bad row is not fatal; its line number and reason are stored as a tuple in skipped, and the next row is read. Other errors, such as a missing file, still stop the program because they signal a setup problem. On the damaged sample the loader returns 8 objects and 4 skipped lines; on the full file 420 and 0.

Why this is the right answer

The answer follows the actual pipeline step by step and explains why each choice (pathlib, open arguments, DictReader, conversions, narrow except, tuples) prevents a crash or a wrong result.

Essay 22
Chapter 5 · 5.3 Responsibilities, classes and UML (Unified Modeling Language)

Explain the Single Responsibility Principle, cohesion and coupling, and apply them to the requirement "publish a dashboard with aggregated numbers only".

0 words

Model answer

The Single Responsibility Principle says that a class should have one responsibility, or in Robert C. Martin's words, one reason to change. Cohesion measures how closely the members of a class belong together; it is high when every attribute and method serves the same responsibility. Coupling measures how much a class depends on others; it is low when a change in one class rarely forces a change in another. A first JARVIS draft gave the dashboard requirement to the Agent, because the agent sees every request. The Agent would then have two reasons to change, the loop and the dashboard, which lowers its cohesion and couples the loop to presentation details. The requirement belongs to the Reporter, whose single responsibility is to write the console report, the charts and the dashboard. The Agent keeps only the loop request → intent → tool → result → log.

Why this is the right answer

The three concepts are defined correctly and applied to the course's own design correction, showing how the principle decides where a requirement lives.

Essay 23
Chapter 5 · 5.4 Abstract base classes, polymorphism and clean code

Explain why Tool and Provider are abstract base classes and where polymorphism appears in the agent loop.

0 words

Model answer

Tool and Provider describe what every tool and every provider must be able to do, but neither should ever be used directly. They inherit from abc.ABC and mark their method, run() and parse(), with @abstractmethod. Python then refuses to create an object of a class that still has an unimplemented abstract method: Tool() raises TypeError, and so does a subclass that forgets run(), such as a planned SummarizeTool. The error appears at creation time, on the developer's computer, instead of during a demo. Concrete subclasses such as LogTimeTool and OfflineProvider implement the method. Polymorphism appears in Agent.handle: self._provider.parse(text) works with any Provider subclass, and tool.run(intent.args, self._store) runs LogTimeTool.run, AddTaskTool.run or DailyReportTool.run depending on the object, with no if/elif chain on the intent name. Adding a tool or replacing the offline provider by the ApiProvider does not change the Agent class.

Why this is the right answer

The answer explains the purpose and mechanism of the ABCs (Abstract Base Classes), the moment at which the error appears, and points to the exact polymorphic calls and their benefit.

Essay 24
Chapter 5 · 5.4 Abstract base classes, polymorphism and clean code

Explain dependency injection and why the Agent receives its provider, tools and store as constructor parameters.

0 words

Model answer

Dependency injection means passing the objects a class needs as parameters of its constructor instead of creating them inside the class. The Agent's __init__ receives a provider, a list of tools and a store and keeps them in _provider, _tools and _store. If the Agent created self._provider = OfflineProvider() itself, the provider would be a part it owns (a composition), and replacing it would require editing the Agent. With injection, main() decides which objects to pass: the OfflineProvider today, the ApiProvider in Class 10, by changing one argument. A test can pass a fake provider that always returns the same Intent, or a store that lives in memory, and test the Agent alone, without a network or a database file. This also supports the rubric: abstract base classes used through polymorphic calls, and a design that pytest (https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/VirusTotal) can test.

Why this is the right answer

The definition is exact and the answer shows the two practical benefits in the course (swapping providers and testing in isolation) and the contrast with composition.

Essay 25
Chapter 6 · 6.1 Mean and median in codeChapter 6 · 6.4 Grouping, validation and the tiny-database rule

Explain the rule "the engine is yours, the library is the oracle" and how the validation table applies it.

0 words

Model answer

An engine performs calculations only: StatsEngine and EconEngine receive numbers and return numbers. A test oracle is an independent, trusted source of the correct answer; for the statistics it is Python's statistics module, and for the economics it is the numbers printed by the Phase 1 scripts of Bricks 3 and 4. The engine must never call the oracle inside its methods, because the Mid-Term asks students to write and explain the methods, because a hand-written method can be read line by line when a number looks wrong, and because a check is only meaningful when both sides are independent. The validation table of Brick 6 has one row per method: method, engine value, script value and match. Values are compared with math.isclose and an absolute tolerance of half a unit of the last printed digit. A red row is chased in order: rounding, formula, rows counted. In the class example, 214 $ came from the pilot rows that Brick 3 had excluded. The table is the first unit test; its rows become the asserts of Brick 9.

Why this is the right answer

The answer defines engine and oracle, gives the three reasons for keeping them separate, and describes the validation table, its tolerance and the chase order with the course case.

Essay 26
Chapter 6 · 6.3 EconEngine and the Store

Explain the two strategies an engine method can use for an input that breaks its formula, using break_even_hours and payback_months.

0 words

Model answer

A guard is a condition at the start of a method that handles an input the formula cannot use. The first strategy is to refuse an impossible input with an exception. break_even_hours(monthly_price, hourly_value) divides by the hourly value; a value of zero or less makes no economic sense, so the method raises ValueError with a message that includes the bad value ("hourly value must be > 0, got 0"). The second strategy is to return a documented value for a legitimate extreme result. payback_months(fixed_cost, monthly_saving) divides by the monthly saving; a tool that saves nothing is a real possibility, and the honest answer is "never recovered", so the method returns math.inf, which prints as inf and is larger than any number of months. The rule is: impossible input → exception; legitimate extreme → documented value. Both behaviours are written in the docstrings and later protected by tests (pytest.raises for the first, == math.inf for the second).

Why this is the right answer

The answer names both strategies, ties each to its method with the economic reason, and states the general rule and how it is tested.

Essay 27
Chapter 6 · 6.3 EconEngine and the StoreChapter 6 · 6.4 Grouping, validation and the tiny-database rule

Explain the tiny-database rule and why the import into data/jarvis.db must be idempotent.

0 words

Model answer

data/jarvis.db is a small SQLite (https://www.sqlite.org/VirusTotal) file committed to GitHub and written by every teammate and later by the scheduled job. The tiny-database rule keeps that workable with five habits: stay under 1 MB (megabyte); run VACUUM before every commit so empty pages are reclaimed; keep one writer at a time, pulling before running the assistant and committing right after (a conflict is solved by taking GitHub's version and running the command again, never by merging two .db files by hand); export the table to CSV (Comma-Separated Values) so a reviewer sees a readable diff; and never commit secrets, raw personal logs or message contents. The import must be idempotent, which means that running it twice gives the same result as running it once. The UNIQUE (date, staff_id, routine, start_hour) constraint with INSERT OR IGNORE achieves this: duplicates are skipped. Without it, every start of the assistant would add another 420 rows, about 30 KB (kilobyte) each time, and the file would pass the 1 MB (megabyte) limit within weeks.

Why this is the right answer

The five habits are listed with their purpose, idempotence is defined correctly and the answer explains both how it is obtained and what happens without it.

Essay 28
Chapter 10 · 10.1 Tests with pytest, edge cases and the oracle

Explain what a unit test and a regression are, and describe the three steps of a test and the oracle test for StatsEngine.

0 words

Model answer

A unit test is a short function that calls one unit of the program, such as StatsEngine.median, with a known input and compares the result with the expected value; an automated suite runs all of them with one command (python -m pytest -q). In software testing, a regression is a defect in behaviour that used to work and stopped working after a change, which is different from the statistical regression that fits a line. A good test has three steps: prepare the input (xs = [4, 9, 1, 7]), call the method once (result = StatsEngine.median(xs)), and check the result (assert result == pytest.approx(5.5)). The expected value must come from outside the code under test. The oracle test compares the engine with an independent source: assert StatsEngine.std_dev(xs) == pytest.approx(statistics.stdev(xs)). The engine itself never calls statistics, otherwise the test would compare the code with itself.

Why this is the right answer

The answer gives correct definitions, distinguishes the two meanings of regression, shows the three steps on a concrete example and explains the purpose and the condition of an oracle test.

Essay 29
Chapter 10 · 10.2 Tracebacks, the debugger, validation and the bug log

Explain the four-step procedure for reading a traceback and the difference between a symptom and a root cause.

0 words

Model answer

A traceback lists the frames of the call stack from the oldest call at the top to the most recent at the bottom. Step 1: read the last line, which gives the exception type and message, for example ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: ''. Step 2: read the frame just above it, which shows the statement that raised the exception. Step 3: move up to the first frame in your own files; frames inside Python or installed packages almost never contain the defect. Step 4: ask where the wrong value came from, following it back from the data file through the loader and the parser to the first place that should have rejected it. The symptom is what the user saw ("the morning brief stopped at 06:30"); the root cause is the defect that produced it ("the loader converted minutes with int() without checking for an empty cell"). Restarting the workflow fixes the symptom only. The cause is fixed at the boundary, and the bug-log entry is closed only when a test fails before the fix and passes after it.

Why this is the right answer

The four steps are given in the right order with a concrete example, and the symptom/cause distinction is explained with its practical consequence for fixing and closing a bug.

Essay 30
Chapter 10 · 10.4 From results to a decision, the report and the sprints

Explain the difference-in-differences estimate of the e-mail pilot and compute the expected impact in hours and dollars per month.

0 words

Model answer

Comparing the pilot group before and after day 10 mixes the effect of the assistant with anything else that changed in the same period. The comparison group S4–S5 did not use the assistant, so its change estimates what would have happened anyway. The pilot group went from 35.85 to 13.73 minutes per run (−22.12); the comparison group went from 34.67 to 34.10 minutes (−0.57). The difference of the changes, (−22.12) − (−0.57) = −21.55 minutes per run, is the estimated effect of the assistant; economists call this design difference-in-differences (https://learn.mru.org/lessons/introduction-differences-differencesVirusTotal). Subtracting 2 minutes of human review leaves 19.55 minutes saved per run. With 100 runs per month: 19.55 × 100 = 1 955 minutes = 32.6 hours per month, and at 28 $ per hour about 912 $ per month. The recommendation reports this impact with its risks: 14 days, five people, a possible novelty effect and the quota of the free tier.

Why this is the right answer

The answer explains why the comparison group is needed, performs each step of the computation correctly and places the result in the recommendation with its limits.
